Chile developed an NDC in 2015 and another one five years later (2020), in advance of its long-term strategy (2021) and framework law on climate change (2022). A complementary NDC has been prepared for 2022 to strengthen it and to refer to the new regulations that have been generated and, therefore, to the new commitments made in the Strategy and the Law. It should be added that the 2020 NDC is still in force and the process of updating it has already started.

The commitments in the 2020 NDC are more ambitious than those in the 2015 NDC in terms of mitigation (reduction of the greenhouse gas emissions budget, carbon neutrality and black carbon by 2030 and 2050), adaptation (new adaptation sectors are added), finance (targets linked to economic growth and international monetary contributions are removed) and additional information (a chapter on clarity, transparency and understanding was added).

The Long-Term Strategy outlines mitigation efforts for each sector and includes a sectoral allocation of emissions and a black carbon budget for 2020-2030, including the energy sector (51% of the country's GHG). For adaptation, the Long-Term Strategy indicates that there will be 11 Sectoral Adaptation Plans with long-term goals and targets by sector. This is in line with the NDC and its proposed targets. In addition, other government instruments add targets and goals.

Chile has identified and developed a series of general public policies (National Climate Change Action Plan 2017 - 2022 and Framework Law on Climate Change) and sectoral policies (mitigation actions in the energy sector, waste, transport, AFOLU, construction, urbanisation and public infrastructure, and the financial sector) that affect Chile's climate change emissions.

A specific national strategy has been formalised through the Long-Term Strategy, which sets broad mitigation targets and identifies the Plan de Acción Nacional and the Ley Marco de Cambio Climático as key policies to address the impacts of climate change. It also sets a sectoral emissions budget consistent with the mitigation targets and contributions of the NDC 2020.

The energy sector's 2017 mitigation plan, developed before the NDC (2020), is being updated, along with the infrastructure sector's plan. Sectors like transport, health, cities, agriculture, and mining are preparing their first mitigation plans, as required by the Framework Law on Climate Change. These drafts include emission reductions and outline the measures needed to achieve sectoral targets, aligned with national strategies such as the NDC and the long-term strategy.
Chile has had a National Climate Change Adaptation Plan (PNACC) since 2014, which was submitted to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) on 7 September 2017.

Chile has developed eight sectoral climate change adaptation plans (Forestry, Biodiversity, Fisheries and Aquaculture, Health, Infrastructure, Cities, Energy, and Tourism) prior to the NDC, Long-Term Strategy, and the Law. Four more plans are in preparation (Water Resources, Mining, Coastal Areas, Transport). These plans follow the sectors identified for adaptation in the National Climate Change Plan 2008-2012, the National Adaptation Plan (2014), the National Action Plan 2017-2022 and the Law.

Both the 2014 National Climate Change Adaptation Plan and the 8 sectoral plans developed before the NDC and the Framework Law are being updated, but plans for fisheries, aquaculture, biodiversity, health, infrastructure, and cities have not been updated in 5 years. Of the 4 newer sectoral plans, 3 are in public consultation, while the transport plan has completed this phase but is not considered 'completed'.

In 2020, Chile's GHG emissions (excluding LULUCF) were 105,552 kt CO2 eq, a 116% rise since 1990 but 4% lower than in 2018. The energy sector, driven by fossil fuel use and fugitive emissions, is the largest contributor, accounting for 51% of the GHG balance and 75% of total emissions. Chile has implemented public policy tools to reduce emissions in this sector, with targets aligned to reduction measures, responsible parties, deadlines, and expected outcomes.

The country has various institutional mechanisms for horizontal coordination, such as the National Climate Change System (SISCLIMA) and the Intersectoral Commission of the Presidential Cabinet for Climate Action. The country's horizontal interaction has mainly taken place through the Intersectoral Commission on Climate Change (CICC) of the National Climate Change System (SISCLIMA), where key issues of the National Climate Change Policy are addressed. Since its establishment in 2016, the Commission has held regular meetings, averaging two per year.

The National Climate Change System (SISCLIMA) has regional and local coordination bodies through nine Regional Climate Change Nodes, which enable the participation of governorates, municipalities, and environmental authorities in promoting, supporting, and assisting the implementation of climate actions. The legal and regulatory framework of Costa Rica is aligned with the requirements of the Paris Agreement, specifically Articles 2 and 4. Additionally, when ratifying the Agreement, the country committed to meeting all its obligations concerning reporting and transparency. The topic of Climate Change is present in various planning instruments of the country such as the Plan Nacional de Desarrollo e Inversión Pública, the Plan Estratégico Nacional, among others. Conducting the analysis considering only the main actors (MINAE, Directorate of Climate Change, MIDEPLAN, National Meteorological Institute) and from the literal interpretation of the laws or regulations, no gaps or overlaps in their competencies were identified. However, it is important to clarify that these bodies are not responsible for executing climate actions; the implementation work is associated with other public institutions and is assigned through policies and plans.

Within Ministerio de Ambiente y Energía (MINAE), there are several vice ministries, including the Vice Ministry of Gestión Estratégica, which oversees the Dirección de Cambio Climático. However, it has limited operational staff and lacks a dedicated budget.

Costa Rica's long-term strategy is outlined in the Plan Nacional de Descarbonización 2018-2050. Ethiopia has responded by establishing a national fund, the Climate Resilient Green Economy Facility (CRGE Facility), as a mechanism to mobilize finance from various sources, including domestic and international, and drive investments to build resilience and support green growth. We have given this item  a rating "Early implementation" because Ethiopia still needs to attract and mobilize finance to support its climate compatible development agenda.

Ethiopia has mechanisms to track private climate finance domestically that established the Public-Private Partnership Directorate General (PPP DG) in the Finance Ministry and the Ethiopian P4G National Platform Framework for seeking available resources from the P4G Global Hub. However, we have given this item a rating of "Early Implementation" because of the non-issuance of these reports on a regular and public basis.

Ethiopia has a Constitution, Proclamations and regulations to address climate change. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "advanced implementation". 
Ethiopia has several primary legislation or Proclamations and Secondary legislations.

Ethiopia's legislative framework is consistent with the Paris Agreement because the Paris Agreement was ratified as the primary law by the House of People's Representatives, and the definition of powers and duties of the executive organs of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia Proclamation No. 1263-2021 article 28 and 72 was updated based on the Paris Agreement. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation.".

Ethiopia prepared a Climate-Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) Strategy at the national level and a guideline to help sectors, regional and woreda integrate the Climate-Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) into their development plans. The guideline is communicated to key economic sectors to ensure they follow it when preparing strategic plans. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "advanced implementation.".

The Ethiopian Parliament has a Standing Committee for Natural Resources and Environmental Protection that looks to provide high-level direction, guidelines, and support to the implementation of NAP-ETH and perform a biannual performance evaluation of NAP-ETH. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation".

Based on Proclamation No.982/2016, Article 4, Sub-Article 3, SAI of Ethiopia has the power to undertake financial, performance, environmental, information technology, control, special, and other audits of the offices and organizations of the Federal Government. SAI of Ethiopia has established the Environmental Audit Directorate and has conducted audits since 2022 that have climate change issues as their main focus. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "advanced implementation.".

The Ethiopian Constitution guarantees the right to a clean and healthy environment & recognize the right to sustainable development to handle claims related to climate change. The EPC Proclamation No. 300/2002 and the updated ESIA proclamation in 2024 provide mechanisms for environmental protection & enforcement. The EPA is a governmental regulatory body that plays a key role in developing & enforcing environmental laws. However, still it needs improvements & rated Early implementation.

Entities have responsibilities assigned to them for climate change activities, including leading, coordinating, and monitoring these activities and providing transparency. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation.". The main entities responsible for climate change activities are: Ministry of Planning and Development, Ministry of Finance, Environmental Protection Authority, and Ethiopian Meteorological Institute. A CRGE Forum is also established at national level.

The main entities responsible for climate change activities have clear roles and responsibilities that are set out in legislation, regulation and CRGE sectors strategies, and through the Budget process. These are the Ministry of Planning and Development, Ministry of Finance, Ethiopia Meteorology Institute, Ministry of Agriculture, Health Ministry, Ministry of Urban and Infrastructure, and Ministry of Water and Energy. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation"

Ministry of Planning and Development is a key government institution that works on climate change issues. The Ministry of Finance mobilizes domestic & international, public & private finance to support Ethiopia's CRGE. The National Meteorology Agency is responsible for collecting climate data & providing weather and climate information. The Ethiopian Environmental Protection Authority is the federal institution for managing the environment.

The CRGE governance structure is based on the new definition of powers and duties of government bodies in proclamation 1263/2021. The Ministry of Planning and Development is mandated to coordinate the sectoral government bodies to effectively implement and manage the low emission and climate resilient green development strategy within the national development planning framework. Therefore, we have given this item score  of "Advanced Implementation"

Ethiopia submitted its Long-term low greenhouse gas emission development strategies (LT-LEDS) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change in June 2023. It also aligned with the Paris Agreement on Climate Change. Therefore, we have given this item score rate "Advanced implementation." There is also an official government documents of Ten Year Development Plan a Pathway to Prosperity.2021-2030 that establishes a national long-term strategy to address climate change.

Ethiopia's Long-Term Low Emission and Climate Resilient Development Strategy (2020-2050) LT-LEDS and Ten Year Development Plan: a Pathway to Prosperity, 2021-2030 are aligned with Ethiopia's Nationally Determined Contribution Updated 2021. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation."

Ethiopia's long-term strategy, the Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy, demonstrates a strong commitment to integrating climate change actions with the achievement of various SDGs beyond just SDG 13 (Climate Action), by prioritizing a green growth pathway that aims to reach net-zero emissions by 2050, thereby positively impacting goals related to poverty reduction, food security, health, and sustainable development across sectors. It meets the criteria "Advanced implementation."

Ethiopia's first Nationally Determined Contribution Technical Report was published in July 2021, which is less than five years ago, and among the aims was to establish linkages to other development frameworks and protocols such as the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, etc. The report specifically identified synergies between international and national development goals, related indicators, and climate change adaptation. Therefore, it meets the criteria "Advanced implementation".

Scientific institutions and different experts from government institutions such as Addis Ababa University, the Ministry of Agriculture, the former Environment, Forest, and Climate Change Commission (EFCCC), etc., as well as non-government institutions and international institutions like UNDAP, participated in the process of Ethiopia's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) technical report in 2021. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation".

Ethiopia's National Adaptation Plan (NAP),Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) strategies and Ethiopia Long Term Low Emission and Climate Resilient Development Strategy (LT-LEDS) consider climate risks in a number of ways, including identifying risks, prioritizing mitigation and adaptation, monitoring and evaluation, and integrating with national planning.  Therefore, this item meets the criteria for a rating of "advanced implementation.".

At the national level, the governance of the CRGE Ministerial Steering Committee is chaired and co-chaired by the Ministry of Planning and Development (MoPD) and the Ministry of Finance (MoF), respectively. The members of the CRGE governance include the public sector, which directly contributes to climate change at the federal and regional levels, and all development partners. As a result, we rated this item as having "Advanced implementation."

We have seen the CRGE Forum's Engagement Reports from 2019 to 2024 and Minutes of the CRGE Forum Technical Working Group (TWG) Meeting held in 2024 and 2025, but according to Ethiopia's First Biennial Update Report (FBUR) Under UNFCCC-2024, there is no frequent interaction among members, and instability and frequent government organizational restructuring are also factors in having smooth interaction with the members. We have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation".

According to Ethiopia's LT-LEDS, vertical coordination mechanism at the national level integrating the governance of CRGE will re-strengthen a unified CRGE Ministerial Committee, chaired and co-chaired by the Ministry of Planning and Development and the Ministry of Finance respectively. The members of the CRGE governance include the public sector, which directly contributes to climate change at the federal, regional, Zonal and Werada level and all development partners. "Advanced implementation"

Before 2024, constraints and gaps in the implementation of climate change activities reported within the Roles & Responsibilities of Stakeholders for the NDC Implementation Assessment Report of 2022 and in the BUR of Ethiopia include inadequate coordination & limited institutional setup, which are significant barriers. Recently, a dynamic platform that fosters dialogue and collaboration, the CRGE Forum TOR, was prepared & has practiced in 2024. We have given this item "Advanced implementation".

Ethiopia has institutional mechanisms to allow stakeholders to participate in climate change planning and implementation. These mechanisms include the Ministry of Planning and Development (MoPD), the Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) mechanisms, the Long-Term Low Emission and Climate Resilient Development Strategy (LT-LEDS), and the Inter-Ministerial Steering Committee. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation."

Ethiopia has proclaimed a public-private partnership (PPP) proclamation in 2018, and the preparation of general and sector-specific implementation guidelines for public-private partnerships in 2019 at the Ministry of Finance General Directorate Director has been established to lead PPP at the national level, and in the recent 2025, there is a legal platform to engage civil society and MoU academia in climate action. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "advanced implementation."

Ethiopia's First Biennial Update Report (FBUR) under the UNFCCC has clearly identified gaps and constraints, including that because of financial limitations, there is inadequate engagement of key actors and participation of local communities and civil society. However, during this assessment, we have got some meeting minutes and reports showing that there is regular interaction between government and other stakeholders. "Advanced implementation."

Ethiopia's government has identified groups and sectors that are most vulnerable to climate change. The government has also developed a National Adaptation Plan (NAP-ETH) to address these vulnerabilities. Vulnerable groups are, Women and female-led households, Smallholder farmers and pastoralists, People living in food-insecure households etc. Sectors most vulnerable to climate change agriculture, forestry, health, transport, power, industry, water, and urban. Advanced implementation

The National Adaptation Plan (NAP-ETH) of Ethiopia emphasizes the importance of vulnerable groups participating in climate strategy and policy decision-making. Article 44 of the Constitution of Ethiopia also grants all persons the right to a clean and healthy environment. The reports of meetings that are showing the participation of the national community of practice for gender equality and social inclusion in climate change and engagement of CSOs are also available. Advanced implementation

Ethiopia's Updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and National Adaptation Plan (NAP) Implementation Roadmap expressly include provisions on reducing harms and ensuring equitable benefits to vulnerable groups. Therefore, this item meets the criteria for a rating of "Advanced implementation".

Ethiopia has monitoring mechanisms in place to track progress towards its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) and national climate overarching law, primarily through its "Climate Resilient Green Economy" (CRGE) strategy, which includes a robust monitoring and evaluation (M&E) system that integrates with other national development plans and leverages data from various sectors to assess progress on climate action goal, this system also incorporates the National Adaptation Plan (NAP-ETH).

The Ministry of Planning and Development - Ethiopia is the designated institution and national focal point of UNFCCC for coordinating the country's reporting to the UNFCCC, including the National Communications, National GHG Inventory, and BUR. The National Communications Report of Ethiopia is a document that provides information on the country's efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change. It can be used to inform decision-making and identify areas for improvement. Advanced implementation.

Ethiopia has updated its National Communication (NC3) submitted in January 2023 and the Biennial Update Report (BUR) in June 2024. We have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation" since the Biennial Transparency Report (BTR) is yet under preparation.

Ethiopia's CRGE Strategy Implementation Progress Assessment Report (2011-2019) that can show the achievement of national climate objectives is published in 2020. This report is available on the Ministry of Planning and Development's website. Because of resources, the report is issued once every five years, and it is impossible to follow up on the current progress of Ethiopia's national climate objectives. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Intermediate implementation".

The 1995 Federal Constitution of Ethiopia grants citizens the right to access information and participate in environmental policy. The Environmental Impact Assessment Proclamation No.299/2002 article 15 of Ethiopia also includes provisions for public participation in the EIA process. Bu we have not found any easily accessible and easily understandable public report (official language) by the society related to climate change. Therefore,we have given this item a rating of "Early implementation."

Ethiopia submitted its first Nationally Determined Contribution to the United Nations Forum on Climate Change in 2015. Ethiopia refers to the second Nationally Determined Contribution as an update of the first Nationally Determined Contribution. This was updated and submitted its final NDC in July 2021. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "advanced implementation.".

The first Nationally Determined Contribution set a target to reduce emissions reduction target of 64% by 2030. The updated Nationally Determined Contribution target is for a 68.8% reduction of emissions by 2030, which is more ambitious compared to its first NDC. Ethiopia's updated NDC includes a detailed adaptation baseline and 2030 targets. The first NDC did not have a quantified baseline and targets. As a result, this item meets the criteria for a rating of "Advanced implementation."

Ethiopia's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) includes sectoral targets for emissions reduction and climate action in several sectors. These targets are broken down in the NDC. Sectors covered in NDS include agriculture, forestry and land use, water, energy, transport, industry, waste, and buildings. The NDC clearly defines objectives for mitigation and adaptation in key sectors. Therefore, this item meets the requirements for a rating of "Advanced implementation.".

Ethiopia has a number of policies and strategies to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, including the Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) strategy, the Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy (LT-LEDS), and the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) with the aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to 64% by 2030, net-zero by 2050, and to 69% by 2030, respectively. Accordingly, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation".

Ethiopia has a number of policies and activities to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, including the Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) strategy, the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), and the Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy (LT-LEDS). It has identified the key activities to achieve the goal, which include reforestation, renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable land management, food security, climate-resilient infrastructure, and education. Advanced implementation

Ethiopia's Climate Resilience Strategy for Agriculture and Forestry, National Green Development Program, Climate Resilience Strategy for Energy and Water, and Climate Resilience Strategy for the Transport Sector are aligned with the country's national strategies. These strategies are part of the Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) strategy, which is a key component of Ethiopia's 10-Year Development Plan. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation".

Ethiopia has submitted its National Adaptation Plan (NAP-ETH) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in 2019. Accordingly, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation".

Ethiopia's National Adaptation Plan (NAP-ETH) focuses on the sectors that are most vulnerable to climate change. The sectors that NAP-ETH focuses on are agriculture, forestry, health, transport, power, industry, water, and urban. Therefore, this item meets the requirements for a rating of "advanced implementation".

Ethiopia has developed and updated its National Adaptation Plan-Ethiopia (NAP-ETH) in 2019 and other climate change strategies in the last five years. Therefore, this item meets the requirements for a rating of "advanced implementation.".

Ethiopia's climate policy for the national forest sector includes the National REDD+ Strategy (NRS) and the National Forest Sector Development Program (NFSDP). These policies are designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, improve forest management, and promote sustainable development. We have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation"

Ethiopia's National Forest Sector Development Program (NFSDP) aims to increase forest cover from 15.7% to 20% by 2020 and 30% by 2025. It is clearly detailed into specific actions like sustainable forest use, alternative energy sources and Urban forests to achieve the general mitigation objectives for the forest sector. Because of this, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation."

Ethiopia's National Forest Sector Development Program, Volume II: Program Pillars, Action Areas and Targets clearly identified the forest sector challenges and action program areas and implementation strategies. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation".

The national government of Ethiopia has established the National REDD+ Strategy of the forest sector and established a measurement, reporting, and verification system at the federal and regional levels in order to monitor and evaluate mechanisms for assessing the outcomes of the strategy to achieve the mitigation objectives for the forest sector and support the review and decision-making process. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation.".

Ethiopia's National Adaptation Plan (NAP-ETH) considers the country's key vulnerabilities in agriculture when designing strategies to improve agricultural productivity. We have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation"

We have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation" because the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) Implementation Roadmap contains several actions related to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) to improving access to potable water (prioritized by four regions); these actions are designed to increase access to safe and clean water for rural and urban households in a climate-resilient manner.

The "One WASH Strategy" and the "WASH Implementation Framework" signed by the Ethiopian Ministries of Ministry of Water and Energy, Health, Education, and Finance in 2013 include defined inputs, activities, outputs, and roles for each ministry, essentially coordinating all WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) efforts under a single program, with each ministry responsible for specific aspects. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Advanced implementation".

Ethiopia's government has designed policies & strategies to increase agricultural productivity & adapt to climate change. These strategies include Ethiopia's National Agriculture Investment Plan, Agricultural Extension Strategy of Ethiopia & Climate-Smart Agriculture Investment Plan for Ethiopia. We have given this item a rating of "Intermediate implementation" because of the national strategies, not specific detail required for implementation-specific actions like inputs, activities, output...

The One WASH Strategy and the WASH Implementation Framework in Ethiopia explicitly identify several key challenges that hinder the implementation of WASH policies and the achievement of set objectives, including limited financial resources, lack of capacity at various levels, climate change impacting water availability, and poor community awareness and behavior change practices etc. But we haven't found measures identified to address these challenges; and the impacts.Intermediate implementation

For each strategy, there are sections called "key risks/barriers to success and systemic issues and related bottlenecks," which include information about some implementation challenges. This information is not detailed and does not cover the impacts of those challenges. Therefore, we have given this item a rating of "Intermediate implementation.".

Ethiopia's Climate-Smart Agriculture Investment Plan includes established monitoring and evaluation mechanisms with specific targets and indicators, outlining how the success of climate-smart agricultural practices will be tracked across key areas like productivity, adaptation, and mitigation. For both monitoring and evaluation, key indicators and periods for monitoring are established. But we have not got whether the results are used in the review and decision-making.

Ethiopia has established evaluation and monitoring mechanisms in place to assess the outcomes of the One WASH Strategy and the WASH Implementation Framework, but there is some inadequate data quality, a lack of timely reporting, limited stakeholder engagement, insufficient integration of findings into decision-making processes, and a lack of clear accountability mechanisms for acting on M&E results. We have given this item a rating of "Intermediate implementation".

The national budget includes various sectoral budget allocations for the implementation of mitigation & adaptation projects associated with the relevant ministry's agenda; see evidence (3) below. This is apart from the $9.7m budget allocation the Ministry ; 17% of which has been allocated to the CCD. Apart from this, there are no evidences for the identification of carbon-intensive actions nor identification & calculation of subsidies that negatively affect the achievement of climate goals.

Globally there is no definition of climate finance, however in Fiji's context, the definition of climate finance exists in the National Climate Finance Strategy although there is no formal climate taxonomy for direct climate finance in Fiji. In addition, climate finance budget tagging system is underway and a draft typology is being developed. Moreover, the National Measurement Reporting and Verification System is still underway and is being developed.

assessment_comment: As the country is not included in the Annex II of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has no obligation to provide financial resources to other countries. In this sense, the assessment of this item is not necessary.

As the country is not included in the Annex II of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has no obligation to provide financial resources to other countries. In this sense, the assessment of this item is not necessary.

As the country is not included in the Annex II of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has no obligation to provide financial resources to other countries. In this sense, the assessment of this item is not necessary.

Fiji's Climate Finance Strategy has identified the country's needs for international climate finance: (i) The identified needs are detailed; (ii) Costs have been estimated & documented; (iii) Identification of the needs are systematic; (iv) The needs has been reported & publicly available in the Climate Change Portal. The forward address of the Strategy noted that the Strategy should be the starting point for anyone looking to support Fiji's climate and development agenda.

The Fiji Government identified climate finance sources through the development of the National Climate Finance Strategy. Government is able to mobilize the climate funds through the Climate Change Division as the National Designated Authority (NDA). The NDA is capable of preparing the projects & documents needed to access funds. The Fiji Climate Finance Snapshot shows that the Government was able to mobilize the climate finance sources successfully, however the outdated report was noted.

As per the mandate of the MoF, international climate funding received directly by the government, are tracked & tagged through due processes in place to be able to oversee the disbursement & release funds. This is dependent on compliance with an adhoc checklist. Activities for the funds are tracked through Project Contract Agreements/Workplan/LoA. Objectives for the use of the funds can be found in the same documents.

The national government is fulfilling its reporting requirements for the the financial support received and needed through the reporting obligations and templates provided by the donor agencies that support their initiatives. As per the UNFCCC Article 13, reporting obligations of developing countries, Fiji is preparing its BUR which will be submitted in 2025.

The National government is able to identify potential private climate finance sources through the National Climate Finance Strategy, and mobilize private climate finance through various sources; firstly,  through use of innovative financing instruments such as the green bonds and blue bonds in the capital market; secondly through carbon markets, i.e. through the World Bank, the National Development Banks in order to sell Fiji's carbon credits to other countries.

There are no mechanisms currently in place to track private climate finance, however, there are fiduciary requirements of the central bank for bond issuance which is used to track funds accessed through the private sector.
According to the Climate Change Division, there are no private climate financing reports developed.

Fiji has developed its first ever "Climate Change Act 2021". The formalized legislation framework is sufficient as it provides the ability to mandate/support climate actions planned by Government - The Act covers relevant aspects relating to Governance, Mitigation, Adaptation, Oceans, Financing & Private Sector Engagement. The Act also introduces a system for the measurement, reporting & verification of greenhouse gas emissions & for related matters.

Section 7, subsections 1-3 of the Climate Change Act 2021 provides full effect of Fiji's obligations under the Paris Agreement. The formalized legislation is consistent with the requirements of the Paris Agreement as it: (1) NDC's are enshrined into the legislation, including the main principles under Article 4; (2) incorporates the overarching goals established in Article 2; & (3) recognizes the transparency and reporting obligations established by Article 13.

The Climate change Act 2021 contain provisions for mainstreaming climate change. Section 18 to 26 stipulates the Climate Change Obligations of State Entities including climate change requirements in National Budget Submissions. Regulations & guidelines are currently being formulated to support the mainstreaming efforts of the Government.
There are independent standing committees that engage in matters related to climate change including the Public Accounts Committee and the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights.
The Climate Change Adaptation Actions Cooperative Audit currently in progress.

There are provisions in the Climate Change Act 2021 to involve the judiciary if breach has been identified or committed. However, provisions of this Act will only enter into force when the appropriate regulations have been developed which is currently in progress and pending gazette process. This is expected to be completed by 2026.

The national government structure responsible for addressing climate change is the Climate Change Division under the Ministry of Environment & Climate Change. The Climate Change Division coordinates climate-informed development planning, climate finance and engagement in international climate change negotiations. The Division supports line Ministries increase their capacity to address the impacts of climate change, while supporting cross-sectoral efforts to increase access to climate finance.

The Climate Change Act & National Climate Change Policy is operationalized through the NAP, NDCs, & Low Emissions Development Strategy, coordinated and monitored by the Climate Change Division. Moreover, the NDP captures Fiji's climate responses from the mentioned planning instruments & commitments & provides actionable strategies for implementation. The NDP further requires that these strategies are to be implemented through an Implementation Handbook, developed by the respective Ministries.

The responsibilities for leading, coordinating, implementing, monitoring, and ensuring transparency in Fiji's national response to climate change are clearly defined in the "National Climate Change Policy (NCCP) 2018-2030" and the "Climate Change Act 2021." The policy and act set forth a structured framework to avoid gaps and overlaps.

The National Climate Change Coordinating Committee is established by Fiji's Climate Change Act 2021. The Act specifies that one of the functions of the Committee is to respond to climate change requests for support from its members. The Act further states that the Committee has the power to mobilize other governmental actors. While members of the Committee consist of Permanent Secretaries of Ministries & the Director responsible for Climate Change, the Act allows nominations of other members.

Pursuant to Article 4(19) of the Paris Agreement, Fiji developed its Low Emissions Development Strategy (LEDS) to provide long-term multi-sectoral guidance for achieving net-zero national carbon emissions by 2050. Other documents established by government include the National Adaptation Plan, National Ocean Policy and the National Climate Finance Strategy.

Mitigation targets in the Updated NDC(Pg.4) are linked to Section 4 of the LEDS(pg.40) where sector-specific targets and measures are comprehensively discussed, including recommendations on policies & priority actions. The LEDS makes reference to the IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories as a mitigation mechanism to account for Fiji's anthropogenic GHG emissions and removals (4.7.4-pg158).This aligns with the Updated NDC(Sect.5c-pg.12) and Article 4.14 of the Paris Agreement.

Chapter 2.4 of Fiji's Low Emissions Development Strategy is dedicated to achieving the SDG's. The LEDS notes that climate change is a cross cutting issue across all the SDG's, however acknowledging potential trade offs between sustainable development & net zero. It is worth noting that developing countries report on specific SDG indicators related to their context. Please refer to Fiji's Voluntary National Report.

The CommonSensing project captures the vulnerability, adaptability & exposure of Viti Levu & pending other regions. The sea-level projection tool by NASA has supported analysis for Western Division. Real time measurements plotted by COSPPac, dependent on GNSS stations to support analysis of sea level rise. Since these assessments have only been conducted at certain geographical locations in Fiji, therefore ranking stands at early implementation. The revised CVA is currently being finalized.

Fiji currently has two GNSS stations with a value of half a million USD per station, and is therefore in need of more GNSS stations that would provide sufficient scientific data for informed decision making. Therefore, scoring has been assessed as 'Early Implementation'. In addition, Fiji is currently working with the Government of Japan to design a multi-hazard early warning system. The system is currently in its design phase for Suva region only.

Fiji had developed its Vulnerability Assessment in 2017 with World Bank support, where identified vulnerabilities were addressed in the National Adaptation Plan. Fiji has a Relocation Guideline, SOP & Trust Fund Financial Management Policy Guideline which came into effect in 2018 & 2023, respectively. There are no provisions on these guidelines on how children, cultural artefacts and burial grounds are to be relocated, however, revisions to capture this is currently in progress.

Fiji has its National Climate Change Coordination Committee consisting of the permanent secretaries of Ministries, the Director Climate Change & other nominated members. The Permanent Secretary Climate Change is the chairperson of the committee. Consultations by the Coordination Committee, with relevant experts & stakeholders, including the private sector, CSO's youth organizations & vulnerable communities, is permitted under Section 12, sub-section 10 of the Climate Change Act 2021.

The National Climate Change Coordination Committee have convened with meetings as per requirements of the Climate Change Act 2021, with issues related to climate change policies and activities discussed. Also, as per the the Climate Change Act 2021, there are focal points defined in the relevant agencies that are part of the mechanism. The next meeting is scheduled for 23 October 2024 prior to the Fiji delegation departing for COP29.

The appointment of Focal Officers from responsible state entities in the vertical coordination mechanism are required in the Climate Change Act 2021. Since it is mandatory to have focal points in each Ministry, there is well representation.

The appointment & composition of focal officers is required under Section 13 of the Climate Change Act 2021. Climate change issues related to mitigation, adaptation, oceans & finance are addressed through the various steering committees. These steering committees include the NAP steering committee, Fiji Relocation Taskforce, & National Oceans Policy Steering Committee.

Climate Change Act S12, ss 10(c) has formalized the engagement with stakeholders such as the private sector, CSO's, vulnerable & at-risk communities etc., in a consultative form. Prior to the Act, stakeholders were involved in the design and implementation of climate-related activities, e.g. design and implementation of the NAP. With the current Act, approval of cabinet papers for climate related activities requires endorsement of stakeholders, specifically by CSO's.

The various policies of the Climate Change Division such as the NAP Steering Committee (SC). Additionally for relocation efforts, the Fiji Government has established the Fiji Relocation Taskforce. The TOR for the NAP SC & Fiji Relocation Taskforce SC, mandates the consultation & engagement of stakeholders, such as CSO's, private sector & academia. For NDC 3.0, the NAP SC & LEDS SC (inactive now) will be used as well as other sectoral SC's, if required.

The CCD involves the stakeholders in its decision making process in the relevant committee meetings. In addition, cabinet papers are required to be endorsed by the stakeholders before submission of the papers. Endorsement by the civil society is required prior to other major decisions such as the relocation of communities and implementation of the NAP. However it has been noted that despite the division sending invites to the private sector, they continue to be absent from these meetings.

The Climate Change Division directed a multi-sector task force in 2017 to integrate adaptation & risk management in carrying out the Climate Vulnerability Assessment (CVA). Through the CVA, the Government has identified all relevant vulnerable groups, which include women, children, elderly, people with disabilities, minority groups & low income groups. The CVA will be updated upon endorsement of the draft Risk Vulnerability Assessment Methodology (to be endorsed by October 2024).

The main mechanism for the engagement of vulnerable groups in the decision making for climate strategies, policies & plans are in the form of taskforces & SC's. As noted in G7.A, the main vulnerable groups identified in the Climate Vulnerability Assessment are women, children, elderly, people with disabilities, minority groups & low income groups - their needs have been considered in the development of strategies, policies and plans (the main ones being the NCCP, LEDS, NAP, NCFS & NOP).

Equity has been considered in the three main policies, strategies & policies: i.e. Climate Change Act 2021 under Section 5 of the Act; Updated NDC under Question 6 of the updated NDC & National Adaptation Plan Section of the NAP.

The NDC Roadmap has a section on Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV), guiding the process for developing the MRV system. Currently, the Climate Change Division uses a manual MRV system for which the IPCC reporting template is used as a guideline. The National Climate Change Coordination Committee is another mechanism established by the government, for the monitoring of relevant sector plans, with particular performance indicators as per Section 12(9(d)) of the Climate Change Act 2021.

OAG assess this component based on the monitoring of NAP implementation. The feedback from the NAP Steering Committee meetings informs the design of the new NAP. Furthermore, an independent research was conducted, assessing the private sector's knowledge and involvement in relation to the formulation process and feedback, for the design of the new NAP.

Fiji has already submitted three National GHGI to the UNFCCC as part of the first, second and third national communication. In addition, Fiji submitted its National Inventory Report (NIR) to the UNFCCC in May 2024 and is expected to submit its BUR in February 2025.
Fiji has its Climate Change Portal and all updates on climate change are uploaded on the hub.

The information hub has accessibility options for persons with disabilities. There are readily available links that easily maneuver the general public to publications, even to non-government websites such as the UNFCCC websites, containing national communications and reports submitted to the UNFCCC as part of its reporting obligations. In addition, the information hub is easily understood as it is in plain English language.

Fiji submitted its intended Nationally Determined Contributions (INDC) to the UNFCCC Secretariat on the 5 November 2015, which was endorsed as Fiji's first NDC on 22 April 2016. The updated NDC was submitted to UNFCCC in 2020. Therefore, Fiji has complied with Article 4(9) of the Paris Agreement, which requires that "Each Party shall communicate a nationally determined contribution every five years".

Fiji provided an update to its existing NDC pursuant to Article 4.11 of the Paris Agreement that includes: (1) a reaffirmation of its 2030 target - i.e. to reduce 30% of BAU CO2 emissions from the energy sector by 2030; (2) a commitment to achieve net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050; (3) up-front upfront information to facilitate clarity, transparency & understanding; (4) a commitment to enact its Climate Change Act Bill by 2021; & (5) a commitment to operationalize its NAP.

Fiji's updated NDC includes Sectoral Targets as outlined in the NDC document itself: (1) 3 mitigation targets in the energy sector from the initial NDC with subsectors of transport, industry & electricity demand-side subsectors; (2) 1 mitigating target as updated in the 2020 NDC; (3) 8 adaptation targets in Agriculture, Public Infrastructure, Health, Environment & Forestry as updated in the 2020 NDC. Total of 12 targets in the updated NDC.

Through the Fiji Low Emission Development Strategy (LEDS) 2018-2050, Fiji identified public policies that impact the countries emissions. Chapter 4 of LEDS identifies specific targets & measures for 8 major sectors. Within each sector, there is a section on existing policy & regulatory framework. Therefore, Government has effectively mapped existing policies and regulatory framework that impact the countries emissions for each identified sector.

The Low Emissions Development Strategy (LEDS) is the National Strategy for accomplishing the emission mitigation objectives for Fiji. The strategies & goals are coherent with the commitments set in the NDC and the strategies are comprehensive with key policies identified to implement the strategies & achieve the goals. This is comprehensively covered in the policy recommendations, priority actions and high level costing for each of the 8 identified sectors in the LEDS.

The FIJI LOW EMISSION DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY 2018-2050 aims to achieve zero carbon emission in the following sectors: (1) Electricity & other energy generation & use; (2) Land transport; (3) Domestic maritime transport; (4) Domestic air transport; (5) Agriculture, forestry, & other land use; (6) Wetlands (i.e., coastal wetlands, also referred to as blue carbon); (7) Waste; & (8) The cross-cutting sectors of tourism, commerce, industry, & manufacturing.

National Adaption Plan was developed to build on Fiji's existing adaptation activities, integrate climate change into every aspect of national decision-making, fulfil Fiji's adaptation-related commitments to the UNFCCC, specifically Article 7(9) of the Paris Agreement, which Fiji ratified in 2015, and operationalize the adaptation-related components of the NCCP at all levels.

Fiji government has identified several key adaptation sectors that are critical in addressing the impacts of climate change. The national adaptation plans and strategies cover these sectors comprehensively and these are: Food and nutrition security; Health; Human Settlements; Infrastructure; and Biodiversity and the Natural Environment.

Fiji developed its National Adaptation Plan in 2018 to cover the period of five years ending 2022. Since then, a progress report has been developed by the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change. The updated National Adaptation Plan is in its draft stage and is yet to validated.

According to Fiji's Low Emissions Development Strategy 2018-2050, the main policy documents for Fiji's energy sector include: (1) The National Energy Policy; (2) Fiji's NDC's submitted to the UNFCCC; and (3) Fiji's National Development Plan. Review of the policy documents noted that they have properly accounted for reductions in emissions within the Energy Sector and the policies include objectives for reducing emissions in the sector.

Fiji's NDC Implementation Road map 2017-2030 details specific actions aimed at achieving general mitigation objectives including for the energy sector. These actions are categorized into short-term, medium-term, and long-term mitigation actions and are supported by necessary enabling elements such as capacity building, and technical assistance from Fiji Competition & Consumer Commission as they are price regulators in Fiji.

The Fiji NDC Implementation Roadmap 2017-2030 outlines several challenges to the implementation of policies and the achievement of goals for the energy sector. These challenges are identified in terms of governance, coordination, resources, and capacity-building, as well as the need for strengthening the Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system.

The Fiji NDC Implementation Roadmap 2017-2030 outlines established monitoring and evaluation mechanisms for assessing the outcomes of plans or programs to achieve mitigation objectives for the energy sector. These mechanisms support the review and decision-making process through a comprehensive Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system which is currently manually done and yet to be digitized.

According to Fiji's National Adaptation Plan, the main policy documents for Fiji's Agriculture sector include Fiji's National Development Plan (NDP). Review of the NDP noted that it has been designed for the adaptation of the sector and the strategies have considered Fiji's key vulnerabilities in their design. Assessment stands at intermediate implementation as the realization of its execution (in order to determine success or failure) is yet to be determined.

Fiji's Water Sector Strategy 2050, aims to ensure reliable and safe water and wastewater services while enhancing climate resilience, infrastructure, health, & economic sustainability. One of the strategic pillars is climate resilience - Forward address to the strategy notes that management of water & sanitation must change if Fiji is to meet the threat of climate change, and the only option is adaptation. Assessment stands at intermediate implementation due to pending realization of benefits.

Fiji's NDP details specific strategies aimed at achieving a competitive, resilient and sustainable agriculture sector. However, these strategies are yet to the translated to specific actions through the implementation handbook, to be developed by the Ministry responsible for Agriculture as the new NDP 2025-2029 has just been introduced. Nonetheless, the earlier version of the NDP aimed at promoting self-sufficiency for production & exports, and climate proofing investments.

According to the forward address of Fiji's Water Sector Strategy 2050, the strategy have identified critical and urgent investments to build climate adaption. Response Strategies are noted in pages 18-44 of the strategy, in order to achieve the strategic outcomes for the country. The strategic responses in the strategy have considered climate resilience as they are one of the strategic pillars in the strategy. Benefits realized from implementation of the responses is too early to measure.

The National Development Plan 2025-2029 outlines several challenges to the implementation of policies & the achievement of goals for the Agriculture Sector. Coupled with the impacts of climate change, challenges identified include poor infrastructure, particularly farm access roads, inadequate drainage systems, poor farm access roads, heavy rainfalls, impassable roads isolate farms, improper drainage systems. Realization of benefits of strategies to address challenges yet to be determined.

Fiji national government has mapped out the challenges to implementing policies and achieving goals for the safe water and wastewater services sector. Major challenges identified include: Aging Infrastructure; Climate Change; Financial Viability; and Environmental and Economic Sustainability. Realization of benefits of strategies to address challenges yet to be determined.

The Cour des comptes is France's SAI. Focusing solely on its 2024 annual public report, 17 audits were fully dedicated to climate change adaptation, with contributions from nearly 60 rapporteurs.

In 2008, the General Direction for Energy and Climate (DGEC) was created and attached to the Ministry for Ecological Transition to focus on climate issues. In 2022, an interministerial body, the General Secretariat for Ecological Planning (SGPE), was created to coordinate national strategies concerning climate, energy, biodiversity, and the circular economy. Additionally, the independent High Council for Climate (HCC) was set up to advise the government (see appendix 1 2.7).

The founding decrees of the DGEC and the SGPE define their responsibilities. The Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan (PNIEC), submitted to the European Commission in 2024, states that the plan is prepared and led by the DGEC "in close cooperation with the SGPE for impacts on various sectoral policies". 
Since May 2022, a decree has assigned the Prime Minister the role of "responsible for ecological and energy plan", which enlights coordination at the highest level.

The SGPE indicates that streamlining work has been undertaken, giving the example of the digital and data roadmap for ecological planning that was published at the end of 2023. 
More generally, however, there is no published source of reference that would assess the extent to which there are potential gaps and overlaps in responsibilities for the different issues of French climate policies. This point has therefore not been assessed, as it would require in-depth analysis.

The SGPE, which reports to the Prime Minister, "is responsible for coordinating the development of national strategies on climate, energy, biodiversity, and the circular economy," as set out in its founding decree. The HCC's 2024 annual report highlights that "the articulation of the various components of climate policies under the aegis of the General Secretariat for Ecological Planning [SGPE] constitutes an important factor of coherence."

The 2019 Energy and Climate Act set the goal of carbon neutrality by 2050, in line with the Paris Agreement. The French strategy for achieving zero net emissions by 2050 is known as the "national low-carbon strategy" (SNBC). In accordance with the Paris Agreement, the SNBC is submitted to the UNFCCC.

The LTA is due to be updated shortly to reflect recent changes in the NDC, with more ambitious targets set for 2030 as part of France's EU commitments. For 2050, the target of zero net emissions remains unchanged. A draft SNBC 3 has been submitted for prior consultation.

Since 2004, the French General Commission for Sustainable Development (CGDD) has been monitoring the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including SDG 13 on climate. The 2024 integrated national energy and climate plan (Pniec) submitted to the European Commission recalls the objectives of ecological planning, which directly echo several SDGs. The draft SNBC 3 states that "adaptation and mitigation options must [...] avoid conflicts of impact with sustainable development objectives".

Météo-France in particular produces maps and projections, but climate services for overseas territories remain insufficient. Risk data is limited, as noted in the 2024 reports of the Cour des comptes and the High Council for Climate. France still lacks a nationwide diagnosis of vulnerabilities to climate change. However, PNACC 3 plans a national impact portal by 2026 developped by Meteo France and implementation of climate services for overseas territories like those for mainland France.

The Cour's 2024 Report underlines that French institutions rely on strong scientific bodies, like Météo-France, for climate decisions. Its expertise shaped the TRACC (reference warming trajectory for adaptation to climate change), a key adaptation tool. However, efforts still needed to be made to improve the interface at regional level. The third National Climate Change Adaptation Plan (PNACC 3) addresses this, aligning with the Cour's recommendation and set for implementation in 2024-2025.
This point has not been assessed, as it would require an in-depth analysis that is beyond the scope of this audit.
The General Secretariat for Ecological Planning (SGPE) reports directly to the Prime Minister, and involves the most relevant decision makers.

The SGPE regularly publishes documents on climate change policies. It constitutes an importante factor of coherence in climate policies, as noted by the High Council for the Climate in 2024. It should be noted that the Cour des comptes has not yet assessed the effectiveness of horizontal coordination mechanisms: in keeping with the general spirit of ClimateScanner, the rating for this audit point relates only to a criterion of implementation, not performance.

Tools exist to strengthen coordination with local authorities on climate issues. These include territorial climate-air-energy plans (PCAET), regional climate-air-energy plans (SRCAE) and regional plans for planning, sustainable development and territorial equality (SRADDET).
This point has not been evaluated, as it would require in-depth analysis.

France has multiple participation mechanisms complementing the parliamentary debate on the Environmental Impact Report of the State Budget (RIEB). These include public consultations, working groups updating energy-climate strategy, and the new ecological planning commission created in 2023. High-emitting sectors must now submit emission reduction roadmaps (per the Climate and Resilience Law). The academic community, like the HCC, contribute to climate strategies. French SAI is involved.

The participation mechanisms identified in point G6A involve a wide range of participants. For example, the consultation process associated with the future French climate and energy strategy involves citizens, academics, as well as economic players (businesses).
The participation mechanisms identified in point G6A enable regular interaction.

The 2024 Cour des comptes report highlights gaps in health data on vulnerable groups and recommends action to protect them from climate risks. PNACC 3 provides specific actions for children, sick people, and low-income groups, addressing fuel poverty and inequality. The government, through the Secretary of Finance (SEFIN), has an active portfolio with various bilateral and multilateral climate financing sources. Currently, the country lacks the capabilities and clearly defined mechanisms to oversee the use of international climate funds, so it is not possible to track the use of international funds clearly and transparently.
The country has not established mechanisms to report on the use of international climate finance, so it does not report on funds intended for public use.

The country does not yet have a mapping of private financing alternatives. Although the General Provisions of the Budget have established that public institutions must consider the climate change approach in preparing projects to be funded by the government with national and international funds, there are no mechanisms or incentives to mobilize private climate financing.
The country does not yet have a mechanism to track or monitor private financing.

Given that the country still does not have a mapping of private financing alternatives or a mechanism to track or monitor private financing, no reports have yet been prepared on the use of private climate financing.

The country has a Climate Change Law (Decree 297-2013), It was drafted in 2013 and published in the Official Gazette (La Gaceta) in 2014. However, the law is considered generic and insufficient because it predates the guidelines established in the Paris Agreement.

The country's current regulatory framework was established in 2014 and is therefore not aligned with the Paris Agreement. However, the State Secretariat for Natural Resources and Environment (SERNA) is updating the regulatory framework in accordance with the provisions of the Paris Agreement.

The current Climate Change Law has certain requirements for connecting short-term planning, such as the National Adaptation Plan (NAP), which needs to be updated every five years. However, Honduras is in the process of developing the National Decarbonization and Climate Resilience Strategy of Honduras (NDCREH) as a planning tool for medium and long-term mitigation, along with its synergies to adaptation.

The National Congress of the Republic (Parliament), through the Organic Law of the Legislative Branch (Decree 363-2013), establishes the formation of the Environment and Climate Change Commission, however, it has not had the prominence to debate issues of climate change and prepare reports on government actions related to climate.

In 2023, The Superior Court of Accounts, as the Supreme Audit Institution (SAI), conducted a specific audit on climate change. Six reports were prepared with respective recommendations for various institutions selected based on stakeholder analysis, which allowed for an understanding of their direct competencies in climate change management, according to the prioritized sectors in the country.

The country's judicial bodies lack clarity regarding the recognition of climate rights. The Supreme Court of Justice (SCJ) of Honduras has a Judicial Circuit with national jurisdiction over organized crime, the environment, and corruption, but it does not specify climate-related matters. SCJ Decision No.8-2023 established the jurisdiction of this court, without specifying in detail aspects of climate justice, climate rights, and climate crimes.
There is a National Direction of Climate Change, which is under the Secretary of State in the Offices of Natural Resources and Environment (SERNA).

There is an internal regulation of the National Directorate of Climate Change (NDCC), which establishes its functions and responsibilities including actions to lead, coordinate implement, and provide transparency to the national responses related to climate change.

Among the overlapping constraints limiting the actions of the Honduran State on climate change, the following can be mentioned: the assignment of the NAP preparation and climate change mitigation measures to the Secretary of Finance and to SERNA, as well as gaps related to GHG, The Information System for Forest Management and Monitoring (SIGMOF), the Public Expenditure Monitoring System for Climate Action, and the National Framework for Safeguards for Climate Change Initiatives for REDD+.

The country is supported by the Interinstitutional Climate Change Committee (ICCC) and the Interinstitutional Technical Climate Change Committee (ITCCC), both of which serve as permanent bodies responsible for leading, directing, and coordinating national actions for the adaptation to and mitigation of the negative impacts of climate change.

Honduras has a National Climate Change Strategy, developed in 2010. It was not submitted to the UNFCCC and does not establish a specific timeline for its implementation. Currently, the State of Honduras through SERNA, is in the process of formulating a long-term strategy, known as the National Strategy for Decarbonization and Climate Resilience of Honduras (ENDRCH), which encompasses goals for 2030 and 2050.

Since the National Climate Change Strategy was developed in 2010, it does not align with the NDCs. Nevertheless, the commitments obtained in the NDC 2021 and Paris Agreement serve as the basis for preparing the ENDRCH update. These commitments are already integrated into the models, and the results of the ENDRCH's models form the foundation for establishing the commitments for the NDC 2025 update.
Honduras' National Climate Change Strategy is not aligned with the SDGs, as it was developed in 2010, and is therefore outdated.

The country has the Interinstitutional Climate Change Committee (CICC) as a horizontal coordination mechanism, chaired by the President of the Republic, and composed of the highest authorities of the institutions responsible for the prioritized climate change sectors.

The Interinstitutional Climate Change Committee (CICC) does not have a working dynamic that allows for frequent interaction with its members. For example, it does not hold regular meetings, lacks a defined work plan, and does not promote within public, private, and community institutions the implementation of approved actions, policies, and strategies related to mitigation and adaptation, or any other actions to reduce the effects of climate change.

The Association of Municipalities of Honduras (AMHON) is an association that brings together the 298 municipalities in the country and is part of the Interinstitutional Technical Committee on Climate Change (CTICC), therefore, it is considered that there is a balanced level of representation that allows vertical coordination, in addition, the Climate Change Law in its article 13 establishes all the institutions that are part of the CTICC and in numeral 17 it indicates that at the discretion of the committee it can convene other members of organized civil society for purposes of the issue being discussed, thus giving greater vertical representation.

The Interinstitutional Technical Climate Change Committee (CTICC) lacks a working dynamic that allows interaction with its members, does not hold regular meetings, and has no defined work plan. It has not developed or promoted regional programs on climate change or communicated progress on its actions. The new Climate Change Law is establishing a new governance structure and forming new subcommittees based on the country's needs.

The Interinstitutional Committee on Climate Change (CICC) allows the participation of different interested parties across different sectors: public institutions, autonomous institutions, municipalities, associations, foundations, private companies, organized civil society and academia.

The Interinstitutional Climate Change Committee (CICC) allows for the participation of organized civil society, the private sector, and academia, represented by the Higher Education Council, which includes both public and private universities.

There is no interaction among the different institutions that make up the CICC, as they lack a consistent working dynamic and do not hold regular meetings. Currently, SERNA and other related entities are developing the National Climate Empowerment Strategy (ENACE), in accordance with Articles 6 and 12 of the Paris Agreement, to raise awareness, build capacity, and promote participation and public access to climate information.

The most vulnerable groups to climate change are identified in the National Climate Change Adaptation Plan and in the NDC, and the most vulnerable groups are: women, youth, Indian peoples and Afro-Hondurans, specifically those who live in extreme poverty and with their basic needs unmet. In the update of these instruments that the State of Honduras is carrying out through SERNA, the most vulnerable groups are being incorporated into climate adaptation and mitigation actions.

There are no mechanisms to involve vulnerable groups in the decision-making process for climate strategies, policies and plans. However, SERNA and other related entities are developing the National Climate Empowerment Strategy (ENACE), in accordance with the provisions of Articles 6 and 12 of the Paris Agreement, for awareness-raising, capacity building, participation and public access to climate information.
The Climate Change Law generally considers the principle of equity, while the National Climate Change Adaptation Plan and the NDC address equity aspects focused on vulnerable groups

Currently, Honduras, with the CBIT (The Capacity-building Initiative for Transparency) project to strengthen climate transparency capacities, within the framework of article 13 of the Paris Agreement, is in the process of creating the National Climate Change Monitoring System (SNMCC), as a tool to collect, monitor, evaluate and report progress in the implementation of climate actions.

By not having monitoring mechanisms to track the instruments for climate action, therefore, there are no feedback mechanisms to strengthen monitoring and improve the formulation of climate policies; however, in the SNMCC that is being developed, a structure and indicators will be incorporated to monitor the implementation of climate action.

Honduras is committed to complying the frequency of report submissions as transparency mechanisms, presenting to the UNFCCC in 2020 the Third National Communication on Climate Change and the First Biennial Update Report (BUR) and in 2024 it presented the Second Biennial Update Report (BUR 2), which should have been presented in 2022; The fourth communication will be presented in 2026 together with the second BTR.

At the national level, there is no transparency mechanism that provides information on the fulfillment of national climate change objectives. However, the forestry and energy sectors have monitoring and tracking systems for their climate objectives and in accordance with their competencies. Currently, Honduras is developing the National Climate Change Monitoring System (SNMCC) as a national integrated transparency system for climate action.

Honduras is developing the National Climate Change Monitoring System (SNMCC), which will include, among other things, two (2) information output modules: one to standardize the process of preparing and submitting reports to the UNFCCC, and another to facilitate and disseminate information to different types of audiences at the national level.
THonduras completed its first update of the NDC in 2021, as stipulated in Article 4, Paragraph 9 of the Paris Agreement.

The energy and agriculture sectors are the most important and generate the most greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the country. Both sectors have specific objectives, targets, and actions to reduce their emissions.

The sectors included are: Agro-Food and Food Sovereignty, Human Health, Infrastructure and Socioeconomic Development, Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, and Water Resources.

Currently, the Secretary of State for Natural Resources and Environment (SERNA) is in the process of updating the legal and operational framework, including the National Climate Change Adaptation Plan.

It is assessed as incipient implementation because there are no established objectives or detailed metrics for emissions reduction. However, there are plans to develop the National Energy Plan aligned with the country's commitments to reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

The country has policies that contemplate the adaptation of the Agriculture and Food Security Sector, specifically with the National Strategy for Adaptation to Climate Change for the Agri-Food Sector of Honduras 2015-2025; It also has the State Policy for the Agri-Food Sector of Honduras 2023-2043 and the National Long-Term Food and Nutrition Security Policy (PSAN) and National Food and Nutrition Security Strategy (ENSAN): PyENSAN 2030.

It is assessed as an intermediate level of implementation, as not all policies include specific and responsible actions for their execution to achieve the adaptation objectives for the Agriculture and Food Security sector.

In the absence of an Adaptation Strategy for the Infrastructure Sector, there are no specific actions with indicators to measure the achievement of the general adaptation objectives for the Infrastructure and Economic Development Sector. Only the National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change outlines some general adaptation actions for this sector.

In general, the National Strategy for Climate Change Adaptation for the Agro-Food Sector of Honduras 2015-2025; the State Policy for the Agro-Food Sector of Honduras 2023-2043; the National Long-Term Food and Nutritional Security Policy (PSAN) and National Food and Nutritional Security Strategy (ENSAN): PyENSAN 2030 have identified the challenges in implementing adaptation actions for the Agriculture and Food Security sector.

There is no specific mapping of the adaptation challenges for the Infrastructure Sector; in general, the National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change has identified the gaps for the establishment of strategic guidelines and actions for adaptation.
The country's climate change adaptation policies, strategies, and plans have mechanisms for monitoring and evaluating their actions. So we considere evaluate as intermediate stage.

The country has not established monitoring and evaluation mechanisms to assess climate policies, specifically the actions aimed at achieving adaptation objectives for the Infrastructure and Economic Development sector. The National  Adaptation Plan outlines a framework for monitoring, tracking, and evaluating itself, including strategic guidelines and actions for the adaptation of the Infrastructure and Economic Development sector.
