The Act LX of 2007 is in place to establish the legal and institutional framework; providing mandate to develop a strategy on climate change.
Act XLIV of 2020 on Climate protection is in place to provide mandate to climate action planned by the Hungarian Government.
The European Climate Law with the objective of climate neutrality in the European Union by 2050, aims to achieve negative emissions thereafter, and establishes the legal framework for achieving climate neutrality.

EU ratified the Paris Agreement in October 2016.
The main relevant regulatory framework, the European Climate Law was approved in 2021. NDCs are enshrined into the legislation, including the main principles mentioned in article 4 of the Paris Agreement; the European Climate Law incorporates the overarching goals set in article 2 and recognizes the transparency and reporting obligations established by art 13 of the Paris Agreement.

There are more detailed provisions, with the specification of sectors, actors, and the climate aspects considered in cross-sectoral policies. Objectives and action lines are closely linked to GHG emission and climate change aspects.

Committee on Sustainable Development deals with climate change issues, climate policy, environmental issues. Occasionally the committee calls public hearings, but does not produce reports on governmental actions related to climate. Ombudsman for Future Generations is elected by the Parliament, may initiate/participate in investigations, turn to the Constitutional Court or the Curia of Hungary. National Council for Sustainable Development is initiated by the Parliament to work as advisory body.

The State Audit Office of Hungary (SAO) is planning to launch an audit that has climate change as its primary focus in 2024. In the last 5 years audits included mitigation or adaptation aspects as central topics (audit related to SDG6, air quality) and several analyses focused on climate change policy.

The Fundamental Law sets out the State's duty to preserve natural resources for future generations. Legal instruments can be used to take action against climate actors, but national courts have not adjudicated climate change claims yet. Possibilities offered by actions for failure to act have not been exploited yet, plaintiffs tend to resort to actions for annulment.Currently there is an ex-post review procedure before the Constitutional Court on shortcomings of the climate legislation.

The designated single national entity currently is the Ministry for Energy Affairs. Tasks and responsibilities are regulated in the articles 23-26 and articles 63-67 of the Operational and Organizational Rules of the ministry. Within the Ministry for Energy Affairs, a Climate Policy Department has been established that plays a coordinating and supervisory role in the national system. The head of this department is Hungary's current UNFCCC Focal Point.

The national government has assigned responsibilities for climate change activities including planning, coordinating, implementing, and monitoring these activities and providing transparency in article 63 of the Operational and Organizational Rules of the Ministry of Energy Affairs.
Nevertheless there is opportunity for improvement to define monitoring in more specific terms with a wider scope and transparency responsibilities with more focus on domestic reporting too.

The Climate Policy Department at the Ministry of Energy Affairs is responsible for leading, steering and coordinating national responses to climate change, and with authority to mobilize other government bodies at national level. It is supervised by high-ranking government officials, but it is not evident if the coordinating body gains inputs from working level government officials.

Hungary has submitted its climate-related long-term strategies (LTSs) to the European Union in accordance with the Paris Agreement (art. 4 (19)). The strategies define green-house-gas emissions reduction targets for 2030, 2050.

Hungary officially presented and regularly updated its commitments since the European Comission officially updated the NDC on behalf of the European Union and its Member States on 16 October 2023. 
Hungary's LTS contains provisions that are conducive to the results expressed in the NDC indicating the ways and measures to reduce the GHG emissions.
The LTS does not fully cover all the mechanisms and activities expressed in the NDC. Relevant documents are under revision at the Ministry.

There are references to SDGs in the long-term strategy and they identify which SDGs - namely SDG2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 - are connected to climate change and what are the positive impacts (co-benefits and synergies), but do not indicate ways to leverage the positive impacts and/or minimize the negative ones. UNFCC Guiding Principles to Develop Long Term Climate Strategies require the LTS to be consistent with the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

The risks associated with climate-related impacts have been considered and updated in the last five years. The sixth chapter of the Eighth National Communication and Fifth Biennial Report of Hungary contains detailed assessment of vulnerabilities and climate change impacts.

Green Economy Model and HU-TIMES model were used to outline long-term trajectories. The NCDS and NECP were based on consultation involving professional organizations. The draft NECP was discussed by the National Environment Council in May 2023, academic representatives appointed by the President of the Hungarian Academy of Science. In 2020, the Hungarian Scientific Panel on Climate Change (HuPCC) was established, to summarize the latest knowledge on climate change related research results.

Climate change risks (e.g: damage to forests, soil erosion, safety of ground water resources) are incorporated in several governmental planning instruments, these considerations are rather systematic and comprehensive analysis of the relevant climate vulnerabilities and risks for the achievement of the national objectives, targets, and contributions.

Horizontal coordination mechanism is supervised by high ranking leadership in the government and relevant actors are involved in the process. Department for Climate Policy at the Ministry of Energy is responsible for the coordinating the work of the inter-ministerial working groups on decarbonisation and adaptation, cooperates with the relevant departments of the Ministry for Agriculture, develops the harmonization of the sectors of effort-sharing decision.

LIII. of 1995 defines the tasks and responsibilities of the National Environment Council that is the government's advisory, proposing or consulting body in the preparation of decisions containing environmental policy. However evidence of regular meetings, discussion of relevant issues is missing.

Act. LIII. of 1995 regulates the participation of adequate representativeness of subnational regions, counties or local governments, prescribes the participation of National Environment Council in the process of  regulation and other governmental decisions concerning environmental issues.

National Environment Council is the government's advisory body, proposing or consulting body in the preparation of decisions containing environmental policy and resulting in a national or regional impact. LIII. of 1995 regulates the participation of adequate representativeness of subnational regions, counties or local governments, prescribes the participation of National Environment Council in the process of  regulation and other governmental decisions concerning environmental issues.

The right to participate in decision making of climate strategies and plans is guaranteed by law for the public. The current long-time strategy (NTFS) and the National Climate Change Strategy-II set the goals in order to achieve climate awareness and partnership (e.g. County Climate Change Platforms, consultation forums, online platform). However, there are no comprehensive, detailed rules on how to ensure and manage participation in the design and implementation of climate-related activities.

National Climate Change Strategy sets goals for stakeholder engagement.During the preparation of the current long-term strategy and the NECP (National Energy and Climate Plan), public consultation and wide-ranging technical consultation took place with the participation of academia, industry, research institutes, NGOs and relevant stakeholders from public administration.However,the public consultation on the revised NECP did not fully comply with the requirements of the framework.

Stakeholder forums or platforms are mainly organisations that list and register programmes for climate protection. According to the NCCSII evaluation report, the majority of the partners interviewed perceive the relationship with climate policy ministry as well-established but decreasing in intensity, with the relationship currently being weaker or minimal.
Until 2021 there was active interaction with the Hungarian Scientific Panel on Climate Change (HuPCC) and the National Environment Council.

The government - based on vulnerability assessments - identified vulnerable groups and considered their needs in the Second National Climate Change Strategy.
KEHOP Plusz operational program's just transition priority aims to create new jobs and reduce emissions in the most carbon-intensive counties, which have a high proportion of workers in transition industries and coal-fired properties.

For legislative documents, opinions of disadvantaged groups should be represented in the consultation process in accordance with Act CXXXI of 2010. Laws/regulations do not ensure the involvement of relevant social groups in case of non-legislative documents.
For programmes supported by the European Structural and Investment Funds, social consultation is carried out in accordance with EU requirements.
National Climate Law does not address vulnerable groups. NDC, climate strategies, policies and plans incorporate an equity perspective, in order to contemplate the needs of vulnerable groups.

Law and government decrees stipulate standardized guidance on international monitoring and reporting. On national level measurable indicators and targets are elaborated. Nevertheless, the systematic, complex monitoring and evaluation of adaptation-related objectives, measures and climate impacts is currently lacking. A complex climate policy-oriented Monitoring and Reporting System is being planned and prepared.

Analysis and data from many institutions support climate change policymaking (e.g. National Adaptation Centre, Regional Centre for Energy Policy Research, HungaroMet, National Adaptation Geo-information System).The information produced by the monitoring mechanisms is used as feedback for improving climate change policies. A complex climate policy-oriented Monitoring and Reporting System is being planned and prepared.
As EU member state, Hungary prepared and submitted its National Communications and Biennial reports to the UNFCCC.

There are no official websites (or other tools) that can provide overall information for the follow-up on the progress towards national climate objectives. Documents on government's former website are hardly accessible, the official climate policy site (klima.kormany.hu) has not been updated. Climate policy information can be accessed from various sources. Updated and complete information can be obtained on EU-websites (on EU-funded developments) and on UN-websites (GHG emissions) in English.

Climate policy information (overview, risks, policy goals, measures, data, implementation, assessments, etc.) can be accessed from various sources. However, the information sources can not be easily found by the public. The provided information is not in a format and language that non-experts can easily understand. Reports on EU-funded measures and achievements and short, understandable summary of the use of public funds can be publicly accessed.

Hungary updated and communicated the nationally determined contribution every five years as EU member state. Submission dates to UNFCC site are: 05/10/2016, 18/12/2020 and 19/10/2023.
Last update was submitted by the European Commission on behalf of the EU and its member states and listed in the NDC Registry of UNFCC.
Hungary has already updated its first as well as the second NDC.

Sectoral plans and programs cover the GHG-emission reduction in the main sectors and detail the actions needed to achieve the reduction. assessment_comment:
In 2019, Ireland committed to a series of green budgeting reforms to better embed climate and environmental goals within the budgetary process. Progress to date includes:
- launch of Irish Sovereign Green Bonds 
- a system of identification and tagging of climate and environmental expenditure in the REV
- annual reporting of the use of additional carbon tax revenues for climate and just transitionary measures
- a February 2023 review by the Irish Government Economic and Evaluation Service of fossil fuel subsidies and other potentially climate-harmful supports
Appendix 6 of the REV identifies budget allocations for (a) climate and environmentally favourable expenditure and (b) climate and environmentally unfavourable expenditure. 
Appendix 7 of the REV identifies allocations from ring-fenced increases in the carbon tax rate. A separate annual report provides greater details.
Ireland has made financial commitments to climate action, including dedicated funding streams e.g. the Climate Action Fund, carbon tax allocations and a growing international climate finance contribution. 
Intermediate implementation is the assessed category because 
 - 	Ireland assigns funds in national budgets for achieving climate goals and these funds align with the Government plans/strategies
 - 	Ireland identifies carbon-intensive actions in budgets
 - 	While IGEES has identified perverse subsidies, this work needs to be followed up by an action plan.

Ireland does not have a formal or nationally developed definition of climate finance in domestic law or policy. However, there are early efforts to identify and categorise climate-relevant public expenditure through green budgeting reforms. International climate finance is reported under OECD DAC criteria. 
In addition, a recent working paper commissioned by the Climate Change Advisory Council (Byrne, 2024) reviews available mitigation and adaptation finance options and references the EU taxonomy, indicating engagement with emerging classification systems. The EU taxonomy for sustainable activities is a classification system that defines criteria for economic activities that are aligned with a net zero trajectory by 2050 and the broader environmental goals other than climate.

Ireland does not have developed systems to track and account for different types of direct climate finance.   

These developments reflect an early-stage effort to define and track climate finance.

Ireland does not have a formal or nationally adopted definition of climate finance in domestic law or policy. However, recent public finance reforms have introduced green budgeting practices that attempt to classify and tag climate-relevant public expenditure. These efforts include assessments of expenditure that contributes indirectly to climate goals, even where mitigation or adaptation is not the primary objective. This tagging approach is detailed in the Department of Finance's April 2025 paper and the Green Budgeting in REV (Revised Estimates for the Public Services) 2024.
The EU taxonomy for sustainable activities is a classification system that defines criteria for economic activities that are aligned with a net zero trajectory by 2050 and the broader environmental goals other than climate.

Ireland does not have developed systems to track and account for different types of indirect climate finance.   

These developments reflect an early-stage effort to define and track indirect climate finance.

The CSO produces reports on fossil fuel subsidies.  The report for 2023 noted that
 - 	Fossil fuel subsidies were  - 4.9 billion in 2023, up from  - 4.7 billion in 2022 and  - 2.8 billion in 2021. Higher levels in 2022 and 2023 occurred as a number of temporary Government support measures were introduced in response to rising energy prices.
 - 	Direct fossil fuel subsidies such as Household Energy Credits accounted for 23% of total fossil fuel subsidies in 2023, while indirect subsidies such as the VAT rate reduction on natural gas accounted for 77%.

The Government in Ireland does not publish regular reports on the use of domestic climate finance. However, the Central Statistics Office does publish reports on fossil fuel subsidies. 

It is assessed that systems in place support a categorisation of 'early implementation'.

Ireland's commitments for international climate finance are expressed in its 8th National Communication and Biennial Reports to the UNFCCC. Commitment in 2015 to provide  - 175m between 2016 and 2020 was achieved by 2018. Announcement at COP26 in 2021 of a commitment to increase climate finance to  - 225m per year by 2025.
Ireland has formally expressed commitments to international climate finance. In 2022, it published its International Climate Finance Roadmap, setting a clear public commitment to provide at least  - 225 million annually by 2025 and support for the most climate vulnerable countries. These commitments:
 - 	Are formally expressed in official policy documents, including in Ireland's Biennial Reports and submissions to UNFCCC.
 - 	Reflect annual increase over the past decade and are delivered through new appropriations in each annual budget (which meets the handbook criteria of "new and additional").
 - 	Includes a pledge of doubling ICF from 2020 levels by 2025, demonstrating an upward trajectory. 

These elements meet all the criteria for advanced implementation under the Climate Scanner Guidance.

Ireland has clear and functioning mechanisms to allocate and disburse resources committed for international climate finance (ICF):
 - 	Resources are formally allocated through Vote 27 (International Cooperation) in the annual Revised Estimate Volume (REV). This includes budgeted amounts aligned with Ireland's commitment of  - 225 million annually by 2025 for climate-related development finance. 
 - 	Disbursement is actively tracked: The REV reports climate finance disbursed in prior years (2021, 2022 & 2023 in the 2025 REV) showing actual flows. 
 - 	Progress is being made towards commitments - Ireland has scaled up ICF from  - 88.3 million in 2020 to  - 159.2 million in 2023, with further increases planned. This upwards trajectory is consistent with the 2025 target. 
 - 	Public Policy Impact indicators are included in the REV, demonstrating the government's intent to monitor not just spending but also the development outcomes of ICF. 

These systems of budgeting, disbursement and performance tracking demonstrate a mature approach, justifying a score of advanced implementation as per the climate scanner handbook.

Ireland has established formal mechanisms for regularly reporting on its international climate finance (ICF) commitments:
 - 	The government reports biennially through the UNFCCC Biennial Reports, which include detailed breakdowns climate finance contributions, delivery channels and sectors supported. These are publicly available. 
 - 	Ireland also participates in the EU's aggregated climate finance reporting to the UNFCCC, which reflects its commitments and disbursements. 
 - 	At national level, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Irish Aid issue annual ICF summaries, often accompanied by press releases (e.g. the 2023 statement showing  - 159 million in climate finance). 
 - 	The Revised Estimates Volume (REV) includes historical disbursement data. 

These reports and updates are publicly available and published on government websites (gov.ie, Ireland.ie and UNFCCC.int), meeting transparency and accessibility expectations. Ireland's routine, multi-channel reporting and transparency mechanisms meet all three climate scanner criteria for an assessment of advanced implementation.

A 2024 OECD report found that "To date, all of Ireland's climate finance has been sourced from public funding. Despite some attempts to involve the private sector, engagement has been limited. This is partly related to the fact that there is less private sector engagement in adaptation than mitigation. Ireland aims to meet 2025 climate targets through public sources."
Ireland is mobilizing domestic private climate finance through a variety of mechanisms, including grants, loans, and green bonds. 
 - 	SEAI (Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland) grants support individuals and businesses to invest in sustainable energy solutions. 
 - 	The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, through schemes like forestry initiatives, also plays a role in mobilizing climate finance by incentivizing land management practices that contribute to carbon sequestration and biodiversity. 
Irish Sovereign Green Bonds are designed to provide investors with the financial features of a standard Irish government bond combined with sovereign green bond market practices. ISGB proceeds are allocated to eligible green projects which generate a positive environmental benefit.
Budget 2025 includes a number of green tax measures for e.g. Electric Vehicles, Energy efficiency in homes, Green tax credits for businesses, Green agriculture initiatives.
There is a range of strategies for mobilising domestic private climate finance but lack of success in raising international private climate financing.

In Ireland, tracking private climate change finance primarily relies on voluntary initiatives and reporting frameworks, rather than a centralized, mandatory system. While there's no comprehensive, publicly available database specifically tracking all private climate finance, some key elements and initiatives contribute to its tracking and accounting: 
Businesses and financial institutions are encouraged to disclose their climate-related financial risks and opportunities through various reporting frameworks like the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
The government's Climate Action Plan sets overall targets for climate finance, but tracking of private finance is largely reliant on voluntary disclosure and reporting by private actors. 
Organizations like the Central Bank of Ireland and the EPA are involved in research and analysis related to climate finance, including its role in the Irish financial system and the potential for green finance. 
The EPA is developing Ecosystem Accounts to assess the value of natural resources and their contribution to the economy, indirectly informing climate-related investment. 
Some sectors, such as renewable energy, have specific schemes like the Renewable Energy Support Scheme (RESS), which tracks the deployment of renewable energy and associated funding. 
There is no centralised comprehensive system in Ireland for tracking private climate finance. The elements that do exist support a score of early implementation.

With respect to reporting, the Government annually reports its climate finance yearly contributions to the European Union, to the OECD Development Assistance Committee and to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. 
In addition, the Department of Foreign Affairs publishes an annual Climate and Environmental Finance Report, providing comprehensive information regarding funding sources, thematic and geographic priorities, and disbursement channels. This report details the levels, channels, and focus of funding provided by the Irish government to support climate action and environmental protection in developing countries. 

While some level of reporting takes place, there is no mechanism for Government to report on private climate finance and its achievements.  The elements that do exist support a score of early implementation.

There is a climate change legal and regulatory framework in Ireland to support the achievement of mitigation and adaptation goals. Ireland is also subject to European climate law which sets the overall goal for Europe's economy and society to become climate-neutral by 2050, setting the intermediate target of reducing net GHG emissions by at least 55% by 2030, compared to 1990 levels.

The legal and regulatory framework in Ireland is aligned with the main mechanisms and rules established by the Paris Agreement. In particular, the 2021 Act is assessed to have a high degree of consistency with the Paris Agreement. The Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 requires
- carbon budgets (every five years)
- sectoral emissions ceilings (contained within carbon budgets)
- climate action plans (annually)
- a national long-term climate action strategy (every five years)
- a national adaptation framework (every five years).

Ireland is also subject to European climate law which sets the overall goal for Europe's economy and society to become climate-neutral by 2050, setting the intermediate target of reducing net GHG emissions by at least 55% by 2030, compared to 1990 levels.
Article 4.16 of the Paris Agreement provides for parties, including regional economic integration organisations and their member states, to act jointly to fulfil their obligations under the Agreement. A nationally determined contribution (NDC) is set for the EU and its member states. In addition to setting emissions targets at an aggregate level, the EU NDC specifies the individual targets allocated to each EU member state.

National legislation contains some provisions for mainstreaming climate change considerations into national and sectoral plans. 
Section 6 of The Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 authorises the Government to request appropriate ministers to submit sectoral adaptation plans for approval, specifying the adaptation policy measures proposed for the sector in question. 
  
Section 6A of The 2021 Act authorises the Minister to set ceilings for GHG emissions in different sectors of the economy. Ministers are required to comply with the sectoral emissions ceiling that applies to the sector for which they have responsibility. 
 - 	The Government agreed sectoral emissions ceilings in July 2022, for each 5-year carbon budget period, for the highest emitting sectors i.e. Agriculture, Transport, Electricity etc.     
Section 14B of the 2021 Act requires each local authority to prepare its own climate action plan, every five years, specifying the mitigation and adaptation measures it will adopt.
Annual Climate Action Plans include analysis by sector  -  they set out sector-specific actions to ensure compliance with carbon budgets and sectoral emissions ceilings. 
Mainstreaming is evident in the NDP review published in July 2025. Chapter 7 of that review outlines how the NDP review has factored in considerations of climate, and how explicit capital allocations for climate related activity are being made through the Infrastructure, Climate and Nature Fund.

There is a Cabinet Committee on Climate Action, Environment and Energy whose membership includes the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste, along with the ministers from the major departments. Other ministers are invited to attend as required. It provides a forum for the discussion of climate policies and delivery mechanisms. The Cabinet Committee is supported by a senior officials group from across government.
Separately, there is a Joint Oireachtas Committee on Climate, Environment and Energy. Membership of the joint committee includes nine deputies from Dáil Éireann and five members of the Seanad.
The predecessor of the current committee (the committee on environment and climate action) met in public over 120 times between May 2021 and November 2024 and published a number of reports on climate-related areas.
Under Section 14A of the 2021 Act, Government ministers are held to account by the relevant joint Oireachtas committees. The Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government shall, at the written request of a joint committee, attend before it to give an account, of matters including progress under the most recent approved climate action plan.
Climate action matters are also discussed regularly by other relevant Oireachtas committees, including the Committee on Agriculture and Food; and the Committee on Transport. 
Committee members have access to a 'Climate Action Hub', which includes climate related information, research and analysis.

OCAG has conducted a number of performance audits in recent years, where climate change was a central aspect of the audit: 
 - 	Adapting flood risk management to climate change impacts (Chapter 4, 2023 Annual Report)
 - 	Performance of certain residential retrofit schemes (Chapter 8, 2022 Annual Report) 
 - 	Greenhouse gas related financial transactions (Chapter 9, 2018 Annual Report)

In addition, there are two ongoing performance audits in the climate change area  -  one on the Climate Action Fund and another on the approach to achieving carbon neutrality in Ireland.

Several important cases relating to climate change have been considered and adjudicated on by the judiciary. 
 - 	A prominent case, Climate Case Ireland, involved a high court challenge by Friends of the Irish Environment (FIE) against the government's climate action plan. 
 - 	In February 2025, the High Court issued a decision in a case taken by FIE seeking to quash the Government's Climate Action Plan 2023 and Annex of Actions. 
 - 	A July 2025 High Court decision [McGowan & Anor v An Comisiúin Pleanála] recognised that "the climate emergency represents a critical risk to human and natural life on earth. 
 - 	In May 2025, the High Court [Massey v An Bord Pleanála] refused leave to appeal a planning decision. 
 - 	In January 2025, a High Court decision [Coolglass Windfarm Limited v An Bord Pleanála] quashed a decision by An Bord Pleanála (ABP) to refuse an application to build a 13-turbine wind farm in County Laois, sending it back to the planning body for a fresh determination.
 - 	In July 2024, the High Court referred a challenge by An Taisce to the Nitrates Action Plan, to the European Court of Justice.
As in other jurisdictions, climate litigation has been increasing in Irish Courts over recent years. A number of High Court decisions re. planning appeals have reinforced the importance of climate action and the need for Ireland to comply with climate action obligations.

It is assessed that a government structure does exist in Ireland to address climate change issues. The following are the key elements:
 - 	A minister of Government has been appointed to lead a department (the Department of Climate, Environment and Energy) with responsibility for addressing climate change. 
 - 	The Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act 2015 established the Climate Change Advisory Council to provide independent advice to Government on climate action.
 - 	There is a Cabinet Committee on Climate Action, Environment and Energy whose membership includes the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste, along with the ministers from the major departments. Other ministers are invited to attend as required. The Cabinet Committee is supported by a senior officials group (chaired by the Department of the Taoiseach) comprising officials from across government, which meets separately in advance of the committee. 
 - 	The Climate Action Delivery Board is jointly chaired by the secretaries general of the Department of the Taoiseach and the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications. Its membership includes the head civil servants of the government departments with responsibility for key climate action areas. 
 - 	Other key groups within the overall climate action governance structure include: a climate action modelling group; a climate communications coordination committee; a climate action hub; and a climate action unit network.

The remit of the Climate Action Delivery Board includes providing leadership to ensure coordinated, timely and effective implementation of the government's climate action agenda. 
A Cabinet Committee on Climate Action, Environment and Energy oversees implementation of programme for Government commitments in relation to, inter alia, the environment and climate action.
The Climate Change Advisory Council is an independent advisory body tasked with assessing and advising on how Ireland can achieve the transition to a climate-resilient, biodiversity-rich, environmentally sustainable and climate-neutral economy. The Council is specifically tasked with advising and making recommendations to Government on climate action plans; the national long term climate action strategy; national adaptation frameworks; and carbon budgets. 
The Department of the Taoiseach oversees the monitoring and reporting process for climate action plans and measures listed in the Annex. Quarterly progress reports are submitted to the Government before being published on the climate action website. 
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) provides environmental data, assessments and evidence to inform decision making and implements effective regulation and environmental compliance systems.
An accountability framework sets out the minister responsible for each of the sectoral emissions ceilings.
The NAF 2024 sets out the lead departments that are responsible for preparation of SAPS for key sectors.

It is assessed that roles and responsibilities for leading, coordinating, implementing, monitoring and giving transparency to national responses to climate change (as set out in G2.B.) are generally well defined and that there aren't any significant gaps or overlaps.
On the issue of transparency, the Climate Change Advisory Council has drawn attention to the lack of regularly published annualised trajectories towards sectoral emissions ceilings  -  it stated that Government departments continue to distance themselves from the responsibilities that they have taken on and may not be demonstrating the necessary levels of ambition to successfully deliver the results required.

The Cabinet Committee on Climate Action, Environment and Energy provides a forum for the discussion of climate policies and delivery mechanisms, usually on the basis of proposals prepared by government departments, which are often subsequently considered by Government. Membership includes the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste, along with the ministers from the major departments. Other ministers are invited to attend as required. The Cabinet Committee is supported by a senior officials group (chaired by the Department of the Taoiseach) comprising officials from across government, which meets separately in advance of the committee.
The Climate Action Delivery Board is jointly chaired by the secretaries general of the Department of the Taoiseach and the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications. Its membership includes the head civil servants of the government departments with responsibility for key climate action areas. Its key responsibilities include to provide strategic direction and leadership for the climate change agenda and to oversee and report to Government on progress in implementing actions from the annual climate action plans.

Preparation of a long-term climate strategy is a requirement of both national, EU and international law.
Ireland produced a long-term strategy on GHG emissions reduction in 2023 and this was updated in 2024. Both versions were submitted to the UNFCCC.

Long term strategy
Ireland produced a long-term strategy on GHG emissions reduction in 2023 and this was updated in 2024. Both versions were submitted to the UNFCCC.  

Three EU NDCs have been submitted to the UNFCCC to date. The Current EU NDC was submitted to the UNFCCC registry in October 2023.

For GHG emissions, the target in the October 2023 EU NDCs is a net domestic reduction of at least 55% in GHG emissions by 2030, compared to 1990; and to achieve a climate-neutral EU by 2050.
Re. the EU ETS, the October 2023 EU NDC set a target for the EU to reduce emissions from ETS sectors by 62% from 2005 levels by 2030.
The October 2023 EU NDC cited Regulation (EU) 2023/839 which sets a Union-wide binding target of 310 Mt CO2 net removals in the LULUCF sector. Each Member State is allocated a binding national target for 2030 for the increase of net GHG removals which together will deliver the collective EU target of 310 Mt CO2 net removals.

Overall, it is assessed that the long-term strategy (LTS) contains provisions that are conducive to achieving the targets set out in the EU NDC. The reference to the EU ETS target in Section 8.2 of the LTS is out of date as it refers to the December 2020 EU NDC target of a 43% reduction in emissions by 2030, rather than the October 2023 EU NDC target of a 62% reduction by 2030. While there is reference in the LTS to the ambition cycles under the Paris Agreement, this isn't a major focus of the document.

This item assesses the extent to which the long-term strategy (LTS) identifies linkages between SDG 13 (climate action) and the other SDGs; and indicates ways to leverage the positive effects and minimise the negative ones.
In accordance with the Climate Scanner Handbook guidance for assigning a score for this item, it is assessed that 'early implementation' is the appropriate category because there are references to the SDGs in the LTS, but it doesn't (a) identify particular SDGs, (b) state whether impacts are positive or negative or (c) indicate ways to leverage the positive effects and/or minimise the negative ones.

In June 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency published Ireland's first National Climate Change Risk Assessment (NCCRA). The NCCRA provides a comprehensive national overview of the potential risks and opportunities posed by climate change for Ireland. NCCRA integrates scientific and technical knowledge with input from expert stakeholders, to identify, assess, and prioritise climate change risks to build a comprehensive understanding of risks.

In June 2025, the EPA published Ireland's first National Climate Change Risk Assessment (NCCRA). It focuses on the risks to Ireland from hazards caused, intensified, or influenced, by climate change. It was prepared on behalf of the EPA by KPMG Ireland. The NCCRA integrates scientific and technical knowledge with input from expert stakeholders, to identify, assess, and prioritise climate change risks to build a comprehensive understanding of risks.
The methodology was developed in consultation with two expert working groups which focused on climatic and socioeconomic considerations (Working Group 1) and thematic considerations (Working Group 2). WG 2 provided expert scientific and policy advice and insights to identify appropriate themes and associated elements at risk, and to determine key criteria that underpin the NCCRA framework.
The expert groups included scientific bodies such as the EPA, the CSO, the CCAC, DCU, the GSI, the Irish Climate Analysis and Research Units (ICARUS, Maynooth University), the Marine Institute, and Met Éireann.
The methodology included that (a) it should incorporate the most up-to-date available science and information, and (b) it should follow international best practice and take lessons learned from existing NCCRA processes.  
It is assessed that the NCCRA methodology included a broad level of participation by scientific institutions, and an extensive use of available scientific information in the risk mapping.

The key national long and medium-term planning instruments that address climate change are 
 - 	The National Planning Framework
 - 	The National Development Plan
 - 	The National Adaptation Framework 2024
 - 	The Climate Action Plan 2025

National Planning Framework - while the document includes reference to climate risks, it does not appear that climate risks were considered in a systematic and comprehensive way. 
NDP - it does not specifically deal with climate-related risks.
National adaptation framework - Ireland's primary adaptation policy response to the impacts of climate change challenges is set out in the second statutory National Adaptation Framework (NAF) which was approved by Government and published on 5 June 2024. 
Under the NAF, 13 priority sectors under 7 lead departments are required to prepare Sectoral Adaptation Plans (SAPs) under the Climate Act by Q3 2025. Each SAP identifies the key risks faced across the sector and the approach being taken to address these risks and build climate resilience for the future.
Climate Action Plan 2025 - While the document includes reference to climate risks, it does not appear that climate risks were considered in a systematic and comprehensive way. It notes that the new National Climate Change Risk Assessment (subsequently published by the EPA in June 2025) will set out priority climate risks and establish a strong, common basis for national and sectoral climate change risk assessment in Ireland.

It is assessed that there are appropriate horizontal co-ordination mechanisms in place across the most senior levels of Government and that the most relevant actors are included.

There is a Cabinet Committee on Climate Action, Environment and Energy whose membership includes the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste, along with the ministers from the major departments. Other ministers are invited to attend as required. It provides a forum for the discussion of climate policies and delivery mechanisms. It oversees implementation of the programme for Government commitments on the environment, climate action, energy and emergency planning. It is supported by a senior officials group from across government, which meets separately in advance.

The roles of the Climate Action Delivery Board includes to provide strategic direction and leadership for the climate change agenda and to oversee and report to Government on progress in implementing actions from the annual climate action plans.

Other mechanisms for horizontal coordination across Government include a National Adaptation Steering Committee and a Climate Action Unit Network.

The key horizontal coordination mechanisms are the Cabinet Committee on Climate Action, Environment and Energy and the Climate Action Delivery Board.

Jamaica mobilizes private climate finance through PPPs, tax incentives, and blended finance but faces gaps in sector-specific strategies and project development. Key mechanisms include grants and loans (DBJ), direct equity investments (US$4.9M in 2024), credit lines, fund-level investments, and tax incentives like GCT exemptions, import duty reductions, and income tax credits for renewables. Despite progress, scalability challenges remain in private climate finance mobilization.

Current systems provide an overview of activities in government-supported projects, but purely private activities are not comprehensively documented.

The current reporting frameworks focus largely on public and international development partner contributions, with no dedicated mechanism to track private climate finance flows, specific private sector projects, or their outcomes. The audit supports Vision 2030 Jamaica National Development Plan, Goal 4, and National Outcomes 13 and 14, focusing on sustainable management of resources and hazard risk reduction. This is in a context where climate change adaptation is seen as crucial for aligning Jamaica's long-term goals with the UN SDGs and reducing climate vulnerability.

Jamaica does not currently have documented domestic climate litigation cases. Legal actions published by the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) focus on general environmental enforcement, such as breaches of permits and pollution violations. Jamaica participated in international legal proceedings before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on climate obligations, but there is no evidence that national courts adjudicated climate-related claims.

The Ministry of Economic Growth and Job Creation (MEGJC), Climate Change Division (CCD) coordinates Jamaica's climate response locally, regionally, and internationally. Jamaica also established a Climate Change Advisory Board, a Climate Change Focal Point Network, and a National Transparency Working Group to monitor and oversee environmental and climate change plans and activities.

The Climate Change Division oversees national climate initiatives under the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement. In addition, Appendix A of the Climate Change Policy Framework sets out the roles and responsibilities of the leading and supporting institutions for executing key climate actions.

There are no contradictory or overlapping mandates. The CCPF and Terms of References for the Climate Change Advisory Board (CCAB) and Focal Point Network clearly delineate roles for coordination, implementation, and oversight. However, while responsibilities are well-defined and not inherently contradictory, the large number of actors increases reliance on effective coordination to avoid operational inefficiencies and ensure real-time data sharing and transparency.

The Ministry of Economic Growth and Job Creation, through its Climate Change Division (CCD), leads Jamaica's climate change response. The CCD oversees climate initiatives, serves as the Designated National Authority for the Green Climate Fund, and mobilizes other government bodies via the Climate Change Focal Point Network (CCFPN). It coordinates monitoring, reporting, and verification efforts to ensure a unified national approach to climate action.

Jamaica's Long-Term Emissions Reduction and Climate-Resilience Strategy (LTS) for 2050 was completed in November 2023 and has been approved for submission to the UNFCCC by way of Cabinet Decision No. 29/24.

Jamaica's LTS (2050) and NDC (2020) are highly compatible and mutually reinforcing. The LTS effectively operationalizes the NDC's medium-term goals while expanding the ambition for 2050 in alignment with international climate targets. The LTS extends the NDC goals into the mid-century timeline, explicitly referencing the NDC as its baseline. Both strategies emphasize sustainable development co-benefits, gender mainstreaming, and climate financing, reinforcing coherence.

Jamaica's 2050 Long-term Emissions Reduction and Climate Resilient Strategy incorporates a holistic approach to climate action that goes beyond SDG 13-Climate Action to integrate and advance multiple SDGS (SDGs 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15 and 17). By embedding economic, social, and environmental sustainability into its strategy, it aligns climate resilience with broader sustainable development objectives ensuring that climate actions yield co-benefits across multiple dimensions of development.

Jamaica's long- and medium-term planning instruments incorporate climate risks, particularly through Vision 2030, the LTS 2050, National Communications, and Circular 34. These frameworks mandate climate risk consideration across sectors and national investments. The extent of integration is comprehensive, with both qualitative and quantitative approaches to risk reflected in policy, sector strategies, and financial regulation.

The Climate Change Policy Framework 2023 establishes mechanisms to facilitate horizontal (within national government) coordination through the Climate Change Focal Point Network and the Climate Change Advisory Board. Both the CCFPN and CCAB operate under the leadership of the Climate Change Division within the Ministry responsible for climate change, ensuring high-level government oversight.

assessment_comment: There is need for increasing the capacity and expertise at both the national and parish levels. Although local representatives are included, their involvement needs to be strengthened through targeted capacity-building efforts. There is need for tools and mechanisms to integrate climate change considerations into local decision-making. The framework suggests that a local government network be developed to address weak parish level coordination.

Vertical coordination is recognized in policy and some structures include local actors. However, the Local Government Network remains under development and there is limited evidence of regular interaction, such as meeting minutes or reports. Without a formal, documented mechanism for consistent engagement, the dynamic of vertical coordination remains weak and insufficiently operational.

The CCD, as national focal point, coordinates implementation of the CCPF, which establishes mechanisms like the CCAB and CCFPN for stakeholder engagement and cross-sectoral integration. The CCAB provides technical policy advice, while the CCFPN supports mainstreaming climate change into sectoral plans and facilitates implementation of climate actions across ministries and agencies.

The Climate Change Policy Framework, Biennial Update Report and National Communications all indicate that civil society, the private sector and academia are represented in the participation mechanisms for stakeholder engagement in the design and implementation of climate strategies, policies and plans.

Jamaica has institutional mechanisms for stakeholder engagement in climate strategies, such as the CCAB and the CCFPN. However, inconsistent interactions were noted, with the CCAB holding fewer than required meetings and limited evidence of CCFPN's activities. Capacity-building efforts were often led by external entities, reducing feedback integration. The government aims to enhance regular collaboration and secure funding to improve stakeholder engagement.

Jamaica has identified vulnerable groups including women, youth, the elderly, rural communities, and small-scale farmers in its climate policy and reports. The Climate Change Policy Framework and national reports highlight their susceptibility to climate impacts and call for targeted public policies, especially in agriculture, health, and livelihoods. However, further operational detail on how their needs are addressed in implementation is limited.

Mechanisms for climate strategy participation in Jamaica include the Climate Change Advisory Board involving public and private sectors, civil society, and academia. However, local governments and grassroots communities have limited involvement. The NC3 highlights insufficiently structured mechanisms for vulnerable groups like coastal communities and small farmers. The Biennial Update Report stresses the need for broader engagement, especially for women, children, and persons with disabilities.

Jamaica's climate strategies embed equity by targeting vulnerable groups such as women, youth, the elderly, and rural communities. The Climate Change Policy Framework and NDC include gender-responsive measures and emphasize inclusive, sustainable adaptation. Vision 2030 also promotes social protection and equity. These documents establish clear provisions to reduce harm and ensure that climate actions deliver equitable benefits.

Jamaica has formal mechanisms for tracking NDC commitments, including GHG inventories and regular reporting via BURs and NCs, coordinated by the Climate Change Division (CCD). The Climate Change Policy Framework (CCPF) assigns monitoring roles to CCD and the Environment and Risk Management Branch (ERMB), including indicator development and annual reporting to Parliament.

While Jamaica's BUR and NC3 establish processes for using climate monitoring data in policymaking, improvements are needed to make these processes more structured and systematic. Key areas for enhancement include public communication, consistent use of feedback, inter-agency cooperation, and implementation capacity. Both reports emphasize the need for better integration of monitoring feedback into future national climate strategies
Jamaica fulfilled transparency obligations as a SIDS under the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement, having submitted National Communications (NC1-NC3) and the Biennial Update Report (BUR1).

Jamaica's NSDI provides access to climate-relevant data but does not track progress on national climate objectives. The NRIP is non-functional. Public reports exist but are not updated frequently or tied to specific targets. There is no regulation ensuring non-state actors' right to request climate policy information, limiting transparency and public oversight of national commitments.

Jamaica's transparency mechanisms for climate data and policy are not easily accessed or understood by the public. Issues like outdated data, and insufficient coordination hinder accessibility. The Climate Change Division faces challenges in data collection and dissemination, affecting overall transparency and public understanding of climate policy progress. Information on climate action is scattered across various websites and systems.

Article 4.9 of the Paris Agreement requires each party to communicate an updated NDC every five years. Jamaica submitted its updated NDC in June 2020, within the five-year cycle since its previous submission in November 2015, satisfying the requirements of Article 4.9 of the Paris Agreement.

The 2020 NDC reflects greater ambition, both in terms of sectoral scope and the level of GHG reduction commitments. Specifically, the total emissions reduction in 2030 is projected to be 1.8 to 2.0 MtCO2e lower than business-as-usual, compared to a reduction of 1.1 to 1.5 MtCO2e in the 2015 NDC. The 2020 NDC uses updated data and methodologies, applying 2006 IPCC Guidelines and expanding the sectors covered, showing a progression in reporting clarity and transparency.

The 2015 NDC focused solely on the energy sector, promoting energy efficiency, infrastructure modernization and renewable energy. The 2020 NDC expands to include land use change and forestry, while enhancing actions in the energy sector, with consideration of the waste and agriculture. It adopts a cross-sectoral approach by embedding adaptation in mitigation efforts, such as forest preservation for water and soil quality, and renewable energy reducing air pollution, benefiting public health.

Jamaica's BUR and NC3 indicate several public policies have been mapped to their corresponding impacts on national GHG emissions. Jamaica's Long-range Energy Alternative Planning model evaluates emissions trajectories and identifies energy-related mitigation strategies. The LULUCF sector is a significant part of Jamaica's GHG inventory, and the Forest Management Plans are explicitly mapped to their role in mitigation, showing their impact on emissions from deforestation and reforestation.

Jamaica has outlined clear goals and strategies to curb GHG emissions, with a particular focus on the energy, forestry, and waste sectors. Jamaica's pivotal policies have been identified, mapped and aligned with the targets set in the NDC. However, challenges remain in ensuring cross-sectoral coherence, especially in underdeveloped areas like agriculture and waste management. Nonetheless, the strategies reflect a clear commitment to reducing emissions and increasing resilience to climate change.

Jamaica's sectoral plans/programs for emission reduction are comprehensive, covering key sectors such as energy, land use, agriculture, and waste management. Actions to achieve sectoral emission targets include renewable energy capacity, modernizing the energy grid, forest conservation, reforestation projects, improved land management practices, adoption of climate-resilient crop varieties, increasing recycling rates, promoting biogas production. There's alignment with National Strategies.

Jamaica does not have a National Adaptation Plan but has commenced activities to develop one. A Ja-NAP project unit was established and consultants contracted to undertake capacity building activities. Notwithstanding, Jamaica has been engaged in adaptation planning and actions and had developed a Climate Change Policy Framework. Jamaica's Adaptation Communication outlines progress in national adaptation actions highlighting gaps in adaptation, finance, technical capacity, and technology.

Jamaica has prioritized key sectors such as water resources, tourism, agriculture, health, coastal resources, and human settlements in its climate change adaptation strategies. Other sectors like transport, energy, forestry, fisheries, finance, and waste management are also recognized as important for adaptation efforts. The adaptation plans are comprehensive, covering critical sectors for resilience and aligning with national goals like Vision 2030 and Climate Change Policy Framework.

In the last five years, Jamaica developed and updated several adaptation plans, sector-specific strategies and policy frameworks. Jamaica also developed 15 location-specific disaster risk management and climate change adaptation plans.

Jamaica's national policies for the energy sector, specifically in electricity and transportation, consider the reduction of emissions and have set clear objectives toward this goal. The objectives in the electricity sector are well-defined with concrete targets for renewable energy adoption and energy efficiency. The transportation sector has specific targets for EV adoption but could improve the detail around biofuels and public transportation initiatives.

The strategies and actions outlined in Jamaica's renewable energy and electric mobility policies demonstrate a well-structured approach to achieving the 2030 targets. The IRP and EV policy include detailed implementation plans, roles, and responsibilities for stakeholders aimed at achieving the set targets of 50% renewable energy share by 2030 and 12% private and 16% public EV penetration by 2030, along with the complete conversion of the government vehicle fleet to EVs.

Key challenges include securing investment for renewable projects, managing grid stability with increased intermittent renewable sources and upgrading the transmission and distribution network. The EV policy identifies barriers like high initial costs of EVs, limited charging infrastructure and public unfamiliarity with EV technology. The policies attempt to map out challenges/mitigation strategies that  will require continuous effort and adaptation to emerging technological and market condition

Jamaica established monitoring and evaluation mechanisms across its energy and transportation policies. These mechanisms were to ensure that the progress towards renewable energy adoption, EV penetration, and emissions reductions were systematically tracked.

Jamaica's water sector adaptation policies address climate vulnerabilities like droughts, floods, and sea-level rise, focusing on resilience and resource management. The Climate Change Adaptation Plan and National Water Sector Policy integrate climate resilience emphasising Integrated Water Resources Management and vulnerable communities. Detailed actions include early warning systems, hazard management and maintenance standards, supported by a vulnerability assessment to target key risks.

Jamaica developed the Disaster Risk Management Policy and Strategy that is designed to integrate DRR and CCA into national development. This policy addresses vulnerabilities, especially to natural hazards like hurricanes, flooding, and drought, aiming to minimize disaster impacts through resilience-building measures. The National DRM Plan further supports this framework by providing a detailed approach to  managing risks across the national, parish, and community levels.

For inputs and activities, actions include establishing early warning systems, mandating additional storage facilities, enforcing no-build zones, and implementing grey-water systems for reuse. For outputs and roles, the Adaptation Plan for the water sector assigns roles to multiple agencies, including the Water Resources Authority and the MEGJC. The actions are relatively robust as they specify responsible entities for implementation and outline required outputs.

Jamaica's disaster risk management frameworks establish clear roles and expected outputs for key agencies such as ODPEM and local authorities, especially in hazard mapping, community preparedness, and disaster risk financing. However, while specific activities and institutional responsibilities were identified, inputs, such as detailed resource allocations, were not consistently articulated across all actions, resulting in a partial fulfilment of comprehensive planning elements.

Jamaica has clearly mapped key implementation challenges, including funding constraints, coordination gaps and limited technical capacity. Measures to address these, such as capacity building, resource mobilization, improved coordination, and international support, are identified across multiple documents (DRM Policy, NC3, BUR1, AdapCom). These are consistently recognized as barriers to achieving adaptation goals, showing a structured approach to diagnosing and addressing implementation hurdles.

Jamaica has clearly mapped water sector adaptation challenges, including funding gaps, coordination issues, and limited technical capacity. The Water Sector Adaptation Plan and National Water Policy outline measures such as capacity building, financing, and coordination to address these. Impacts, such as delayed action and reduced resilience, are acknowledged. This reflects a structured approach to identifying and tackling key barriers in adaptation implementation.

Jamaica's Disaster Risk Management framework includes a well-defined monitoring and evaluation (M&E) system. The DRM Policy and associated plans specify responsible agencies, key performance indicators, and processes for both annual monitoring and mid-term and end-of-plan evaluations. The framework also outlines mechanisms for using M&E results to inform decision-making and improve disaster risk management strategies.

Jamaica's water sector has defined monitoring frameworks, with key indicators, responsible bodies, and provisions for periodic reviews set out in the Water Adaptation Plan and National Water Policy. These mechanisms support tracking adaptation progress and institutional accountability. While operational details vary, the framework reflects a structured, ongoing approach to monitoring and informing water sector adaptation.

assessment_comment: The government in its budget has provided for climate actions across sectors to realize the adaptation and mitigation goals. However, the budgets do not identify carbon-intensive actions. Additionally, it has not identified or calculated the perverse subsidies

The government has no taxonomy on what can be considered as direct climate finance. Additonally the governemnt does not have a finance tracking system. However,climate finance was tracked manually up to year 2018

The government has no taxonomy on what can be considered as indirect climate finance. Additionally, the government does not have a finance tracking system.  The National Treasury issued a Circular in 2020 requiring all government entities to track and report on their climate expenditures. However, climate finance was tracked manually up to 2018.

The Government considered climate finance tracking in its Integrated Financial Management System (IFMIS) but the segment is not yet operationalized. The National Treasury last published a report on climate finance expenditures in 2021 for the Financial Year 2017/2018. The National Treasury issued a Circular in 2020 requiring government entities to track and report on their climate finance expenditures but the Circular has not been implemented

As the country is not included in the Annex II of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has no obligation to provide financial resources to other countries. In this sense, the assessment of this item is not necessary.
