The Government has identified sources of international climate finance funding and has a breakdown of funding pegged on adaptation and mitigation interventions as presented in the Second NDC. However, there is no segregation of international and government funding in the cost of activities per sector. It is presented as a block figure in the Implementation Matrix of the NCCAP.

The National Policy on Climate Finance has outlined the alternative sources of international climate finance and the possible activities they can support. The National Treasury has been designated for the Green Climate Fund and the National Environment Management Authority as the National Implementing Entity (NIE) that has been accredited by the GCF to access funding for the implementation of eligible activities approved by the GCF.The government has mobilised funds from international sources

Except for the Financing Locally-Led Climate Action Program in which the National Treasury specifically mobilizes climate finance from donors and disburses to the county for local-level climate action, mobilization of climate finance in the country is not targeted. While at the entity level, the funds are used on climate action, the National Treasury mobilizes them as a donor fund without tagging it as climate finance. Tracking of climate finance then becomes a challenge

The governement does not have a reporting mechanism in place for international climate finance received. However,reporting is done as per the specific requirements of the donor.This is done according to reporting frameworks of the donors.

The Government has enacted Climate Finance Policy in which one of the proposed interventions for mobilizing climate finance is to develop robust and flexible public financial instruments to support and leverage private sector investments in low carbon and climate resilient activities. In this regard, the government has drafted Kenya Sovereign Green Bond Framework which once finalized will be used to mobilize private finance.

The National Treasury issued a Circular in 2020 requiring all non-state actors to report on their climate finance expenditures. The circular has guidance on how to tack and report on climate finance;however, it remains unimplemented.

The National Treasury issued a Circular in 2020 requiring all non-state actors to report on their climate finance expenditures. The circular has guidance on how to tack and report on climate finance;however, it remains unimplemented.
The country has enacted the Climate Change Act, which is very comprehensive

The Climate Change Act has incorporated the overarching goals of Art.2 of Paris Agreement where under Part 3 (Objects and Purposes), National and County Governments are obligated to enhance adaptive capacity and promote low carbon technologies to reduce GHG emissions. The Act has provisions on internal reporting requirements but is silent on international reporting. The Act has also not enshrined the requirements of Art.4 on preparation of Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).

The Climate Change Act provides for mainstreaming of climate change into sectoral strategies, action plans and other policy documents both at national and county levels of government. Section 6(a) of the Climate Change Act mandates the National Climate Change Council to ensure the mainstreaming of the climate change function by the national and county governments

There is the Departmental Committee on Environment, Forestry and Mining in the National Assembly whose mandate as per the Second Schedule of the Standing Orders cuts across the following subject areas: climate change, environment management and conservation, forestry, mining and natural resources, pollution, waste management. However, the a review of its activities shows that the Committee only discussed climate change issues during the enactment of the Climate Change (Amendment) Bill, 2023.

SAI Kenya is currently undertaking an audit on Implementation of the National Adaptation Plan under the Global Cooperative Audit on Climate Adaptation Actions (CCAA). The SAI has also conducted other climate change related audits in the areas of: disaster risk management, forest conservation and water resources management.

Kenya has Environmental and Lands Court which was Established under the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 to hear and determine disputes relating to the environment and the use and occupation of, and title to land. According to the UNEP's 2023 Global Climate Litigation Report, Kenya recorded two (2) climate change litigation as of December 2022
Kenya has a clear governance structure for climate action which is well outlined in the Climate Change Act

The Climate Change Act has established three levels of responsibilities. The National Climate Change Council is mandated with overall leadership while the Cabinet Secretary responsible for climate change is responsible for formulation of policies, strategies and actions. The Directorate of Climate Change is responsible for coordination. NEMA on the other hand has the responsibility for monitoring and enforcement of climate duties.

The roles of the different government actors in climate change are clearly defined hence there are no overlaps. Sections 6,8,9(8)(2-g), 15(5)(a-f), 17 and 19 details the responsibilities of each actor.

The Climate Change Act establishes the National Climate Change Council Chaired by the President and his Deputy as the Vice-Chair. The Council's membership is composed of key government ministries, private sector and civil society representatives, and a representative of marginalized and vulnerable groups. The Council provides an overarching national climate change coordination mechanism. However, the Council currently is not yet constituted.
The Country has  produced a long term strategy for the period 2022-2050

LTS is elaborate and consistent with the actions identified in the NDC for reduction of emissions up to 2030 and even up to 2050.The said actions and activities are detailed across all the sectors that contribute to emissions. The NDC mitigation ambition raising mechanism is included in the LTS.
The Long Term Strategy (LTS) makes minimal reference to SDG. Only SDG 6, "clean water and sanitation" is referred to.

The Technical Analysis Report,2020 for the updated NDC and Adaptation Technical Analysis Report in 2023 have mapped the risks and impacts of climate change across the following sector i.e. agriculture,tourism, population, urbanization and housing, gender, vulnerable groups and youth and manufacturing and trade. However, the mapping is general, focusing only on likely impacts.

The mapping of risks makes reference to reports and data produced by scientific bodies such as IPCC and academia; however, there is no evidence of direct involvement of scientific bodies in the mapping of risks.

The vision 2023 IV Medium Term Plan has mainstreamed climate change in the form of flagship projects targeting adaptation and mitigation without highlighting the climate risks. However, Climate Change Action  Plans highlight climate risks in each priority sector. The National Adaptation Plan also highlights climate risks

Climate Change Act, Section 5 establishes the National Climate Change Council which is charged with overarching national climate change co-ordination. The Council is chaired by the President. Membership of the Council, however, excludes the Ministry of Agriculture, despite agriculture sector being the large contributor to emissions and most vulnerable to climate change in the Country. While established in the Act, the Council is yet to be constituted.
The National Climate Change Council is not yet constituted

Section 7 (2)  of the Act, provides for representation of the County Government in the National Climate Change Council through the Chairperson of the Council of Governors. However, mechanisms to facilitate operational vertical coordination at technical level does not exist. Besides, the Council is yet to be constituted
The National Climate Change Council is not yet constituted

One of the guiding principles of climate action in the Country as outlined in Section 4(2)(f) of Climate Change Act is ensure participation and consultation with stakeholders in accordance with the Schedule. However, the Schedule only limits it seeking of views which mostly happens during planning stage.

The Act provides for representation of the youth, civil society organizations, vulnerable and marginalized groups and the academia in the National Council for Climate Change. However, the Council is not yet constituted.
The Council is yet to be consitituted

The Government has not done mapping of the vulnerable and marginalized groups. However, interviews with various government entities revealed that ad hoc mapping is always done for inclusion in public participation during implementation of climate change activities.

As a guiding principle, Section 4(2)(d) requires all government entities to ensure equity and social inclusion in allocation of effort, costs and benefits to cater for special needs, vulnerabilities, capabilities, disparities and responsibilities. The Act also provide for representation of the vulnerable and marginalized groups in the National Climate Change Council, which is the the overarching climate change coordination body in the country. However, the Council is yet to be constituted.

The National Climate Change Action Plan (2018-2022), the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and the National Adaptation Plan (2015-2030) has tried to address the equity consideration as far as vulnerable groups are concerned

A monitoring mechanism for climate action is elaborated in the Climate Change Act, 2016. However, operationalization of the same has not been done. Data is requested from actors on a need basis only as a way of facilitating UNFCCC reporting requirements
Monitoring as currently done is only for data collection purposes and does not provide for feedback

Kenya submitted the Third National Communication and first Biennial Update Report in December 2024. The Second National Communication was in 2015 hence the Third National Communication should have been submitted in 2019.

The climate Change Act, 2016 has provisions for reporting on climate actions both by national government entities and county government. It also requires reporting to Parliament on progress on climate action. However, these provisions are yet to be implemented

The Ministry of Environment, Climate Change and Forestry used to operate a Climate Change Knowledge Portal from where the public would access information on climate change. However, website was not operational by the time of the assessment
Kenya submitted its updated NDC in 2020

Mitigation targets on emission reduction have been increased from 30% to 32% by 2030
Prioritized Adaptation Programmes in the 2nd NDC have been expanded and are specific to each sector
The 1st NDC identified financial requirements for mitigation and adaptation measures as a block figure while the 2nd NDC has the inclusion of financial commitments including own source (13%) and international support (87%) 
The NDC provides additional information for clarity, transparency and understanding

Kenya implements its NDC through the National Climate Change Action Plan (NCCAP). NCCAP 2018-2022 had priority climate change actions with objectives and targets for each of the main mitigation and adaptation sectors. An updated NCCAP covering the period 2023-2027 is currently under developed and follows the same approach.
The Government has mapped key mitigation policies across the mitigation sectors as presented in the Third National Communication and National Climate Change Action Plans.

Kenya has developed the National Long Term Low Emission Development Strategy,2022-2050. The strategy has clearly set out goals and strategies on how greenhouse gas emissions will be reduced. Actions to be implemented in all the sectors contributing to GHG emissions are clearly laid out.

The Strategy is relatively new (became operational in 2023) does not have sector specific implementation plans. However, the Country has sectoral mitigation policies and plans geared towards emissions reduction as mapped out in the Third National Communication
The country has a National Adaptation Plan covering the period 2015-2030
NAP includes all key sectors for adaptation: Agriculture and food security, infrastructure and transport, water and sanitation as well as environment. It includes other sectors as well.

Kenya has not updated its NAP since 2015; however the government relies on using the National Climate Change Action Plan (NCCAP) to respond to any emerging issues in climate change. NCCAP is updated every five years. The last NCCAP covered 2018-2022. NCCAP 2023-2027 has been launched for implementation; however it is yet to be officially signed by the president.
The National REDD+ Strategy, 2021 recognizes the role of forestry in emissions reduction. However, it does not outline specific emission reduction objectives and targets.
The Kenya Climate Smart Agriculture Strategy (2017-2026) outlines goals, objectives and strategies for reduction of emissions in agriculture sector.

The Implementation Matrix in the Kenya Climate Smart Strategy (2017-2026) has information on strategies, activities, indicators and responsibilities. The information on output with clear measurable targets is lacking.
Though not specific to emission reductions, the Strategy outlines strategic objectives, investment area and actions which if implemented will result to emission reduction

There is some mapping of challenges presented as weaknesses in the SWOT analysis under policy legal and institutional framework. Measures to address the weaknesses have been identified; however, impacts of these weaknesses have not been identified
Policy implementation challenges have not been mapped

There is the Kenya Climate Smart Agriculture Monitoring and Evaluation Framework (2018-2027), however; it is biased towards monitoring. It outlines parties responsible for monitoring, indicators to be monitored. The  reporting timelines is also indicated as monthly, quarterly and annually
While the strategy has a chapter on monitoring of REDD+ activities, it is silent on how its implementation should be monitored

The Government has developed various policies and strategies in the water sector, all of which consider issues related to building resilience in the water sector. Key among these policies are: the National Water Policy, 2021; the National Water Resources Strategy (2020-2025); and the National Water Harvesting and Storage Strategy (2020-2025)

The ministry of Agriculture developed a Policy (Agricultural Policy,2021). The policy was developed against the backrop of current impacts of climate change and the challenge this poses to agriculture production.The policy vouches for crop diversification and irrigation to enhance food production and food & nutrition security.Further, the government has developed Climate Smart Agriculture Strategy 2017 - 2026. This strategy details raft of adapatation actions to be undertaken in the sector.

The Agriculture Policy, 2021 only has information on activities and responsibilities for implementation. The Kenya Climate Smart Agriculture Strategy on the other hand has information on the inputs, activities and responsibilities for achieving the adaptation goals and objectives. The outputs are presented the the form of indicators but does not give details of measurable targets
The policy documents have information on intended objectives/strategies, activities for achieving them, responsibility for implementation and to some extent indicators for measuring achievement.
No evidence of mapping of policy implementation challenges found
Policy implementation challenges has not been mapped
No monitoring and evaluation mechanisms

Both the National Water Resources Strategy (2020-2025) and the Water Harvesting and Storage Strategy (2020-2025) have some provisions on monitoring but is silent on evaluation. While these policy documents state what needs to be monitored, they are silent on how actual monitoring is to be carried out. No actual monitoring mechanism was found.

Latvia's approach to tracking direct climate finance is influenced by its membership in the European Union and its participation in international frameworks. While there is no single, nationally developed "taxonomy" of direct climate finance in the public domain, the country adheres to and uses the EU taxonomy.
The EU taxonomy is a classification system designed to help investors and companies determine which economic activities are environmentally sustainable. It is a key component of the EU's broader sustainable finance framework and aims to direct capital toward activities that are essential for the transition to a net-zero economy by 2050.
To be considered environmentally sustainable under the taxonomy, an economic activity must meet certain conditions, for example, it must make a "substantial contribution" to one of six environmental objectives (e.g., climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation).
The government's systems for tracking and accounting are primarily linked to reporting obligations for international funds, but no comprehensive national system exists for all public (including domestic) funds yet.

There is a plan to develop a "green budget" marking methodology by 2026 in Latvia which will be based on the EU's sustainable finance taxonomy regulation.
Beginning in 2026, there is a plan to assess and report on climate-related budget expenditures involving a "Climate Declaration"  that will be attached to the state budget law.

There is no taxonomy established of what can be considered as indirect climate finance.
The EU Taxonomy only covers direct contributions, i.e. activities that directly contribute to mitigation or adaptation under established technical criteria.
There is no national system that allow the tracking and accounting of indirect climate finance.

Latvia has a robust and systematic process for identifying its needs for international climate finance, primarily driven by its adherence to EU regulations. This process is highly detailed, includes cost estimations, and is regularly reported to the European Commission.
Detailed and Costed Needs: Latvia's National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) and its Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) are the key documents that outline its climate goals, a wide range of specific measures, and the estimated costs required to achieve them. 
Systematic Identification: The development of these plans is a structured and systematic process, involving multiple ministries and public consultations. The needs identified in these documents are directly linked to EU targets and national development strategies. The process is not ad-hoc; it is a top-down, government-wide approach to resource allocation for climate action.
Public Reporting: The Latvian government reports its climate finance needs and plans to the European Commission as part of the EU's governance framework. These reports, such as the NECP, are publicly available and transparently communicate the country's strategic and financial requirements for its green transition.
According to the European Commission's assessment of the Latvia's National Energy and Climate Plan it is not clear whether all policies up to 2030 are included in the assessment of investment needs.

Identified Sources: Latvia has a clear understanding of the various international sources available, including the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the Cohesion Fund, the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the Just Transition Fund, as well as other mechanisms like the European Investment Bank (EIB) and Emission Allowances Auctioning Instruments (EAAI - revenue from the auctioned allowances of the Emissions Trading System).
Mechanisms and Structures: Dedicated government bodies, such as the Ministry of Finance, act as the managing authorities for EU funds. These institutions have the necessary expertise, staff, and procedures to interact with EU institutions, prepare required project documents, and manage the application process. For EAAI the managing authority is the Ministry of Climate and Energy.
According to the European Commission's assessment of the Latvia's National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) and the audit:
- the plan does not provide a breakdown for public (including national and international) and private investments;
- the information provided in the plan is not sufficient to assess a potential financing gap with respect to the investment needs, or how this would be filled.
Other instruments, like revenue from the auctioned allowances of the Emissions Trading System, are also used, while in the audit it was found that planning (including mobilization) and usage is not being done in a proper manner.

Latvia has well-developed mechanisms and systems to oversee the disbursement and use of international climate funds, which are largely dictated by the stringent oversight and audit requirements of the European Union.
Tracking Funding: EU-funded projects are subject to rigorous monitoring and control systems. The government can track the international climate funding received, its allocation, and its disbursement to specific projects. Public portals, such as the EU Funds homepage, provide a level of transparency for tracking these funds.
Identifying Activities: The structure of funding programs like the Recovery and Resilience Facility, other Eropean Union structural funds as well as the revenue from the Emissions Trading System ensures that funds are tied to specific, pre-approved projects and activities. It is possible to trace which activities the funds were used for, as demonstrated by the detailed breakdowns in the Recovery and Resilience Plan (e.g., funding for sustainable transport, building renovations, and grid modernization).
Identifying and Accomplishing Objectives: The funding framework requires the government to set clear milestones and targets for each project. The EU's monitoring and evaluation process assesses whether these objectives were met, which provides a mechanism to verify the accomplishment of the intended goals.

Latvia has regular reporting system for the use of international climate finance, fulfilling the demanding requirements set by its funding sources and making this information public.
Mechanisms for Reporting: The government has established formal mechanisms to report on how it has spent EU funds and the revenue from the Emissions Trading System. This includes regular reports to the European Commission as part of the Recovery and Resilience Facility and the broader EU cohesion policy frameworks.
Meeting Reporting Requirements: Latvia's reporting is designed to meet the detailed requirements of the EU institutions that manage the funds. This ensures compliance with established standards for financial and project-based reporting, including demonstrating progress toward milestones and targets.
Regular and Public Reporting: The government issues these reports on a regular basis. These reports are publicly available on government websites and EU portals, providing transparency to a broad range of stakeholders. For instance, reports on the implementation of the EU funds (including Recovery and Resilience Facility) and on the use of the Emission Trading System revenue are public documents.

However, there is limited evidence of a national framework specifically designed to mobilize private climate finance.
Some relevant initiatives do exist, particularly via EU-level instruments such as:
- InvestEU and European Investment Fund (EIF) green financing instruments that co-finance private-led projects in Latvia;
- Support for energy efficiency investments in buildings, which sometimes involve private co-financing (e.g., commercial retrofitting, industrial decarbonization projects).
State-owned development finance institution ALTUM plays a key role by offering financial instruments like loans and guarantees to private sector.
However, these mechanisms are largely EU-driven, not nationally initiated or coordinated by Latvian institutions.

Despite these initiatives, a comprehensive framework to attract private funding seems to be lacking.

Tracking of private climate finance is not a comprehensive, government-wide process in Latvia.
Fragmented Tracking: Tracking is carried out by specific institutions for their own activities. For example, Latvijas Banka (Bank of Latvia) publishes its own climate-related financial disclosures report for its non-monetary policy portfolios, including Scope 3 emissions data. Similarly, ALTUM tracks the GHG emission reductions from the projects it finances through its Green Bonds.
Tracking of private co-financing is likely embedded in individual project-level reporting (e.g., under Resilience and Recovery Facility-funded programs or other EU funded programms), but not rolled up into national-level climate finance accounting.
No National System: There is no centralized, national system for tracking all private climate finance across the country.

Institution-Specific Reporting: Reporting is primarily conducted by the institutions directly involved in mobilizing funds. Latvijas Banka issues annual reports on its climate-related disclosures, and ALTUM reports on the projects funded through its Green Bonds.
Publicly Available but Incomplete: While these reports are public, they do not provide a complete picture of all private climate finance in Latvia. Actions include:

All four elements are present at least partly:

Per the Law on Climate Change Management , the Climate Change Programme secures extra funds for climate governance. These funds, held in a State Treasury account and part of the national budget, support targets in the National Progress Plan, National Climate Change Management Agenda, NECP, and national development programs.

Lithuania does not have a national definition of climate finance. In April 2020, the EU Council adopted a regulation establishing an EU-wide classification system, known as the "taxonomy," which includes the following categories:
a)mitigation
b)adaptation
c)Sustainable use and protection of water resources
d)Transition to a circular economy
e)Pollution prevention and control
f)Protection of biodiversity
National development programs include specific measures covering all taxonomy categories.

A) Lithuanian official documents do not define the term "indirect climate finance." B) Currently, separate data is collected on funded measures, and information on total funds and public expenditures related to climate change is summarized. While "taxonomy" categories exist, expenditures are not assigned to these categories in information systems.

Government reports, though public, don't cover all four categories: direct and indirect climate finance, carbon-intensive budgets, and harmful subsidies. A 2014 Ministry of Environment study addresses harmful subsidies, but no full financial reports exist. The Climate Change Program report details measures and finances, including GHG reduction, but omits harmful subsidies, as they're outside its scope.

Law on Climate Change Management states that the funds of the Climate Change Programme may be used for climate change mitigation and adaption measures in third countries in accordance with the EU legislation, the UNFCCC, the Kyoto Protocol and other international agreements. Since 2011, part of these funds has been allocated annually to projects in developing countries. Commitments are increasing: 4.6 EUR in 2017-2020, 8 EUR planned for 2021-2025.

The 2022-2025 Climate Change Program investment plan allocates 8 000 000 EUR for developing countries. This support leverages public funds to attract private sector investments in low-carbon technologies through bilateral cooperation projects, facilitating technology transfer to developing countries. Annual reports provide information on the planned and actual GHG reductions achieved through development cooperation projects.

Annual Climate Change Program funding reports provide detailed information on state financial support for developing countries. In line with Regulation (EU) No 2018/1999, Article 19(3) and Annex VIII(2), as well as Implementing Regulation 2020/1208 (Annexes III, IV, V), Lithuania prepares and submits reports to the European Commission by September 30 each year, complying with the Paris Agreement's reporting requirements.

In line with the 2021-2027 EU cohesion policy regulations and Strategic Planning Methodology, ex-ante assessments must be conducted before implementing financial instruments. Based on Regulation No. 2018/0196, Article 52 requirements, ex-ante assessments were carried out were carried out to determine financial instrument needs for adaptation and mitigation. All assessments are publicly available on the Ministry of Finance website.

Lithuania has established procedures to mobilize EU climate funds through national planning aligned with EU regulations. The 2021-2027 EU Investment Programme, NECP, and other documents identify funding sources (e.g. Modernisation Fund, JTF, RePowerEU). Dedicated entities (e.g. MoF Green Investment Unit) and structures coordinate planning, while ministries submit expenditure plans under required EU formats.

An annual report on the National Progress Plan details progress fund investments by source, including EU funds. The Ministry of Finance tracks expenditures based on Recovery and Resilience Facility and Cohesion Policy classifications. Data on planned EU funding (2021-2027) is on the EC's DG REGIO website. While reports enhance financial transparency, Lithuania's allocation and impact of EU climate funds are not sufficiently disclosed publicly.

The updated National Energy and Climate Action Plan 2021-30 includes financing certain measures with private funds, such as "Public Building Renovation" and "Expansion of AEI Production Facilities." According to the Ministry of Finance, 1.5 bn EUR in private funds is expected for climate-related measures. The 2023-26 Green Finance Action Plan aims to mobilize public and private funds, targeting an additional 900 million for green projects by 2026. From 2021-2022, 220 million EUR was attracted.

The Climate Policy Group of the Ministry of Environment of the Republic of Lithuania collects financial data on implemented measures by funding sources, including private funds, and submits it to the European Commission. The attraction of private funds through financial instruments is carried out by the private limited company "ILTE," established by the Lithuanian Government. However, ILTE reports do not summarize information on private investments attracted for climate goals.

In order to ensure the implementation in the international agreements and the EU legal acts defined targets for Lithuania, on 30 June 2021 by the Decree No XIV-490 of the Parliament of the Republic of Lithuania approved the National Climate Change Management Agenda  which lays down the targets and objectives for climate change mitigation and adaptation by 2050.

The Environmental Protection Committee of the Lithuanian Parliament reviews climate-related issues annually. In the 2023 spring session, it discussed the 2022 Climate Change Program funds usage report, while in the 2022 spring session, it reviewed the 2021 report and the draft Climate Change Program 2022-2025 investment plan. The National Climate Change Committee also supports coordination of climate efforts, ensuring regular parliamentary engagement on climate policies.

The National Audit Office of Lithuania  conducts audits on various public sector activities, including those related to climate change. While specific audit reports focusing solely on climate change may not be readily available, the office has examined environmental and energy policies, which encompass climate-related issues.

Currently, there is no publicly available data on the exact number of climate change-related cases in Lithuanian courts. However, there have been some legal actions related to climate change, such as international lawsuits involving governments and climate activists, as well as cases regarding corporate responsibility for climate action. One notable case involved a ruling by the Hague Appeals Court recognizing the responsibility of companies to take action against climate change.

Lithuania has established a national government structure to address climate change issues. The Seimas (Parliament), the Government, and ministries - including the Ministry of Environment, Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Energy, Ministry of Economy and Innovation, Ministry of Transport and Communications, Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and others - formulate and implement national climate change management policy within their respective areas of governance.

The responsibility structure for climate change responses- leadership, coordination, implementation, monitoring, and transparency - is clearly defined in Lithuanian legislation. No significant gaps or overlaps in key actors' responsibilities have been identified.

The accountability structure for national climate responses - leadership, coordination, implementation, monitoring, and transparency - is clearly defined in Lithuanian legislation. No major gaps or overlaps in responsibilities among key entities have been identified. However, municipal obligations to conduct environmental monitoring that reliably supplements national data and to submit this data to a unified system are not sufficiently regulated.

At the national level, the Ministry of Environment leads, manages, and coordinates Lithuania's climate change response. It oversees climate mitigation and adaptation policy development and implementation. Within the ministry, the Climate Policy Group prepares strategic documents, drafts legislation, ensures the implementation of mitigation and adaptation measures, and contributes to hydrometeorology policy development.

In 2021, the Seimas approved the National Climate Change Management Agenda to fulfill commitments under the Paris Agreement. It sets Lithuania's climate policy goals for 2030, 2040, and long-term objectives for 2050 in mitigation and adaptation. Mitigation aims to reduce GHG emissions and enhance absorption, while adaptation strengthens resilience and reduces climate vulnerability. The target is to achieve a net 100% reduction in GHG emissions by 2050.

Long-term targets&objektives have been set, with planned measures detailed across sectors: energy sector, transport, small-scale energy, land use, land-use change and forestry, and waste. The agenda and National Energy and Climate Plan clearly state that Lithuania implements EU directives and regulations, fulfilling commitments under the Paris Agreement and the EU NDC. However, some EU NDC provisions are not fully integrated, including marine transport and CO2 reduction targets for new vehicles

The Lithuanian strategic planning system ensures the links between the SDGs and strategic planning documents. Six strategic targets of NPP (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10) have been assigned to achieve the 13th SDG, with specific measures and indicators for progress. The Agenda is closely related to the SDGs. However, while it discusses measures to mitigate climate change, some documents do not provide detailed actions on how to optimally achieve results across sectors, such as agriculture and health.

The Ministry of Environment, together with other institutions, prepared reports summarizing Lithuania's efforts to address the climate crisis and providing future projections. The reports include information on greenhouse gas emission trends, projections until 2100, and climate impact risk assessments across various sectors. Additionally, the "ClimAdapt-LT" project was implemented to enhance public and regional adaptation to CC, providing climate projections for Lithuania from 2030 to 2100.

In May 2023, the National Climate Change Committee was established to provide independent scientific advice to the Ministry of Environment on climate change policy formulation, evaluation, and implementation. The committee consists of representatives from 11 different scientific and academic institutions in Lithuania, including Vilnius University, Vytautas Magnus University, Vilnius Gediminas Technical University, and other institutions.

The National Climate Change Agenda sets short-term (by 2030), medium-term (by 2040), and long-term (by 2050) goals and tasks in climate change mitigation and adaptation. The National Energy and Climate Action Plan for 2021-2030 addresses climate change challenges and outlines measures to tackle them in the energy sector.

Institutional mechanisms exist to coordinate government bodies on CC issues, involving key stakeholders. A working group was established by the Prime Minister's decree, consisting of representatives from the Government and 10 ministries. The group is led by the Prime Minister's advisor and coordinates Lithuania's position on the EU's 2040 climate goal and 2050 climate neutrality, addressing NECP and Green Deal implementation. Parliamentary control is exercised by the EU Affairs Committee.

The working group coordinating the implementation of NECP and Green Deal regularly meets to discuss key related issues. Designated responsible contacts, institutions, and other stakeholders participate in the meetings. At least once a year, the results of NECP implementation and issues are presented to the EU Affairs Committee. This ensures regular interaction, consistency in decision-making, and sectoral alignment. The EC has positively evaluated the inter-ministerial collaboration.

Formal mechanisms enable vertical coordination and joint policy-making across government levels. Municipalities, though lacking a formal agreement, are represented via an association and working groups. The Government aims for climate-neutral ministries by 2030 and supports municipal climate targets. The Environment Ministry promotes greening. Of 60 municipalities, 16 joined the Covenant of Mayors, and 2 are part of the EU Mission for Climate-Neutral & Smart Cities.

Through the working group activities, conditions were created for regular interaction among group members. However, there is a risk that the participation of local authorities may be fragmented, as there is no document ensuring regular and consistent interaction between central and local authorities.

In Lithuania, mechanisms exist to involve various stakeholders in the development and implementation of CC policies, strategies, and plans. The National CC Committee, as an advisory body, ensures the participation of academic representatives in the policy creation, evaluation, and implementation processes. The government's consultation and legislative alignment procedures allow stakeholders - such as the public, NGOs, private sector, experts, and academia - to participate in these processes.

Civil society, the private sector, and academia are represented through the National Climate Change Committee and public consultation procedures, including proposal submissions, participation in working groups, surveys, interviews, discussions, and conferences. All stakeholders were involved in the National Energy and Climate Plan update process, ensuring their inclusion and representation.

Mechanisms like the National Climate Change Committee and public consultations enable regular dialogue between authorities and stakeholders on climate issues. They provide access to draft documents, discussions on key policies, and opportunities to submit feedback. Inputs from consultations were considered in the National Energy and Climate Plan, with a summary showing stakeholder impact. However, the Committee remains largely formal, meeting only once a year without major decisions.

The National Climate Change Management Agenda and the National Energy and Climate Plan partially identify vulnerable groups affected by climate change, but not all needs are clearly addressed. Energy-poor households, socially vulnerable groups (seniors, children, chronically ill, single parents, unemployed) are mentioned, but coastal areas and remote rural communities are not prioritized. A Social Climate Plan is planned to assess vulnerability and define targeted support measures.

Formal mechanisms ensuring the systematic and meaningful participation of vulnerable groups in decision-making on climate strategies, policies, and plans are not clearly defined. While legislation drafting rules and the Ministry of Environment's public participation procedures allow for public involvement, there are no specific provisions or processes guaranteeing the inclusion of vulnerable groups.

The National Climate Change Management Agenda and the National Energy and Climate Plan address damage reduction and ensuring fair benefits for vulnerable groups. These documents outline tasks and measures, including financial incentives, support, and awareness initiatives to reduce energy and social poverty. However, only measures targeting energy poverty are clearly defined. Without a comprehensive identification of all vulnerable groups, it is unclear if all are adequately covered.

In Lithuania, monitoring and reporting follow EU requirements. Mechanisms are in place to track progress on national climate commitments and legislation implementation. These include indicator monitoring, regular reports, GHG accounting, emission forecasts, and climate policy assessments. Processes are defined by EU regulations and national laws, such as the Strategic Management Law and the CC Management Law. The Ministry of Environment coordinates progress monitoring and timely reporting.

The energy sector plays a key role in this transition, with a focus on increasing energy efficiency, expanding renewable energy sources, and promoting low-carbon technologies.

NECAP outlines existing and planned measures in the small-scale energy sector until 2030, their impact on GHG reduction, energy savings, preliminary funding needs, and financing sources. Malta's National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) demonstrates a strong commitment to climate action, with investments in various sectors. However, climate-related spending in the national Budget remains fragmented, making it difficult to assess alignment with climate targets. As alerted by the European Commission, general energy subsidies relying on fossil fuels remain in place. The NECP notes that there are currently no detailed plans to phase out energy subsidies, citing Malta's insularity as a key constraint. Nonetheless, the Climate Action Authority contends that Malta's goal is to phase out inefficient energy subsidies, particularly those that do not address energy poverty or support a just transition, in line with COP Decision 1/CMA.5. Additionally, the NECP does not specify sectoral investment needs, leaving potential financing gaps unclear. In this context, the Government is still in the process of better quantifying the cost of inaction on climate change and the cost of adaptation. Thus, like global trends, national climate change budgets are on the increase but likely not commensurate with the investment needs. Forward-looking, the Climate Action Fund (CAF), established under the Climate Action Act (Cap. 643), is intended to centralize and transparently manage climate-related budgeting and planning. Yet, it is still awaiting the enactment of the legal framework required to become operational.

Malta has not adopted a specific definition or taxonomy for direct climate finance in its policy frameworks or official communications to the UNFCCC. Instead, direct climate finance is primarily tracked and reported in line with the requirements of the Governance Regulation (EU) 2018/1999, which mandates the tracking and reporting of climate-related investments as well as the use of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) auctioning revenues. Additionally, revenues and expenditures related to climate finance are reported annually through the Financial Estimates included in the Government's budget documents. This suggests
that a system for tracking and accounting for direct climate finance is in place. However, Malta's climate-related revenues and expenditures are embedded within broader sectoral or EU funded budgets, particularly in areas such as energy, transport, and the environment. This presumably makes it highly complex to define, identify, and systematically track direct climate finance in an exhaustive manner.

Malta has not adopted a definition of indirect climate finance within its policy frameworks or official submissions and communications to the UNFCCC. Instead, the reporting requirements under the Governance Regulation (EU) 2018/1999, which mandates the tracking and reporting of climate-related investments as well as the use of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) auctioning revenues potentially contribute towards improved tracking of indirect climate finance.

Malta adheres to international reporting obligations such as the Biennial Transparency Report submitted to the UNFCCC and EU reporting obligations under Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 on the Governance of the Energy Union and Climate Action. Among other requirements, the Governance Regulation calls for the monitoring and reporting of climate-related investments, progress in financing climate-related policies and measures, as well as updates on the use of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) auctioning revenues. In addition, climate finance is reflected in official budget documents, such as the annual Financial Estimates, which are published and made publicly available each year. However, climate-related revenues and expenditures are typically embedded within broader sectoral budgets or EU fund-related allocations. As a result, the mechanisms for the classification of budget lines covering the four categories of direct climate finance, indirect climate finance, carbon-intensive budgets, and perverse subsidies are still being developed.

As indicated in Malta's First Biennial Transparency Report, despite not being classified as an Annex II country under the UNFCCC, Malta, as a developed country listed in Annex I of the Convention and as a member state of the European Union, has been actively contributing to global efforts. Its contributions are primarily focussed on providing financial aid and capacity building support to developing countries.

As indicated in Malta's First Biennial Transparency Report, the country has established mechanisms to allocate resources earmarked for meeting its commitments. These mechanisms include, inter alia, financial contributions through established multilateral organisations, such as the Green Climate Fund (GCF), as well as capacity-building and technical support to assist small island developing states. The planned provision of international climate finance contributions is incorporated into Malta's annual budget plans, with the Ministry responsible for climate action policy overseeing the disbursement of these contributions.

As a member state of the European Union, since 2021, Malta is obliged pursuant to Article 19(3) of the Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 on the Governance of the Energy Union and Climate Action and Article 6 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1208 to submit an annual report which provides information on the financial and technology support provided to developing countries.
