Malta's efforts to mobilise private climate finance are still scaling up, with room for stronger market integration via direct incentives and indirect mechanisms. The National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) highlights the need for joint public-private investment, supported by policies, research and innovation, grants, schemes and guarantees. However, as recently highlighted by the European Commission, the NECP lacks clarity on distinguishing and mobilising private investment. Nonetheless, the said Commission assessment acknowledges Malta's robust energy efficiency financing programmes and support schemes, including financial instruments and public guarantees, able to mobilise private investments and additional co-financing. Progress includes inter alia green bonds supported by the Central Bank of Malta, a  - 30M climate action loan agreement between the Malta Development Bank and the European Investment Bank backed by a Market Assessment and Recommendations Report under the Green Gateway Advisory initiative, and interest-free loans under the Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy (EERE) financial instrument under the European Regional Development Fund. The Climate Action Authority is also exploring financing options with local and financial bodies to support the green transition.
The mechanisms to track private finance are still in their early stages.

The reporting obligations under Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 on the Governance of the Energy Union and Climate Action, as well as the Biennial Transparency Reports (BTRs) submitted to the UNFCCC, may be considered as potentially suitable mechanisms for reporting on private climate finance. While Malta adheres to these reporting obligations, it appears that only limited information is currently captured or communicated through these mechanisms regarding the use of private climate finance.
The Chapter 643 of the Laws of Malta - the Climate Action Act and its subsidiary legislation can be considered as a comprehensive legislative framework to address climate change.

Although not prescriptive, the scope and objectives of the Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) are in general consistent with those set out in the Paris Agreement as well as the European Climate Law (Regulation (EU) 2021/1119).
The Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) outlines guiding principles and defines the government's duties and obligations for mainstreaming climate change actions.

Since 2022, the standing committee dealing with issues related to climate change is the Standing Committee on the Environment, Climate Change and Development Planning, which follows the rules and procedures laid down in the Development Planning Act (Cap. 552) and the S.L.Const.02, the Standing Orders of the House of Representatives. In line with the Climate Action Act (Cap. 643), the Minister responsible for climate action policy is required to submit reports annually to the Standing Committee on the Environment, Climate Change and Development Planning on the progress achieved in climate action. Based on publicly available
information, particularly the agenda and minutes of the Standing Committee's meetings, it does not appear that climate-related issues feature as a central focus of its discussions.

Malta's National Audit Office (NAO) is committed to conducting performance audits on climate-related issues. Its latest audit focused on climate change adaptation, specifically evaluating Malta's efforts to address flooding and sea level rise. This work forms part of the IDI-WGEA Global Cooperative Audit on Climate Change Adaptation Actions. The NAO will also take into account the results of the ClimateScanner, aligning them with its current risk-based approach to audit selection.

The Climate Action Act broadly states that the Government must ensure adequate access to justice. It also provides that any person aggrieved by a decision of the Climate Action Authority may appeal to the Administrative Review Tribunal, in line with the Administrative Justice Act (Cap. 490). However, the Act does not include clear provisions that establish mechanisms to guarantee access to climate justice. In addition, there is limited publicly available information on the number of climate-related cases adjudicated locally, or on the extent to which courts and quasi-judicial bodies are handling such claims. Documented evidence showing that judicial and quasi-judicial bodies are actively engaging in climate justice, such as through participation in climate networks, seminars, institutional debates, or educational initiatives, was limited.

The Climate Action Authority is the national body established under the Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) to develop and implement a comprehensive national climate action plan, to coordinate and manage climate action projects across government entities, as well as to fulfil Malta's international and EU climate obligations. In addition, the National Climate Action Council, also established under the Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) is an independent statutory body which aims to provide advice to the Government on Malta's strategic aims relating to climate actions.

The responsibilities and strategic objectives of the Climate Action Authority (CAA) and the National Climate Action Council are clearly defined in the Climate Action Act (Cap. 643). Further information in simple terms on the responsibilities of the CAA and the National Climate Action Council is also available on the website of the Climate Action Authority. Moreover, the Climate Action Act establishes a Climate Action Coordinator within every Ministry.

The roles and responsibilities of the Ministry and bodies involved in climate change are defined, with no substantial gaps identified. The Climate Action Authority fulfils coordination and regulatory function, while the National Climate Action Council provides advisory and consultative services to the Minister responsible for climate action. However, these roles were only recently established and thus any potential
gaps or overlaps may be determined in due course.

The legislation defines the Climate Action Authority (CAA) as the leading entity for regulating and coordinating climate action. The CAA falls under the portfolio of the Minister responsible for climate action policy, currently the Minister for the Environment, Energy and Public Cleanliness. While the CAA is not under the central Office of the Prime Minister, it is yet led by a Cabinet-level minister, implying a high level of political prioritisation and access to high-level decision-making.

In line with the provisions of the Paris Agreement and Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 on the Governance of the Energy Union and Climate Action, the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy was published in October 2021. It was submitted to the UNFCCC on 12 November 2021 and is considered as Malta's long-term strategy that maps out the country vision up to 2050.

Malta's long-term strategy, the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy, was developed in line with the Nationally Determined Contribution dated 2020, submitted by the European Union on behalf of its Member States.

The interlinkages to the Sustainable Development Goals in the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy are too generic and does not include ways to leverage the positive effects while minimising the negative ones.

Malta's First Biennial Transparency Report (BTR) acknowledges the critical role of the Maltese economy-wide Vulnerability & Risk Assessment (VRA), mandated by the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS). The National Audit Office in Malta acknowledges that the VRA should have served as the first in-depth consideration of the interplay between the climate change impacts and the socio-economic realities of the Maltese Islands, establishing priority areas within different economic sectors, in terms of the vulnerability to climate change impacts. The Climate Action Authority contended that such assessment would need to be sustained with more detailed sector-specific VRAs. The BTR mentions other initiatives aimed at assessing coastal risks, namely Coastal SAGE as well as two projects under the flagship of the Technical Support Instrument offered by the European Commission, namely Coastal Cover and Climate MATCH. Project findings are either unpublished or difficult to access.

The Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) emphasises science-based climate action, requiring expert involvement via the National Climate Action Council. The Maltese economy-wide climate Vulnerability and Risk assessment was conducted by an international scientific consultancy, and climate-related projects, such as Climate MATCH, Coastal Cover and Coastal SAGE, actively involve educational and research institutions like the University of Malta as well as other regional or international institutions.

Malta's National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) discusses the impact of climate change on various sectors, including energy, transport, and water management, and details policies and measures to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to climate change effects. Strategically, the NECP identifies the Vulnerability Risk Assessment as an essential tool to identify areas where the greatest adaptation efforts are required. In general Malta's Strategic Plan for Environment and Development (SPED), published in 2015 and currently under review, strategically calls for embedding climate resilience into all planning processes across Malta. It requires that development projects be designed with future climate risks in mind, such as flooding, heatwaves, and sea level rise, ensuring long-term sustainability and safety. It also promotes cross-sector collaboration and regular reviews so that strategies can be updated as conditions evolve, supporting a balanced approach between economic growth and environmental protection.

The Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) establish the Climate Action Authority as the primary entity responsible for coordinating Malta's national response to climate change. Falling under the portfolio of the Minister for the Environment, Energy and Public Cleanliness, the Authority benefits from Cabinet-level leadership, signalling high-level political prioritisation despite not being directly housed within the Office of the Prime Minister. The same Climate Action Act establishes mechanisms to support horizontal coordination. Each head of a government authority, agency, entity, or department deemed relevant to climate action, based on the Minister's designation, is required to act as the point of contact supporting the Climate Action Coordinator within their respective Ministry. In turn, the Permanent Secretary of each Ministry assumes the role of Climate Action Coordinator, responsible for facilitating inter-ministerial consultation and transmitting necessary information to the Climate Action Authority to support its functions. Malta's First Biennial Transparency Report discusses initiatives aimed at integrating climate adaptation measures across various governmental sectors to ensure cohesive and effective responses to climate challenges.

While a mechanism for enabling both horizontal and vertical coordination exists, the recent established Climate Action Authority is actively working to set up the relevant communication channels, particularly with the Climate Action Coordinators and the heads of government bodies.

Notwithstanding that Malta's context of vertical coordination is unique owing to its small scale, the Research Innovation Unit (RIU) represents a specialised initiative and a best practice within Malta's system of local government. The RIU is intended to fulfil the objectives of the Local Government Act (Cap. 363), specifically in advancing climate change research and promoting sustainable urban development. Its mission is closely aligned with key international and EU frameworks. However, while the RIU is an important component of Malta's climate governance landscape, its position within the Local Government framework could be strengthened and supported with the necessary resources.
While initiatives like the Research Innovation Unit (RIU) demonstrate promising practices at the local and regional level, their current legal position may highlight structural gaps.

The Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) stipulates that long-term strategies, plans and regulations shall be prepared in consultation with social partners, civil society, non-governmental organisations and the public. It is also within the responsibilities of the National Climate Action Council to consult every stakeholder concerned including the civil society, particularly the voluntary organisations in the sector related to climate action. In addition to the structures established under the Climate Action Act, the Climate Action Authority actively collaborates with a broad range of stakeholders through workshops, public consultations, and participatory campaigns. Ongoing mechanisms include tailored stakeholder meetings during the development of national strategies, direct feedback channels through the Authority's website and social media. The Authority is also working to institutionalise more frequent and structured dialogue opportunities.

The Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy and the National Energy and Climate Plan outline the approach taken to consult and engage with key stakeholders, including social partners, non-governmental organisations and the civil society, and thus demonstrate that the mechanisms in place observe the representation of the civil society, the private sector and the academia.

While the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy and Malta's National Energy and Climate Plan demonstrate that mechanisms are in place, limited information is publicly available regarding the structural and functional aspects of these mechanisms, particularly on the existence of stakeholder engagement bodies or platforms. Furthermore, the processes and systems that ensure regular, meaningful, and inclusive interaction between stakeholders and the CAA are insufficiently detailed.

The Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) acknowledges the importance of safeguarding the interests of vulnerable groups when formulating and implementing climate policies. Malta's National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) acknowledges the importance of addressing social vulnerabilities and recognises energy poverty as a critical issue, highlighting the importance of identifying and supporting vulnerable households to ensure equitable access to energy services. Malta's commitment to developing a Social Climate Plan (SCP) to access the EU Social Climate Fund resources is currently under discussions between all relevant stakeholders, with the draft Plan issued for public consultation in May 2025 and focussing on alleviating financial burden for the vulnerable groups in two specific sectors, namely building and transport. Malta's First Biennial Transparency Report (BTR) acknowledges the key role of the Maltese economy-wide climate Vulnerability and Risk Assessment (VRA). The VRA was the first in-depth consideration of the interplay between the climate change impacts and the socio-economic realities of Malta, establishing the vulnerable areas within different economic sectors.

The Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) stipulates that long-term strategies, plans and regulations shall be prepared in consultation with social partners, civil society, non-governmental organisations and the public. Similarly, the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy, the National Energy and Climate Plan and the Public Consultation Document - Malta's Social Climate Fund Plan outline the approach taken to consult and engage with key stakeholders, including social partners, non-governmental organisations and the public, highlighting that insights and feedback gathered were carefully evaluated and considered. Nevertheless, there
is no explicit reference to mechanisms which ensure the inclusion of vulnerable groups in the decision-making process.

The Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) considers equity as a key guiding principle in climate action emphasizing that climate actions must be inclusive, non-discriminatory, and promote gender equality. This aligns with the European Union's commitment, as stated in paragraph 27 of its updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) to promote a human rights-based and gender-responsive approach to climate action, ensuring social justice, fairness, inclusiveness, and the full, equal, and meaningful participation of women in climate-related decision-making. Malta's Low Carbon Development Strategy and National Energy and Climate Plan recognise the principle of equity in a generic manner, underlining that any transitions to carbon-neutrality must offer support to communities, groups, and individuals facing socio-economic challenges.

The Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) provides for monitoring mechanisms to track progress toward achieving Malta's commitments pursuant to International and EU obligations. These mechanisms are embedded within the core regulatory functions of the Climate Action Authority, including, inter alia, arrangements to track progress and compile Malta's inventory of greenhouse gas emissions and removals. Separately, the Climate Action Act mandates the National Climate Action Council to submit an annual report to the Minister responsible for climate action policy, detailing progress in climate action. The Minister shall then report to the House of Parliament on a yearly basis the progress registered in climate action and refer reports, strategies and policies to the Standing Committee on the Environment, Climate Change and Development Planning.

Data collected for Malta's Greenhouse Gas Inventory are valuable in providing insights on trends of emissions, which influence the development of policies both directly and indirectly. In this context, as acknowledged in both Malta's First Biennial Transparency Report and Malta's National Inventory Document of Greenhouse Gas Emissions & Removals - 2025, the need to improve the accessibility of inventory data for policymaking is one of the key considerations for ongoing investment at a national level.

Malta's most recent 8th National Communication, the First Biennial Transparency Report and the National Inventory Document of Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Removals, are up-to-date, publicly accessible and aligned with the global governance framework under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement.

In general, the Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) acknowledges that the Government shall ensure that adequate information is made available to the public, to facilitate public participation in respect of certain plans and programmes relating to the climate system and ensure adequate access to justice. The right of access to climate-related information is guaranteed in accordance with the Freedom of Access to Information on the Environment Regulations (Subsidiary Legislation 549.39) or the Freedom of Information Act - Chapter 496 of the Laws of Malta. The mechanisms that provide updated information on progress towards the
achievement of national objectives related to climate change are continuously being enhanced by the Climate Action Authority, in line with its Quality Service Charter and through efforts to communicate such progress via different media including inter alia its website, digital publications such as a monthly magazine, regular posts on social media and active participation in public events.

The Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) assigns the Climate Action Authority the responsibility of creating and maintaining a framework for knowledge, education, information, and communication to promote climate-conscious behaviour. While Malta's official climate reports, submitted under international and EU obligations, are publicly available on platforms such as the UNFCCC website and the European Environment Agency's Reportnet, the Climate Action Authority continues to develop tools that make national climate action information more accessible to non-experts and civil society. These efforts include:
- Publishing national climate policy documents on its website,
- Providing user-friendly resources such as factsheets and FAQs on technical topics, including the EU Emissions Trading System for Aviation and Maritime Transport, and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism,
- Maintaining a country profile that presents Malta's greenhouse gas emissions and removals using clear descriptions and easy-to-understand statistics,
- Issuing a monthly magazine, The Climate Pulse, which goes beyond statistics and policy to share the latest developments, inspiring stories, and expert insights on climate action, and
- Engaging audiences on social media with tailored communication materials, including infographics, videos, and reels.

As a Member State of the European Union, Malta contributes to the EU's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). On 19 October 2023, Spain and the European Commission submitted an update of the nationally determined contribution of the European Union and its Member States.
Malta's ambition is reflected through the EU's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) submitted to the UNFCCC.
The EU NDC generally demonstrates a coherent and integrated approach to sectoral goal-setting, drawing on existing legislation and complementary policy instruments.

Malta's Biennial Transparency Report, National Inventory Document of Greenhouse Gas Emissions & Removals and National Energy and Climate Plan clearly map the policies currently implemented or adopted in Malta that are expected to impact GHG emissions.

The Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy is Malta's long-term strategy under the Paris Agreement. It aligns with the EU's commitments outlined in its Nationally Determined Contribution and is tailored to Malta's specificities. The strategy sets out mitigation measures across seven key sectors, namely Energy, Transport, Buildings, Industry, Waste, Water, and Agriculture and land use, landuse change, and forestry, to help reduce greenhouse gas emissions and support climate change mitigation. However, monitoring and reporting could be affected by gaps in performance metrics.

Malta's National Energy and Climate Plan references the sectoral plans/programs contemplating the reduction of emissions in the main sectors, and the NECP provides details of how such sectoral plans/programs provide actions needed for achieving the sectoral emissions targets. Nonetheless, although elements of sectoral planning are in place, the element of policy integration within such sectoral plans and programmes remains somewhat unclear and not fully aligned with the national long-term strategy.

Malta has an official national adaptation plan contained in its national adaptation strategy, that is the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS). The LCDS encompasses sector-specific adaptation measures for water resources, infrastructure and transport, land use and buildings, natural ecosystems, agriculture, and fisheries, health issues and civil protection, tourism and cross-sectoral action.

Water resources, infrastructure and transport, land use and buildings, natural ecosystems, agriculture, and fisheries, health issues and civil protection, tourism and cross-sectoral dimensions are the sectors which have been identified in Malta's Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS) as requiring the highest priority in the formulation of adaptation measures, owing to their current vulnerabilities and heightened susceptibility to the effects of climate change on the Maltese Islands. Such identification was based on modelling, research and stakeholders' consultations. Nevertheless, sources such as Malta's country-profile on Climate-ADAPT acknowledge the challenges, gaps and barriers in identifying such sectors. The newly established Climate Action Authority, also through the recent first-economy wide climate Vulnerability and Risk Assessment, shall endeavour to strengthen the identification of the most vulnerable sectors that should feature as a priority in the upcoming national adaptation plan.

The national adaptation plan contained in the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS) is currently in its implementation phase. On a general note, Article 23(2) of the Climate Action Act (Cap. 643) mandates the Minister responsible for climate action to review and update periodically, and at least every five (5) years the national adaptation strategy. In this context, the Climate Action Authority is prioritising the development of a national adaptation plan which will take into consideration the outcomes of the recently finalised Maltese economy-wide climate Vulnerability and Risk Assessment.

Malta's National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP), prepared in line with Regulation (EU) 2018/1999 on the Governance of the Energy Union and Climate Action, sets out objectives to reduce emissions in the energy sector. These objectives focus on transitioning to cleaner energy sources and improving energy efficiency. However, the European Commission's assessment of Malta's final updated NECP identifies some shortcomings.

Malta's National Energy and Climate Plan outlines the intended actions to support the achievement of national objectives and targets. These appear to be generic, with limited scope and timelines. Furthermore, certain actions or measures seem to overlap with those in other sectoral plans, which could potentially lead to ambiguity regarding their ownership and coordination.

The challenges identified (such as limited renewable energy resources, geographical constraints, financial barriers, technological limitations, and energy poverty) are discussed in Malta's National Energy and Climate Plan and the Plan presents measures to overcome the identified challenges. However, while the challenges are mapped out effectively, there could be more depth regarding the impact of these challenges on specific sectors. Albeit the Plan includes an impact assessment, as suggested in the European Commission's assessment of Malta's final updated NECP, the evaluation could be further strengthened through a quantifiable analysis to provide a clearer link between these challenges and their long-term socio-economic implications, effectiveness and financial viability. Additionally, the challenges and responses are spread across different sections of the Plan and key uncertainties remain regarding funding, timelines, expected outcomes, and support mechanisms.

Malta's National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) outlines institutional responsibilities for monitoring and evaluation, primarily identifying the Climate Action Authority (CAA) for overseeing implementation. This includes, inter alia, the preparation, coordination, and updating of the NECP, as well as ensuring compliance with both national and international climate-related commitments. The Plan further notes Malta's adherence to EU and international reporting obligations and frameworks, intended to support the monitoring of progress towards climate and energy targets, and a defined reporting and review cycle, including an annual report to Parliament by the Minister responsible for climate action, as well as a comprehensive review and update of the Plan at least every five years, in line with the Climate Action Act (Cap. 643). Nevertheless, although the CAA is developing internal monitoring systems, details on the frequency of internal assessments, the specific methodologies employed, as well as the measurable targets and quantifiable indicators at the level of programmes or measures beyond those required under the EU acquis are not clearly defined.

Malta's national climate adaptation policy framework to address issues related to flooding and sea-level rise is broadly aligned with EU commitments, particularly through adherence to the EU Floods Directive (2007/60/EC). Compliance has been achieved through various measures, notably the transposition of this Directive into Maltese legislation via Subsidiary Legislation 549.167 - the Assessment and Management of Flood Risks Regulations. Additional measures include the development and publication of the Preliminary Flood Risk Assessment (PFRA) in 2019, and the adoption of the Second Flood Risk Management Plan for the Malta River Basin District (2nd FRMP), published in February 2024. The Flood Hazard Maps (FHMs) and Flood Risk Maps (FRMs) developed in 2020 underpin the 2nd FRMP, reflecting Malta's commitment to identifying and assessing risks and hazards within designated vulnerable catchments. Furthermore, as highlighted in a recent performance audit by the National Audit Office of Malta on climate change adaptation, the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS) addresses vulnerabilities related to flooding and sea level rise; either directly, by tackling specific concerns, or indirectly, by enhancing resilience to climate change impacts.

Malta's 3rd River Basin Management Plan (3rd RBMP), published in March 2024, and the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS) collectively form part of the national policy response to climate change, each addressing key dimensions of water management adaptation. The 3rd RBMP integrates climate adaptation within the broader context of water quality, quantity, and resource management, in line with the EU Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC). The LCDS also emphasizes adaptation as a critical pillar, particularly in sectors deemed highly vulnerable, such as water resources, and outlines seven adaptation measures to directly address the challenges in this sector. It also includes indirect adaptation measures, which contribute significantly to enhancing overall resilience to climate-related hazards affecting water resources. While both the 3rd RBMP and the LCDS independently address similar goals and concerns, particularly the impacts of climate change on water management and the need for adaptation responses, their connection remains relatively indirect. Although they are conceptually aligned, the degree of integration between the 3rd RBMP and the LCDS is limited.

Malta's 3rd River Basin Management Plan (3rd RBMP) and the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS) both address climate adaptation for water resources. The 3rd RBMP outlines direct and indirect actions through its Programme of Measures (PoMs), such as improving water efficiency, reusing treated water, boosting aquatic ecosystem resilience, and enhancing data collection for informed decision-making. The selected
measures were prioritised using a multi-disciplinary evaluation framework to ensure responsiveness to changing climatic conditions and to preserve the recovery of aquatic ecosystems. Governance is supported by the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Water, which promotes cross-sectoral coordination and policy alignment. Implementation is further reinforced by the LIFE16 IPE MT 008 initiative, which includes targeted actions. Malta's Interim reporting on the PoMs specifies responsibility for each measure, clarifying roles and ensuring accountability. The LCDS complements the RBMP with seven direct adaptation measures and additional indirect ones that strengthen resilience to climate related water challenges. However, according to a performance audit carried out by the National Audit Office of Malta on climate change adaptation, adaptation measures outlined in the Malta LCDS currently lack clear ownership, defined timeframes, and specific Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), potentially hindering their effectiveness.

The Second Flood Risk Management Plan for the Malta River Basin District (2nd FRMP) includes a Programme of Measures (PoM) designed to address challenges associated with flooding. The multi-faceted PoM demonstrates a practical orientation, comprising various initiatives up to 2027. These initiatives cover adaptation, mitigation, monitoring, public information, as well as research, studies, and investigations. Overall, the 2nd FRMP has broadly addressed the European Commission's recommendations. Notably, established timeframes for initiatives outlined in the PoM facilitate improved monitoring and evaluation of related
deliverables. However, the recommendation from the European Commission to provide cost estimates for each measure has not been fully addressed within the 2nd FRMP. The Energy and Water Agency contended that the cost estimates for the measures to be considered in the 3rd FRMP shall be made available. Most adaptation measures identified in the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS) are expected to offer direct or
indirect benefits in addressing flooding and/or sea-level rise. However, it transpires that adaptation measures outlined in the Malta LCDS currently lack clear ownership, defined timeframes, and specific Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), potentially hindering their effectiveness. Additionally, the cost implications of these adaptation measures remain unspecified in the policy document.

Malta faces implementation challenges, particularly in capacity building and data availability. These barriers are recognised in key policy documents such as Malta's First Biennial Transparency Report and the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS). Similarly to the LCDS, Malta's 3rd River Basin Management Plan (3rd RBMP) acknowledges data and knowledge gaps as well as capacity limitations as main barriers to implementation. These challenges are discussed within the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Water, which provides a good opportunity for the participating entities to share the lessons learnt on the development and implementation of their measures, hence improving policy development and implementation. The 3rd RBMP's Programme of Measures includes targeted actions to address these barriers, supported by the LIFE16 IPE MT 008 initiative. The latter has enabled project beneficiaries to significantly invest in capacity building and allowed for the execution of pilot studies to enhance operational capabilities and fill knowledge gaps on specific topics.

Malta faces a range of implementation challenges, notably structural and data related. These barriers have been duly acknowledged in official communications or policy documents, including inter alia Malta's First Biennial Transparency Report, the Second Flood Risk Management Plan for the Malta River Basin District (2nd FRMP), the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS) and the performance audit on climate change adaptation carried out by the National Audit Office (NAO) of Malta. These include limited spatial and temporal data on the frequency and typology of flood events, outdated demographic inputs in risk assessments, and the absence of comprehensive cost estimations for both action and inaction. Progress has been made in the 2nd FRMP, particularly in the inclusion of forecasted costs as a criterion for prioritisation as well as the inclusion of appropriate measures to address data limitations, some of which have already been implemented through participation in EU Funded Projects. Broader implementation challenges remain, such as cross-sectoral coordination, unclear policy uptake, and the absence of key performance indicators. The Climate Action Authority, alongside the Climate Action Coordinators within each Ministry and the key stakeholders, is tasked with overcoming these barriers. In this context, the NAO Performance Audit report on climate change adaptation includes recommendations to address the implementation challenges.

Malta's 3rd River Basin Management Plan (3rd RBMP) is jointly monitored by the Environment and Resources Authority (ERA) and the Energy and Water Agency (EWA), with support from national stakeholders. The Plan clearly outlines the roles and responsibilities and sets up a monitoring framework through the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Water (IMC Water) and the National Water Table meetings. The IMC Water tracks implementation progress, identifies obstacles, and reports outcomes to relevant authorities, while the National Water Table multi-stakeholder platform serves as a technical forum for stakeholders to review progress and discuss future actions. ERA and EWA coordinate these efforts to ensure monitoring insights inform policy. Interim progress, including adaptation measures, is reported within the 3rd cycle of
the RBMP. Monitoring is further supported by a range of project actions under LIFE16 IPE MT 008. In contrast, Malta's Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS) lacks a structured monitoring and evaluation system. As highlighted in the performance audit report of the National Audit Office of Malta on climate change adaptation, the measures in the Malta LCDS currently lack clear ownership, defined timeframes, and specific key performance indicators. The recent establishment of the Climate Action Authority signals a positive development aimed at strengthening national-level monitoring and evaluation, particularly of cross-cutting adaptation measures.

The Second Flood Risk Management Plan for the Malta River Basin District (2nd FRMP) benefits from a relatively well-structured monitoring framework for its Programme of Measures, featuring implementation timelines, prioritisation criteria, and biannual multi-stakeholder oversight through the Inter-ministerial Committee on Water and the National Water Table meetings, both jointly coordinated by the Energy and
Water Agency and the Environment and Resources Authority, with the aim of facilitating cross-sectoral dialogue and promoting implementation accountability. Initiatives like LocAll4Flood and CARDIMED showcase effective stakeholder engagement and cross-border collaboration. Their outcomes are routinely presented in platforms such as the National Water Table meetings and inform flood hazard monitoring and risk evaluation by the relevant coordinating and participating entities. In contrast, the Malta Low Carbon Development Strategy (LCDS) currently lacks a systematic monitoring and evaluation mechanism, with limited
detail on key performance indicators (KPIs), costings, and clear institutional ownership of measures. The recent establishment of the Climate Action Authority signals a positive development aimed
at strengthening national-level monitoring and evaluation. In this context, the NAO Performance Audit report on climate change adaptation includes recommendations to strengthen monitoring and evaluation mechanisms.

A National Climate Change Mitigation Strategy and Action Plan (NCCMSAP) was formulated in 2022 through technical and financial assistance from UNEP and GEF. Government approval to implement the NCCMSAP 2022-2030 was obtained in June 2023.

The National Climate Change Mitigation Strategy and Action Plan focuses on reducing GHG emissions across all sectors. The document includes sectoral strategies, targets and actions. However, National Strategies in some sectors are still being revised or formulated.

The NAP process for Mauritius started in 2017. During 2017 to 2022, various consultations were held with stakeholders and the Green Climate Fund to review the proposals in terms of costing and write-up. In 2023, the Ministry decided to re-initiate the development of a NAP as there had been major developments in addressing Disaster Risk Reduction and Infrastructure. As of June 2024, the NAP concept note was still at draft stage and a NAP was yet to be formulated and operationalised.

National Adaptation Plans have not yet been formulated. However, the Government has developed a National Climate Change Adaptation Policy Framework whereby Government has set priority adaptation actions for all the strategic sectors which are the backbone of the country's economy.

The NAP process has been re-initiated in 2023. As of June 2024, Concept Notes are still in draft stage. A National Climate Change Adaptation Strategy and Action Plan, as prescribed in the Climate Change Act 2020, has not been developed yet.

According to the National Climate Change Mitigation Strategy and Action Plan, Energy Industry is the single largest source of GHG emissions. The key mitigation objective by 2030 is to reduce the overall GHG emissions by 40% predominantly by increasing the share of energy generation from green sources to 60% and phasing out the use of coal. (In 2023, the energy sector remains the largest contributing sector and accounted for 78.8 % of total emissions).
2 Sectoral mitigation strategies have been identified and broken down into 11 actions for the Energy Sector.
Challenges to the implementation of policies and achievement of goals for the energy sector have not been mapped.

An online platform, the Mauritius NDC Registry (MauNDC Registry) has been developed to assist in the systematic and regular collection, preparation and reporting of data on climate action and support in Mauritius. However, the system has not been populated as of June 2024. Under the Initiative for Climate Action on Transparency (ICAT) project, the Ministry has sought assistance to Support capacity building of stakeholders for the population of the MauNDC Registry.

The Mexican Government, through the Annex Resources for the Adaptation and Mitigation of the Effects of Climate Change of the Expenditure Budget of the Federation, determines the budgetary programs in order to comply the national climate objectives. In 2023, 187,968.5 million pesos were budgeted in the Annex, but neither the carbon-intensive actions nor the amount of subsidies that negatively affect the achievement of climate objectives were identified.

The Mexican Government, through the Annex Resources for the Adaptation and Mitigation of the Effects of Climate Change of the Expenditure Budget of the Federation, identifies the resources to be exercised by government entities that share objectives, goals or priorities in climate matters. Although there is no specific report on this Annex, it is monitored through the Transparency Agenda Information System of the Special Climate Change Program and the Quarterly Reports.

The Mexican government does not have systems to identify, track, and account for resources not directly allocated to climate change mitigation and adaptation; however, they contribute to achieve climate goals.

In its Public Accounts, the Government of Mexico annually reports on the use of public resources budgeted in its Annex 16 "Resources for Adaptation and Mitigation of the Effects of Climate Change" in terms of climate change, which in 2023 amounted to 192,308.5 million pesos, but the amount spent on carbon-intensive actions or the amount of subsidies that negatively affect the achievement of climate objectives were not identified.

In the First Communication on Adaptation of 2022, Mexico identified financing needs for climate change and designed an architecture detailing the flow of international climate funds; while the 2022 Nationally Determined Contribution suggests that more international financing can increase climate goals, but there are no formal requests for an increase.

Mexico has the Climate Financing Platform and the Climate Financing Architecture to identify sources of international climate financing. For its mobilization, it has the Sustainable Financing Mobilization Strategy, coordinated by the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit, in which it prioritizes access to financing from the Multilateral Funds for the Environment and Climate Change.

In Mexico, the Mexican Agency of International Cooperation for Development  through the National Registry of International Cooperation for Development  tracks international funds received; However, this system does not specifically identify the activities and objectives of the use of funds and the fulfillment of the planned goals.

Mexico has the Climate Financing Platform and the National Registry of International Cooperation for Development through which it publicly informs about the supply and demand of financing and the destination of climate funds. In the case of the Registry, it must publish the results of international cooperation annually, but as of 2023, it did not present the corresponding report.

The Mexican Climate Financing Platform promotes the supply and demand of financing for climate change projects, including co-financing and credits from the private sector, aligning with the Sustainable Financing Mobilization Strategy that establishes the line of action for the creation of innovative sustainable financing instruments in cooperation with the private sector.

In accordance with the Public-Private Partnerships Law, Mexico's Public Procurement System as well as the Portfolio of Investment Programs and Projects must identify those that were carried out in cooperation with the private sector; However, these systems do not identify which of the programs and projects that received support from this sector contributed to the mitigation and adaptation to climate change.
No provisions were identified that establish the preparation of reports on the use of private climate financing, nor their frequency of preparation.

In Mexico, the General Law on Climate Change considers the financial, regulatory, technical, planning, evaluation and surveillance instruments of public climate change policy. The planning instruments of this law include the Agreement through which the update of the National Climate Change Strategy is published, in terms of the General Law on Climate Change; the Special Climate Change Program and the State´s Climate Change Programs.

The General Law on Climate Change was reformed on July 13, 2018, so that Mexico contributes to the compliance of the Paris Agreement, with the aim of maintaining the increase in world's average temperature below 2 °C, relative to pre-industrial levels, and continue efforts to limit this temperature increase to 1.5 °C, relative to pre-industrial levels.

Articles 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 of the General Climate Change Law identify the necessary national and sectoral public policy instruments for the design, implementation and evaluation of the National Climate Change Policy.

The Mexican Parliament has special commissions on climate change, which promote the modification of laws, their compliance as well as the compliance of international commitments, and organize events to debate and produce reports on climate-related actions.
The Supreme Audit Institution of Mexico has carried out at least two audits in the last five years focused on the evaluation of the actions of the Mexican Government on climate change.
By 2023, Federal courts in Mexico had 18 cases on climate change, which were related to probable violations of the right to a healthy environment; However, none of them were sentenced that year.

The first paragraph of article 38, of the General Law on Climate Change, establishes that the federation, the federal entities and the municipalities will coordinate for the integration and operation of the National Climate Change System based on the System's Declaration and its internal regulations.

The General Law on Climate Change establishes that the National Climate Change System will coordinate the national and subnational governments to carry out adaptation, mitigation and reduction of vulnerability to climate change actions. This system is made up of representatives from both levels of government and the Congress with legally recognized powers.

The General Law on Climate Change clearly establishes the responsibilities, coordination and monitoring mechanisms for the actions carried out on the matter. In addition, the roles and responsibilities of each government entity are defined for the correct fulfillment of their powers in the design and implementation of public climate change policy.

In accordance with its Internal Regulations, the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources will have the power to formulate and coordinate the national climate change policy; while the General Law on Climate Change establishes that the National Institute of Ecology and Climate Change will coordinate and carry out studies on climate change and that the National Climate Change System will be the means of coordination for the National Policy on the matter.

In 2016, the Mexican Government submitted its Midcentury Strategy to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, which corresponds to its Long Term Strategy (LTS), aligned with the Agreement through which the update of the National Climate Change Strategy is published, in terms of the General Law on Climate Change.

Mexico's Midcentury Strategy 2016 was not aligned with the latest version of the 2022 Nationally Determined Contribution, as it was aligned with the Contribution issued in 2015 and ratified in 2016, as well as with the Agreement through which the update of the National Climate Change Strategy is published, in terms of the General Law on Climate Change.
The 2016 Midcentury Strategy highlights the interconnections between Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 13 - Climate Action and other SDGs.

The Mexican government maintains the National Atlas of Climate Change Vulnerability, a structured and systematic set of maps showing territorial vulnerability to climate change. This map serves to guide adaptation strategies and decision-making in development planning. It was updated in 2023.

The National Institute of Ecology and Climate Change is the body in charge of the administration of the National Atlas of Vulnerabilities to Climate Change and in its development there is an inter-institutional and inter-sectoral scientific perspective participation.

The Special Climate Change Program includes some changes and impacts of climate change in Mexico, which are considered in the National Atlas of Vulnerability to Climate Change. However, it does not specify the types of risks to which the country is exposed and how they were used to design the objectives of the program.

In the General Law on Climate Change, the National Climate Change System is established as a horizontal coordination mechanism, since it is made up of an Intersecretarial Commission, a National Council with representation of the social, private and academic sectors, the Institute National Climate Change Committee and representatives of the Federal Congress.

In 2024, the First meeting of the National Climate Change System was held, in which issues related to the lines of action of Mexico's Nationally Determined Contribution as well as the National Climate Change Policy were discussed.

The General Law on Climate Change considers that the National Climate Change System has an Intersecretarial Commission on Climate Change and the Climate Change Council, as institutional mechanisms for vertical coordination.
The National Climate Change System held an extraordinary session in 2024 to discuss matters related to the review and update process of the National Climate Change Strategy.

The Climate Change Council is the permanent consultation body of the Intersecretarial Commission on Climate Change, which is made up by the social, private and academic sectors and has among its powers to recommend the carrying out of studies and adopt policies, actions and goals aimed to address the adverse effects of climate change.
The Climate Change Council will be made up at least by fifteen people from the social, private and academic sectors, with recognized merits and experience in climate change.

The General Law on Climate Change establishes that the Climate Change Council will meet twice a year or whenever the Intersecretarial Commission on Climate Change requires its opinion; however, in 2024 there were no means to document their sessions.

The General Law on Climate Change recognizes vulnerable groups such as indigenous people, migrants, children and the disabled, establishing that their rights must be considered in the fight against climate change. Likewise, the National Climate Change Strategy includes actions to identify and serve these populations, although it does not detail their specific needs.

The Government of Mexico must include vulnerable groups in the creation of climate change programs, through consultations and social participation of these groups. For the design of the Special Climate Change Program, a survey that recorded the participation of indigenous people, women and young people, was carried out.

The General Law on Climate Change establishes that gender equity and representation of vulnerable groups must be considered in national programs. In addition, it promotes a gender and human rights approach in territorial planning and risk management, seeking to increase resilience and reduce vulnerability. However, the national programs do not specify which vulnerable populations will be considered for their design and implementation.

The monitoring mechanisms provide information on the climate, emissions of greenhouse gases and compounds, mitigation, vulnerability, risks, population and biodiversity based on indicators, in addition, there is a record of emissions; but its results are not linked to the progress of the indicated commitments by the Mexican Government in the 2022 Nationally Determined Contribution, aligned with the Paris Agreement.

The National Climate Change Strategy, updated in 2024, integrates monitoring mechanisms for its execution, assigns periods and responsible parties to evaluate results, and allows these evaluations to update the strategy. However, it does not detail how the information obtained will be used or how it will influence future updates.

Mexico's Government had the Sixth National Communication on Climate Change of 2018, but it was not updated 4 years after it was issued; It also had the Third Biennial Update Report of 2022, through which it reported the progress made in climate change as of that year.

The Mexican government has a regulatory framework for transparency and access to information, including environmental issues, as well as systems and reports that provide data on monitoring toward national climate goals, which are updated to 2024.

The reports on progress in meeting climate change objectives by the Mexicvan Government are accessible and understandable to the public, but they are dispersed in different repositories, which makes them difficult to locate.
In 2022, the Mexican Government presented the second version of its Nationally Determined Contribution in accordance with Article 4 of the Paris Agreement.

In the 2022 Nationally Determined Contribution, Mexico increased its greenhouse gas reduction goal from 22.0% to 35.0% and confirmed reducing carbon emissions by 51.0%; both goals to be achieved in 2030. Conditionally, it plans to increase them by 40.0% and 70.0%, respectively. In addition, it established 17 lines of action on Adaptation, that are additional to those established in the 2015 Nationally Determined Contribution, but they do not have goals.

In the 2022 Nationally Determined Contribution, Mexico had goals by sector for Mitigation, but not for Adaptation; while, in the Special Climate Change Program, objectives and goals were established without distinguishing their scope of application.

Mexico's National Climate Change Strategy, issued in 2013 with a 40-year scope, defines the institutional and public policy framework to implement climate change mitigation measures at the national and subnational level. Its last update was in 2024.

The National Climate Change Strategy of Mexico, from 2013 with a 40-year vision, establishes strategies and objectives for mitigation and adaptation to climate change; which was consistent with the last update of the 2022 Nationally Determined Contribution.

Mexico has the Special Climate Change Program and the Environment and Natural Resources Sector Program that are aligned with the National Development Plan and the National Climate Change Strategy. These instruments establish objectives to reduce emissions in the main sectors and establish actions, as well as those responsible for their achievement.

There is some work done to report data for FY2023 only; however, there is still alot of updated information to be collected by the Overseas Development Assistance function for FSM in line with the ODA Policy of 2013 (attached).

Currently, the GCF funded NAP project is designed to produce an overarching adaptation plan that includes the GCF and other climate finance and development partners. One of the main outcomes of the NAP will be the development of a national climate finance strategy.  In the GCF updated country program 2024-2027 (page 15), there has been identification of key players and focal points for climate finance that includes the Dept. of Finance, DECEM, ODA, and Dept. of Foreign Affairs.
The national government is not able to fully track private climate finance due to poor coordination efforts between the national government and the CSOs.

The financial information provided from the CCAA Report was obtained directly from the ODA Office.  ODA Portal has not been updated. The Overseas Development Assistance office provides data on finance sources up to FY2021; however it does not include financial data from the CSOs.  Also, per the 2019 FSM climate change and disaster risk finance assessment report, non-government organizations, line ministries and private sector use of donor funds is not reported or acknowledged by the government.  Micronesia Conservation Trust for example is an accredited Entity that can access AF projects up to USD1.0 million and GCF 10.0.  These project funds are not tracked by the FSM government.

The FSM CC Act and DRM&CC Policy of 2013 are expected to be the overarching frameworks for further detailed legislation on climate change. An overarching NAP to better coordinate the implementation, monitoring and reporting of climate change adaptation actions (CCAA) is under development by a GCF funded project called the FSM NAP Planning Project.   The CCCSD now called the Presidential Council for Sustainable Development that oversee CCAA re-organized this fiscal year, and the executive order pending approval from the FSM President. FSMNG Congress Standing Committee on climate change and environmental issues was established in recognition of the relevance and urgency of climate change and its effects.

While climate change has always been a priority of FSM, the DRM&CC policy was designed to address the pressing needs of the country in relation to climate change and disaster risk management.  This policy was also developed to assist in meeting regional and international treaty obligations and objectives that the Government of FSM has agreed as worth pursuing such as UNFCCC, RFA and PIFACC.

JSAPs were developed to mainstream adaptation efforts, and these are being updated under the current NAP process.  Noting that this coincides with the recently updated Infrastructure Development Plans (IDPs) and Strategic Development Plan (SDP).

The Congress of FSM actively engages with climate change issues, by participating in the 139th Inter-Parliament Union (IPU) assembly to champion a climate change resolution, demonstrating legislative action on the global stage.  The President of the FSM address the UN General Assembly to emphasize the urgency of climate action and the severe impacts of climate change on FSM.  The FSM government has the Department of Environment, Climate Change and Emergency Management to address climate change challenges.  The nation is also developing an overarching NAP to adapt to worsening climate change impacts, a process that requires both governmental and parliamentary support.

Office of the National Public Auditor (ONPA), FSM published a Climate Change Adaptation and Actions audit on April 24, 2025, and intends to do a follow up audit in 9 months' time to verify implementation of recommendations.

The FSM judiciary is increasingly poised to adjudicate climate change claims, supported by the nation's proactive engagement in international legal proceedings and its internal climate change legislation. The FSM participated in the International Court of Justice (ICJ) advisory proceedings and passed a Climate Change Act in 2014, indicating a governmental intent to integrate climate change considerations into national policy and legal frameworks which can be a precursor to developing domestic capacity to address these issues in its courts.

The Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) has a national government structure and frameworks in place to address climate change, including the Department of Environment, Climate Change, and Emergency Management (DECEM), strategic plans like the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) that is anticipated to be developed by the on-going FSM NAP Planning Project funded by GCF, and National Environmental Management Strategy (NEMS), and initiatives that involve state governments and community participation. These efforts are supported by key frameworks such as the Strategic Development Plan (SDP) and the Infrastructure Development Plan (IDP), and aim to enhance climate resilience through adaptation, mitigation, and robust governance mechanisms.

The FSM Climate Change Act and the DRM&CC Policy mandated and specified obligations for FSM National Government and the State Governments, including private sector, but did not specify any roles for the Presidential Council for Sustainable Development currently known as the Council.  DECEM as the focal coordinator continues to face challenges to implement the CC Policy due to challenges in operational support from the President's Council and financial support from the FSM Government.

The CCAA audit 2025 identified gaps in the leading, coordination and monitoring of the implementation of the CC Policy. Also, per the Updated Country Program, gaps and needs in institutional operations at both the national and states government levels were identified as cross-cutting needs. Although the FSM Government has not adopted a centralized monitoring and reporting system to track all climate change adaptation donor funded projects and actions, gaps and needs are being monitored and reported by the MEL Action System.  Per the MEL Action System, although progresses are slow, the major gaps in the last 2 years are being addressed. MEL tracks and reports GCF funded projects.  Other donor funded projects are tracked by the other 2 climate chang financing institutions, Adaptation Fund (AF) and Global Environment Facility (GEF).

The Department of Environment, Climate Change and Emergency Management (DECEM) is currently the FSM National Government body with responsibilities for leading, steering and coordinating national responses to climate change, and with authority to mobilize other government bodies.  The Presidential Council called the CCCSD under the 21 Executive Order oversees coordination, implementation, monitoring and reporting of climate change action.  This Council was found to be inactive during the CCAA audit, however currently this council now called the Sustainable Development had amended the 2021 EO which is pending President's approval. MEL Action System tracks, monitors and reports progress of climate change actions and FSM's responses to climate change, however a follow up audit is needed to determine if this GCF Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) system also tracks climate change projects tracked by the other 2 climate financing institutions, Adaptation Fund (AF) and Global Environment Facility (GEF).

The Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) has communicated its long-term climate strategy to the UNFCCC, with its Third National Communication and First Biennial Update Report submitted in October 2022 serving as key official government documents establishing its national strategy to address climate change, aligning with the goals of the Paris Agreement.
The FSM Strategic Development Plans, Infrastructure Development Plans (IDPs) are aligned to its 2022 NDC.
The FSM Strategic Development Plan (SDP) and Infrastructure Development Plan (IDP) and the updated Country Program considered interlinkages between SDG13-Climate and other SDGs.

There is mapping of climate change risks in the FSM documented on several resources like the 2023 Pacific Islands Regional Climate Assessment (PIRCA) report, 2021/2022updates to the World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal for the region and the updated 2022 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).  These mappings include threats from sea level rise, increased temperatures, storm impacts, and their effects on health, food security and infrastructure.
FSM bases the identification of risks on scientific evidence.
The FSM long- and medium-term planning instruments that address climate change incorporate climate risks.

DECEM at the national government level coordinates the implementation of climate change policy, planning, financing and actions and provide technical assistance to the 4 state governments responsible for implementation.  The Presidential Council for Sustainable Development oversees coordination and implementation.  MEL Action System monitors, tracks and reports progress made on climate change conditions, actions and responses to the President's Council while this Council reports to the FSM President.  DECEM continues to be a co-chairman for the Council under the newly amended executive order pending the President's approval.  The Congress Permanent Standing Committee considers and reports on bills, resolutions, and other matters referred to it pertaining to the preservation of physical and natural environment. Our CCAA report concluded that there is a need for improving how climate change actions are coordinated, implemented, monitored and reported.

During the CCAA Audit, the President's Council was found to be inactive.  Currently this council re-organized under a new executive order.  DECEM and the FSM Department of Finance continue to be co-chairman under the new executive order including the 2021.  FSM also has the Congress Permanent Standing Committee.

The FSM has established some institutional mechanisms for vertical coordination of climate change actions, such as Joint State Action Plans (JSAPs) and a national policy framework, but significant barriers to coordination and effective adaptation planning remain, requiring better capacity and a more comprehensive national monitoring system to improve integration across national and state levels.

Climate action in the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) involves mechanisms for vertical coordination that allow for regular interaction between different levels of government and stakeholders, as seen with the FSM Joint Management Network (JMN). The JMN serves as a crucial platform for coordinating climate change adaptation and disaster risk management activities across national government agencies, regional organizations, and non-governmental organizations, ensuring integration and avoiding duplication of efforts at community levels.  Our 2025 CCAA report did not cover vertical coordination.  There is a need to do an audit to determine status of interaction between members.

The FSM has institutional mechanisms for consistent stakeholder participation in climate strategies, including the National Designated Authority (NDA) for the Green Climate Fund (GCF) that consults with states and various civil society actors for its Country Program, and joint state-national action plans developed in collaboration with state representatives and supported by organizations like the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme (SPREP) and the Pacific Community (SPC).

The institutional mechanisms within the FSM include representation from the civil society, private sector, and academia, with state chambers of commerce serving as a key mechanism for private sector representation. These mechanisms ensure diverse stakeholder voices are included in governance and decision-making processes across the nation's various sectors.

The institutional mechanisms are implemented in a way that allows regular interaction between government and other stakeholders.  For example, the FSM established the SDG Working Group to solicit input from civil society and chambers of commerce, and the Protected Areas Network (PAN) demonstrates how communities and stakeholders work together to manage natural resources. A recent UN-backed joint programme further reinforces this by focusing on strengthening partnerships between governments and civil society to improve data collection and achieve Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Identified vulnerable groups in the FSM include elders, children, pregnant women, disability, gender, youth and persons with health complications as well as those working outdoors (i.e., farmers, fishermen), especially the ones on the low-lying islands.

Women's groups, youth groups, traditional leaders and persons with disabilities were key players in the development of the FSM Joint State Action Plans (JSAPs) and the on-going GCF NAP Project intended to develop the FSM NAP.
Climate Strategies, policies and plans are focused on identified vulnerable groups.  Measures and provisions were also focused on reducing harms and ensure equitable benefits from climate solutions.

The NAP was developed through the UNDP-GCF project "Enhancing Montenegro's Capacity to Integrate Climate Change Risks into Planning," employing extensive stakeholder engagement across government ministries, local authorities, private sector, civil society, and academic institutions. Water Resources: Drought management, flood prevention, wastewater quality improvement, integrated water resource management under changing precipitation patterns

Tourism: Infrastructure climate-proofing, seasonal adaptation strategies, diversification of tourism products, integration of climate considerations

The Climate Change (Management) Act 2015 is a significant piece of legislation in Papua New Guinea (PNG) that addresses climate change mitigation and adaptation. Based on this act, the Climate Change and Development Authority (CCDA) was established to regulate this act and  oversee climate-related matters.

These include mitigation efforts (reducing greenhouse gas emissions) and adaptation measures (building resilience to climate impacts).

In addition to Paris Agreement being ratified, Law on Climate Change, as well as policy documents Low Carbon Development Strategy and the Climate Change Adaptation Programme, were developed so as to embed Paris Agreement provisions. It has to be noted that Serbia is an EU candidate country and is in the process of transposition of EU climate acquis that was developed so as to align EU with Paris Agreement.

Spain guarantees, through its Climate Change (CC) National Law and its Adaptation to CC Plan, the necessary instruments and funding to combat CC, including measures and resources from the Next Generation EU Program and the EU's Multiannual Financial Framework 2021-2027, with its ERDF, EAGF, EAFRD, and EMFF funds, as well as the LIFE and HORIZON Europe programs. Additionally, Spain has green funds from the Recovery, Transformation, and Resilience Plan, along with national budget PIMA ADAPTA funds

Spain and the EU regulate and track climate finance with Taxonomy Regulation EU 2020/852 setting climate and environmental objectives and conditions for environmentally sustainable economic activities. In Spain climate measures are financed by the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan, through budgets from Environmental Promotion Plans (PIMA) and with the auctioning of GHG emissions allowances. Other funds for climate finance are the Green Bonds launched by the Spanish Treasury in 2021.

Indirect climate finance, which is not primarily allocated to climate policies but still contributes to climate objectives, follows the same parameters as direct funding and the EU Taxonomy Regulation. The Report on Alignment with the Ecological Transition of the Draft Budget Law analyses whether the contribution of budgetary programs to environmental objectives is direct or indirect, and whether it may create favorable conditions for compliance, even if it does not constitute the main objective

Spain regularly reports on its climate financial commitments with instruments such as National Communications every 4 years and Biennial Reports every two, in the format and guidelines of UNFCCC (Eighth National Communication and Fifth Biennial Report). The Ecological Transition Alignment Report of the Draft Budget Law also contains a wealth of information in this area and includes "the brown dimension", which also analyses expenditure detrimental to the achievement of environmental objectives.

Eighth National Communication details Spain's financial commitments for 2019-2020, amounting to EUR 740 million and EUR 529 million, respectively. In 2021, Spain announced its commitment to increase international climate finance by 50 %, raising it from EUR 900 million to EUR 1.35 billion annually by 2025. Spain's commitments as developed country to increasing financial support for developing ones is outlined in the Spanish Strategy for International Climate Finance, a planning instrument (2023)

Spain's international climate finance cooperation is primarily channelled through financial contributions from the Official Development Assistance (ODA) and the Other Official Flows (OFO). In 2022, the latest year with available data, a total commitment of EUR 740 million was allocated, with EUR 342 million (46 %) still pending disbursement. Of this, EUR 407 million in ODA had 20 % yet to be disbursed, while EUR 333 million in OFO had a significantly higher 79 % remaining to be paid.

The EU and its Member States are the world's largest providers of climate change funding. Spain, as part of its 2023 International Climate Finance Strategy, reports on its contributions through platforms like Climate Summits and public reports, such as UNFCCC National Communications (every four years) and Biennial Reports (every two years), in accordance with UNFCCC formats and guidelines.
