In 2020 the EU adopted the Taxonomy Regulation 2020/852 to facilitate sustainable investments, and in 2021 the Recovery Facility, followed by the Spanish Recovery and Transformation Plan (PRTR). Under this one the Government has launched 6 strategic projects called PERTES, with 100 % CC objective, and planned to engage EUR 41 billion of private funding. Furthermore, the Spanish Official Credit Institute, in its 2022-2027 Strategy, set a target of 40 % of operations with sustainability criteria.

Both the Spain´s Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (PRTR) and the Spain´s Official Credit Institute feature mechanisms to monitor private climate financing. The ELISA National Platform has been launched to assess the implementation of the PRTR measures. Regarding international private climate finance, Spain compiles information sent to both the EU and UNFCCC on the Reportnet Platform and the UNFCCC Website, where the Biennial Reports are published (the latest related to Spain in 2022)

Spain´s Government reports the degree of implementation of the PRTR in Climate Change on the ELISA Platform. Since 2021, all EU Member States must upload information on private climate finance to the Reportnet platform, although it does not yet provide a comprehensive overview of all mobilized funding. Under the UNFCCC, the Framework Convention website publishes the Biennial Reports, with Spain's latest report from 2022. In addition, there are also private monitoring observatories, such as OFISO

Implementation is advanced because since 2021 Spain has had a comprehensive Law on Climate Change and Energy Transition that ensures compliance with the Paris Agreement, facilitates the decarbonisation of the economy and its transition to a circular model, ensuring adaptation to the impacts of climate change. The Law is part of the Spain´s Strategic Energy and Climate Framework, which puts the fight against climate change and the energy transition at the heart of policy action for the first time

According to Article 1 of the Spain´s Law on Climate Change, its purpose is to ensure full compliance with the Paris Agreement by regulating the approval/review every 5 years of the National Energy and Climate Plan and the National Climate and Adaptation Plan, setting targets for greenhouse gas reduction, renewable energy and energy efficiency, and stressing that integrated national plans are the national strategic planning tool that integrates energy and climate policies.

Spain has integrated compliance with its climate targets into its main national policies and strategies, as evidenced by the National Declaration of Climate and Environmental Emergency, agreed in January 2020. This is a signal of the Spanish Government's commitment to an ambitious regulatory and policy framework, in the context of the Paris Agreement, but within the overall EU energy and climate framework, in which Spain participates in compliance with European climate and energy legislation.

The Spanish Parliament has bodies for CC issues such as the Congress's Committee on the Ecological Transition, with competences in climate matters, which approves the non-legislative proposals and deals with draft climate laws, and the Senate's Committee on Ecological Transition, the legislative and monitoring committee on climate matters. In addition, several reports related to climate issues were produced in 2022 and 2023 by the relevant Bureau of Science and Technology of the Spanish Congress

In the last five years, the Spain Court of Audits carried out a special audit with the Climate Change as its main subject, the Audit Report on the action of the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Food and the Environment and the Ministry of Ecological Transition in relation to climate change, approved in 2021. In addition, others reports have been drawn up by the SAI of Spain on protected natural areas, on fire-fighting and desertification, on the management of GHG emissions allowances, etc.

In Spain, the major climate dispute or climate lawsuit was resolved by the Supreme Court in 2023 rejecting the actions of environmental associations against the government's failure to act on the grounds that it did not approve the National Mitigation Plan in 2019, and by the Plan approved later. In 2022, Spain had 17 disputes relating to CC, ranked ninth worldwide. In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights dismissed Duarte Agostinho's application against Portugal and others (including Spain).

Spain has a specific governance structure to address climate change, headed by the Ministry for the Ecological Transition, whose head is Deputy Prime Minister, and the State Secretariat for the Environment, which directs and coordinates climate policies. Below is the Spanish Climate Change Office (OECC), which formulates and drives these policies. In addition, there are other bodies such as the National Climate Council and the Climate Change Policy Coordination Commission.

In Spain, climate change responsibilities are well defined from the highest level (President and Council of Ministers), approving draft laws and submitting them to Parliament, as well as implementing regulations, to the level of policy formulation and implementation undertaken by the Spanish CC Office, in accordance with Royal Decree 503/2024, through the Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Secretary of State for the Environment, which direct and coordinate the national policy of CC.

In Spain, with the current distribution of responsibilities between the Council of Ministers, deciding body, the Ministry for the Ecological Transition, the State Secretariat for the Environment, and the Spanish CC Office, in addition to the General Committee of State Secretaries and Undersecretaries, a cross-cutting and coordinating body, there are no place for internal overlaps or gaps. Collaboration with the regions has also been strengthened with a dedicated coordination commission in CC.

In the Spanish Government climate leadership lies with the Third Vice-President for the Ecological Transition, led by the competence Ministry and the State Secretariat for the Environment, where the main CC policies are coordinated, formulated and implemented. This is done through the Spanish CC Office which is the specific administrative body responsible for coordination between the ministerial departments with competence in this area, such as the Ministry of Health or the Ministry of Transport

In 2020, Spain approved its Decarbonization Long-term Strategy (LTS) for a Modern, Competitive and Climate-Neutra Spanish Economy in 2050, submitted to the UNFCCC, which guides Spain towards climate neutrality in line with the EU's NDC and which is an essential part of Spain's Strategic Energy and Climate Framework, together with the Law on Climate Change and Energy Transition, the Just Transition Strategy, the National Climate Adaptation Plan and the Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan.

In 2023, the EU sent the technical update of its NDC with the new greenhouse gas reduction target (55 %) and the entire energy and climate legislative framework (Fit for 55 package). Spain's LTS is consistent with that objective and with the EU NDC, involving all sectors of the national economy. Although its ambition is currently not fully aligned with the latest update of the NDC, it will be with its imminent revision in 2025 and with the update in 2024 of the National Energy and Climate Plan.

Spain's LTS contains many references to the SDGs, the synergies between them and the analysis of their relations, highlighting SDG 13 (Climate Action) which is "intrinsic to the development of this strategy". The LTS also identifies the SDGs impacts positive or negative in CC but does not indicate how to capitalise these positive impacts or minimise negative ones. The National Energy and Climate Plan also sets out its contribution to the SDGs and sets SDGs 7 and 13 as one of its core objectives

The climate risk map in Spain is the 2021 "Climate Change Impacts and Risks Report" released in collaboration with the scientific community. Include the risk ratio and the assessment of the urgency to address them across a wide range of sectors. Other studies analyse sectors not covered in this report, so the risk map covers all relevant sectors. In addition, a new impact and risk assessment is being prepared covering the whole national territory and analysing cross-border risks and new sectors

The main scientific analysis in Spain on climate issues, the 2021 Report on the Impacts and Risks of Climate Change, was promoted by the Ministry of Ecological Transition but coordinated by the prestigious scientific centre "Basque Centre for Climate Change (BC3)", involving numerous experts in the main fields of CC in Spain's production sectors and natural systems. Another academic involvement in climate decision-making and risk assessment is the Ministry's Advisory Group with 19 experts on CC.

In Spain, major economic planning instruments such as the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (PRTR) or multiannual budgetary plans assess and consider climate risks, contributing to the 2030 climate targets and the 2050 climate neutrality objective. Half of the PRTR funds for Spain have a positive climate and environmental impact. Other strategies include the Spanish Urban Agenda (2019), the National Civil Protection Strategy (2019), the Strategic Health and Environment Plan (2021).

The Spain´s Government has internal coordination mechanisms to manage climate policies and the CC is one of its priorities and a cross-cutting issue, not sectoral as before. For the first time a Deputy Prime Minister is assigned to the Ecological Transition and its first initiative was to declare the Climate and Environmental Emergency. The Ministry participates in the decision-making bodies such as the Council of Ministers and its main climate support body formulates and evaluates CC policicies

Horizontal coordination in the Spanish Government on climate matters is working well given the information available on the operability and effectiveness of the collaboration mechanisms put in place. The interaction on climate matters between the Council of Ministers, the General Committee of State Secretaries, the Delegated Committee for Economic Affairs and the National Climate Council is demonstrated by evidence of their meetings, events and decisions (agendas and minutes of their meetings).

Spain has good vertical coordination mechanisms for managing climate policies (CC). Stand out in this area the National Climate Council established in 1998, as an institutional forum for the participation of all public administrations, organisations and bodies representing social and environmental interests and the Committee for the Coordination of CC Policies, established in 2005, which is the real coordination and collaboration body between the central administration and the autonomous regions

Cooperation between the central government and regional and local governments on climate matters is correct and appropriate, as demonstrated by the operational and effective coordination mechanisms put in place, with evidence obtained from their numerous meetings, events and decisions taken. Highlights the Policy Coordination Committee of CC, the main body for coordination and collaboration between the National Government and the Autonomous Regions on climate and emissions trading policies.

Spain has 3 established participation mechanisms: 1. National Climate Council, an advisory body composed of public administrations and non-governmental actors (civil society, private sector and academia). It´s very relevant but its conclusions are not enforceable. 2. Citizens' Climate Assembly, a citizens engagement forum to reflect and share knowledge on solutions to the CC. It made 172 recommendations on CC for a safer and fairer Spain. 3 Climate Generation, a youth climate engagement program.

In Spain, the composition of the participatory bodies is laid down in rules, but good representativeness is not fully guaranteed. Criteria for representation on the Climate Council give precedence to government and could be improved due to low participation of science or civil society. Only 25 % of non-governmental actors. The Citizens' Assembly involves 100 randomly selected ones, with no guarantee of fair representativeness of these stakeholders (civil society, private sector and academia).

The interaction of participatory bodies could be improved. The Climate Council has few meetings (2 in 4 years) and with more informative and deliberative debates than decisions. The Citizens' Assembly has an impact on the design of climate policies but not on their implementation and monitoring, with little activity and questionable representativeness in votes without discrepancies, etc. The Climate Generation initiative also has little activity with a strong focus on attending climate summits.

Groups vulnerable to climate policies and their needs are identified in Spain by risk, including youth, coal mining, people living near thermal or nuclear power or who live in sparsely populated areas, farmers, general public, etc. In this area, the Just Transition Strategy, to increase the social benefits of the green transition and mitigate its negative impacts should be highlighted, as well as the Energy Poverty Strategy, which defines this type of poverty and sets reduction targets for 2025.

In Spain, the views and perspectives of vulnerable groups to climate change (CC) are heard and taken into account in the climate policies decision-making process through three specific forms of collaboration: 1. Working meetings with organisations defending their interests; 2. Support for the development of studies and manuals on CC risks and adaptation by social organisations; and 3. Encouraging the development of risk and vulnerability CC analysis by other public institutions.

The just energy transition takes place with dialogue and social participation, due to its labour and economic dimension (closure of mines and coal or nuclear power plants, etc.), through agreements guaranteeing employment between government, companies and trade unions. To revitalize areas where the transition is challenging, diagnostics are being developed and Just Transition Conventions with action plans are being signed. The PRTR has just transition objectives with a strong budget allocation.

At national level and as part of the EU, Spain has mechanisms for compliance with its reporting obligations on CC policies and progress. The reports submitted (Regulation EU 2018/1999 on the Governance of the Energy Union and Climate Action, National Communications and Biennial Reports) are further analyzed and reviewed by the European Commission or the UNFCCC. The reviews are made public and allow the identification of progress in climate policies, including measurable indicators and targets.

The detailed information obtained during the climate policies reporting to the European Commission or the UNFCCC and the review reports of those reports is considered to be key to subsequent informed decision-making. As these mechanisms are regular, they allow continuous improvement through a process of feedback, with numerous recommendations identifying aspects that need to be followed up. These recommendations are analysed and taken into account in the next cycle of preparation of new reports.

In Spain, the implementation of global transparency in climate policy is advanced because it has drawn up all its national communications in due time, i.e. every 4 years, since 1994, and the Eighth National Communication was reported in 2022, and the Fifth Biennial Report was also submitted in the same year. Spain has therefore, since the start, complied with its international commitments to submit updated information, stemming from the signature of the 2015 Paris Agreement and the UNFCCC.

The information and documentation on Climate Change available on the Web Pages of the Spanish CC Office and the Ecological Transition Ministry is complete and up-to-date, ensuring transparency and the right of access of non-state actors and the general public to information on climate policies. Transparency is also improved by the Citizens' Information Platform on Adaptation to Climate Change called AdapteCCA.es, the National Gas Emissions Inventory, National Communications and Biennial Reports.

The Ecological Transition Ministry´ web portal contains extensive and accessible information on CC which is regularly updated, as well as numerous strategies, reports and studies on all relevant aspects of the CC. It also highlights the Citizens' Information Platform on Adaptation to the CC, AdapteCCa.es, with a lot of affordable and easily understandable information, as a joint initiative of the Spanish CC Office and the Biodiversity Foundation, both of which are part of the competent Ministry

Spain participates in the CC policy of EU, as an International Economic Integration Organisation (REIOs) of Article 4.16 of the Paris Agreement. The EU presented in October 2023 the latest update of its First NDC in 2015, with the so-called EU NDC 2023 Update, which increases Europe's 2030 climate ambition (Fit for 55 package). Spain, in turn, as a Member State, complies with its obligations laid down in European energy and climate legislation for 2030, the European Energy and Climate Framework.

Path to climate neutrality in 2050, the updated EU NDC submitted to the UNFCCC in October 2023, reflects an increase in ambition with the 2030 emission reduction target of 55 % compared to 1990. It is considered to be a more comprehensive, more transparent and complementary NDC with the European Energy and Climate Framework, established to ensure compliance with the Fit for 55 Package. The previous EU NDC 2015 reduction target, revised upwards in December 2020, was only 40 %.

Sectoral objectives to achieve the overall EU NDC targets are not included in the NDC itself but in other government instruments, such as national plans, programmes or laws, because the contribution of different sectors to meeting the EU targets is defined in the European Energy and Climate Regulation (Fit for 55 Package). In Spain, the new Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan (2023-2030) sets the decarbonization path to 2030 with the contribution of the different sectors of the economy.

In Spain, the 2020 CC Impacts and Risks Report analyses a wide range of sectors, but there are also analyses in sectors not covered by that report and the Spanish CC Office has started the process for a new risk assessment to be completed in 2025. First European Climate Risk Assessment Report identifies 36 climate risks that pose a threat to Europe's energy and food security, ecosystems, infrastructure, water resources, etc. Insights from these assessments will inform strategic policy making.

Spain's strategy to mitigate CC is the new Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan 2023-2030, a key part of the Strategic Energy and Climate Framework with the Energy Transition and CC Law, the Decarbonisation Strategy 2050 (LTS) and the Just Transition Strategy. The recent update of the Plan will make it possible to adapt it to the EU's increased ambition and the acceleration of the energy transition by the PRTR, as Spain has increased the reduction of gas emissions to 32% compared to 1990.

The LTS, under Sectoral Decarbonisation, sets out emission reduction plans and programmes in the main sectors of the economy and actions to achieve this, aligned with national strategies. The new National Energy and Climate Plan includes policies and measures for decarbonisation, noting that the sectors with the highest emission reductions are electricity generation and transport. Other sectoral transitions, with climate-neutrality actions, include the Hydrogen Roadmap, the Biogas Roadmap, etc.

The Spain´s Law on CC and Energy Transition (2021), basic rule on CC, devotes its Title V to adaptation, which cycle runs until 2050 with the LTS, through the National Adaptation Plan 2021-2030 and its First Work Program 2021-2025 that develops it. While the Plan is the roadmap to reduce the damage of CC and build a resilient economy and society and identifies 18 affected areas or sectors, the Program includes concrete development measures, identifies those responsible and provides indicators.

The National Plan for Adaptation to the CC identifies 18 areas of work or sectors of climate action under public or private management, specifying the objectives and the lines of action to achieve them. It identifies 7 cross-cutting aspects to be developed in these areas and the tools for reporting and monitoring adaptation policies and the Plan itself. The 2021 CC Impacts and Risks Report analyses the main impacts of CC by sector and system, linking the risks and the urgency to address them.

The development of the National CC Adaptation Plan is contained in the First Work Program and it´s not planned to update it until the end of its validity in 2030, given the flexibility of the system for implementing these policies. Each Work Program of the two planned (2021-2025 and 2026-2030) builds on the lessons learned from the previous one, putting forward new measures and identifying unforeseen needs. It also highlights the information contained in the Spain´s Eighth National Communication

The new version of the Integrated National Plan for Energy and Climate (PNIEC 2023-2030) raised the decarbonisation target to 81 % and includes the policies and measures to achieve this objective, with a full section dedicated to 'Energy generation'. This is based on renewable sources and two priority objectives, increasing the efficiency of the various renewable energies and reducing the cost of their technologies, through the development of Photovoltaic, Biomass, Wind and Oceanic energy.

The definition and updated design of climate policies for the transport sector is set out in the "Sustainable Mobility Strategy" of the new version of the Integrated National Plan for Energy and Climate (PNIEC 2023-2030), which main strategic lines for this sector are the promotion of public transport, the promotion of electric vehicles and the integration of urban planning with sustainable mobility. Among other objectives, the target is to reach 5.5 million electric vehicles by 2030

In Spain, the new version of the Integrated National Plan for Energy and Climate (PNIEC 2023-2030) sets specific measures for the transport sector, highlighting Measure 2.3. Renewal of the vehicle fleet (50 % of progress); Measure 2.4. Electric vehicle pulse (75 % of progress); Measure 2.10. Energy efficiency in farms, irrigation communities and agricultural machinery (25 % of progress); Measure 3.3. Recharging points for alternative fuels (50 % of progress).

The PNIEC 2023-2030 contains specific measures in the electricity generation sub-sector, highlighting the implementation of Measure 1.3: Adaptation of electricity grids for the integration of renewables (75 % progress); Measure 1.5. Incorporation of renewables in the industrial sector (50 %); Measure 1.9. Technological renovation plan for electricity generation projects using renewable energy (50 %). Measure 1.11. Specific programmes for biomass harvesting (25 %).

In Spain, within the framework created by the new version of the Integrated National Plan for Energy and Climate (PNIEC 2023-2030), concrete initiatives of a strategic nature have been developed to identify the challenges and opportunities in driving the energy transition, highlighting the Self-Consumption Roadmap, Renewable Hydrogen Roadmap, Biogas Roadmap, Marine Wind Development Roadmap, Energy Transmission Network Planning Horizon 2026, etc.

The 2012-2024 Plan for Infrastructure, Transport and Housing includes, among others, a diagnosis of the Spanish transport system of infrastructure and services, of the regulatory framework and environmental and territorial impact, but does not include the requested map of challenges for each measure. The report on "Decarbonising transport" devotes a chapter to the opportunities and challenges of decarbonisation, but does not include a map of challenges for the implementation of the measures.

The main mitigation actions in the transport area are assigned to the bodies responsible for their implementation and monitoring. The update PNIEC 2023-2030 presents under Table A.50 the GHG projections but the specific monitoring actions for the measures approved are not developed in the Plan. This is in line with the European Commission's report on the evaluation of the PNIEC-2021-2030, stressing that the mechanisms for monitoring and evaluating the measures taken are not always established.

The new Integrated National Plan for Energy and Climate (PNIEC) 2023-2030 sets out the bodies responsible for monitoring the main mitigation actions in the area of electricity generation, although the details of the monitoring actions and the assessment criteria are not precisely developed. This is in line with the European Commission's 'Assessment of the PNIEC 2021-2030 report, stressing that mechanisms for monitoring and evaluating the measures taken are not always established or developed.

In the area of human health sector, Spanish Government adopted in 2021 the 'Strategic Plan for Health and the Environment 2022-2026', the main policy plan for reducing the health risks associated to the Climate Change. In addition, there is a 'National Action Plan for Preventive Action against the Effects of Excessive Health Temperature', a 'National Plan for the Prevention, Surveillance and Control of Diseases Transmitted by Vectors' and a 'Strategic Plan for Safety and Health at Work'.

In Spain, the State Meteorology Agency coordinates and develops this component of the National Plan for Adaptation to the Climate Change (2021-2030), working with the most active Spanish investigation groups and the Spanish Office of CC. Its main actions include strengthening climate observation, early warnings and regionalised CC projections. Specifically, for each work programme of the Adaptation Plan, this Agency and the Office of CC have already prepared regionalized projection scenarios.

In Spain, the National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change 2021-2030 (2020) includes the integration of measures into the Strategic Plan for Health and the Environment, with specific measures and lines of action for the prevention and protection of health and with specific actions to prevent the effects of high temperatures on health. It also includes actions in response to infectious diseases and parasitic diseases due to Climate Change and to the impact of Climate Change on workers' health.

In Spain the National Plan for the Adaptation to the CC (2021-2030) contains specific climate objectives and climate scenarios with specific action lines set out in its Annex 1 I.1-Systematic climate monitoring. The most relevant actions include improving the national observation system, observation networks, the spanish contribution to global networks; coordination of observation activities, operating protocols, and standardisation of data dissemination formats.

The first National Plan for Adaptation to CC (2006-2020) identified adaptation challenges addressed by the Plan 2021-2030 in 10 blocks, including resources, governance and monitoring. This Plan contains seven 'cross-cutting aspects' with implementation challenges, such as territorial or social vulnerability. At sectorial level, however, the analysis of challenges is not comprehensive of the entire human health sector, and the information has to be found at subsectorial working documents level.

The Spain´s First Plan for Adaptation to the CC (2006-2020) identified the challenges that have been considered for new Plan (2021-2030). They are presented in 10 blocks, which also include seven cross-cutting aspects with main implementation challenges; however, there is not a specific mapping for every challenge and related action for the entire 'Climate and Climate Scenarios' sector, and this more detailed information is only available at more subsectoral or thematic working papers level.

The Spain´s National Plan for Adaptation to the Climate Change (2021-2030) sets out objectives, indicators and the organisms responsible for monitoring the measures. For the 'Climate and Climate Scenarios' specific sector it is defined who leads each action, and the performance indicators such as the number of observation stations, the contribution of the main networks for climate observation, the availability of up-to-date data, and climate indicators for consultation.

In Spain, for each action planned in the human health sector, the Plan for Adaptation to CC sets out the responsible for the different actions and compliance indicators. The Strategic Plan for Health and the Environment (2022-2026) contains objectives and compliance indicators, many of which are planned but still to be developed. This Plan also includes the Health Impact Assessment of together with an Interdepartmental Monitoring Committee for that Strategic Plan for Health and the Environment.

Led by the Vice President's Office with support from the 2050 Pathways Platform and International Climate Initiative (IKI), the process aims to chart a pathway to net zero that aligns with the Paris Agreement.

The National Climate Change Response Strategy has mapped the climate change impacts in Tanzania. The Strategy identifies key climate risks across various sectors and outlines mitigation and adaptation measures, with Chapters 3 and 5 specifically detailing the risks and strategic responses to enhance resilience and minimize vulnerability.

The country through the National Climate Change Response, indicates the involvement of research and academic institutions, development partners, civil society organizations, and other Institutions in developing of this Strategy. This clearly indicate the involvement of scientific institutions in the process of mapping the risks

The National Climate Change Technical Committee (NCCTC) and the National Climate Change Steering Committee (NCCSC) guide the implementation of the Strategy. The NCCTC gives technical advice to the National Climate Change Focal Point, while the NCCSC gives policy guidance and makes sure all sectors work together.

As of May 2025, Tanzania's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) is not up to date in accordance with Article 4, paragraph 9 of the Paris Agreement. This article mandates that Parties submit updated NDCs every five years. Tanzania submitted its first updated NDC on July 30, 2021. Therefore, the next update was due by early 2025.

Tanzania's updated 2022 NDC is more ambitious than its previous one, in line with Article 4.3 of the Paris Agreement. It raises emission reduction targets from 10-20% to 30-35% by 2030 and expands sectoral coverage. The update also involved inclusive stakeholder participation and aligns with national development goals.

Tanzania's 2022 NDC outlines an overall emissions reduction target but does not specify sectoral targets within the NDC itself. However, national strategies like the National Climate Change Response Strategy provide sector-specific goals in energy, forestry, waste, and transport. These plans support the broader NDC goals through detailed mitigation actions.

Tanzania has mapped national policies impacting GHG emissions through its updated NDC and draft NDC Implementation Plan. These documents align sectoral actions with national development goals and climate targets. The government is also developing a national MRV system to track emissions and policy effectiveness.

Tanzania has set clear Green House Gases (GHG) reduction goals aiming for a 30-35% cut by 2030 and outlined strategies in its updated NDC and National Climate Change Response Strategy. Key policies and sector-specific actions are identified in energy, forestry, transport, and waste. An Measurable, Reportable, and Verifiable (MRV) system is being developed to track progress and policy effectiveness.

Tanzania has sector-specific plans aligned with national climate strategies to reduce emissions. These include renewable energy expansion, forest conservation, low-emission transport systems, and improved waste management. Each plan supports the national goal of cutting GHG emissions by 30-35% by 2030.

Tanzania submitted its National Adaptation Plan (NAP) to the UNFCCC. In April 2013, the country submitted a roadmap detailing its approach to formulating a national adaptation plan, as per the guidelines established by the UNFCCC's Conference of the Parties (COP)
The Government of Tanzania has identified the most relevant adaptation sectors and developed national adaptation plans and strategies addressing these sectors.

Tanzania updated its National Climate Change Response Strategy for 2021-2026 within the last five years, emphasizing adaptation and resilience. The Tanzania Health National Adaptation Plan 2018-2023 is also under review to address climate-related health impacts.

Tanzania's NCCRS 2021-2026 identifies LULUCF as a priority for emission reduction, focusing on forest conservation, afforestation, and sustainable land use. Also, the NDC reinforces these goals through commitments to REDD+ and sustainable forest management.
The NCCRS 2021-2026 details measures such as afforestation, REDD+, and climate-smart agriculture. These targeted actions support the country's broader emission reduction objectives.

The Tanzanian government has identified several challenges hindering the implementation of climate policies and the achievement of goals in the Land Use, Land-Use Change, and Forestry (LULUCF) sector. These challenges are outlined in key national documents such as the National Climate Change Response Strategy (NCCRS) 2021-2026 and the updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).

The National Climate Change Response Strategy (NCCRS) 2021-2026 outlines a comprehensive M&E framework. This framework includes the development of a system to collect, compile, analyze, and evaluate information related to the implementation of the strategy. The Vice President's Office (VPO) is responsible for coordinating these efforts, working through Sector Environmental Sections and Units, Regional Environmental Experts, and Environmental Management Officers from sector ministries and LGAs.

The Country has established public policies to address climate adaptation in the water sector. The National Water Policy (2025) and the Water Sector Development Programme promote climate resilience through infrastructure, integrated water management, and early warning systems. These are supported by the National Climate Change Strategy (2021-2026).

Tanzania's key climate adaptation policies for agriculture include the NCCRS 2021-2026, Agriculture Climate Resilience Plan, (2014), and Climate Smart Agriculture Programme. They focus on promoting sustainable farming, climate-smart technologies, and building farmers' capacity. These efforts aim to enhance resilience and ensure food security amid climate challenges.

The National Climate Change Response Strategy (2021-2026) and the National Water Policy (2025), outline specific actions to meet adaptation goals. These include infrastructure development, early warning systems, sustainable resource management, and institutional capacity building. The actions are tailored to address sector-specific climate vulnerabilities and enhance resilience.

Tanzania's national adaptation policies outline specific actions to meet sectoral objectives. Key plans target agriculture, water, and health through measures like climate-smart farming and improved irrigation. These actions aim to build resilience and reduce climate risks.

The government has identified several challenges in implementing climate adaptation policies, particularly in sectors like agriculture and water. These challenges include limited institutional and technical capacity, inadequate financial resources, data and information gaps, and low public awareness. Addressing these barriers is crucial for achieving national climate goals.

The government through FAO has mapped key challenges in implementing adaptation policies, especially in agriculture. These include limited technical capacity, insufficient funding, and data gaps. Public awareness and institutional coordination are also noted as major barriers.

The National Climate Change Response Strategy (2021-2026) includes a dedicated framework for monitoring progress, evaluating effectiveness, and informing decision-making. However, implementation remains challenged by limited data, capacity, and coordination at various administrative levels.

The Government has established monitoring and evaluation systems to track adaptation policy outcomes, led by the Vice President's Office. These systems include clear indicators and reporting processes for sectors like water and agriculture.

Budget allocation is prepared in accordance with the National Strategy and its Master Plans, National Economic and Social Development Plan, National Security Policy and Plan, and major government policies. Budget for reducing GHG emission and impact of natural disasters and climate change are allocated under "Strategic Program on Coping with Repercussions from Climate Change." However, there is no identification of carbon-intensive actions in the budgets and calculation of perverse subsidies.

However,the Thai government, through the Budget Bureau (BB),has its own system known as the "Budget Allocation Strategy" to determine both direct and indirect climate finance. The BB tracks national direct climate change expenditure through monitoring and evaluation mechanisms mandated by the Budgetary Procedures Act, B.E. 2561 (2018).

However, the Thai government, through the Budget Bureau (BB), has its own system known as the "Budget Allocation Strategy" to determine both direct and indirect climate finance. The BB tracks national indirect climate change expenditure through monitoring and evaluation mechanisms mandated by the Budgetary Procedures Act, B.E. 2561 (2018).

The national government has mechanisms mandated by the Budgetary Procedures Act, B.E. 2561 (2018) to report domestic climate expenditure in accordance with the Budget Allocation Strategy. Although the budget expenditure reports are regularly published and accessible via the Budget Bureau's website, they do not explicitly provide details on direct and indirect expenditures, nor do they classify carbon-intensive budgets or perverse subsidies.

Department of Climate Change and Environment (DCCE) periodically requests line ministries and agencies to report their international support needs. The financial support requirements for mitigation and adaptation actions and enabling environments, as identified by relevant agencies, are included in BUR4, NC4, BTR1 and NDC Action Plan on Mitigation 2021-2030. Besides overall financial support needed, these reports do not provide cost estimates for the identified needs.

Thailand's primary focus is on the Green Climate Fund(GCF).The Thailand Country Program & GCF Handbook has been developed to guide stakeholders to understand GCF processes,national requirements,and project planning for GCF & other climate funds.These tools also mention other potential domestic & international climate funds.For receiving funds like ThaiCI Fund,the government has set a mechanism to mobilize funds through the consideration of a subcommittee under the Environmental Subcommittee.

The financial support for Thailand, excluding global and regional supporting projects, is reported in the NC3, NC4 ,BUR4,and BTR1. These reports provide details on type of support, objectives, descriptions, timeframe and status of project, donors/partners, and the funding amounts. However, results of projects are not mentioned in above reports .DCCE is responsible for tracking the climate funds from UNFCCC and reporting back to the respective agencies.

The projects that received international support have put in place a mechanism, such as a steering committee, to consider and provide guidance/comment on the project management concerns, project activities as well as budgets. Moreover, the government reports the international financial support received through the NC, BUR and BTR, which are published on the UNFCCC and DCCE websites according to a mandatory schedule. However, there is no evidence showing how funds have been spent, and the report meets the donor's reporting requirements.

The government has developed incentives to encourage GHG reduction efforts by offering benefits to entrepreneurs, aimed at promoting private sector investment in GHG reduction. These incentives include (1) tax benefits or customs duty reductions/exemptions for the Voluntary GHG Emission Reduction Project, and (2) tax benefits for investments in the Thailand ESG Fund (TESG). However, there is insufficient information available on mapping alternatives for private funding.

Thailand's private climate finance tracking operates through various mechanisms within its broader climate policy framework, with key roles played by the Bank of Thailand, the financial regulator & the Securities and Exchange Commission of Thailand, the capital market regulator. The Thai Greenhouse Gas Management Organization also supports/promotes private sector, through carbon market & green bond. However, there is no centralized database to track climate investment across various agencies.

Thailand's private climate finance tracking system operates through various mechanisms within its broader climate policy framework, with key roles played by the central bank, Securities and Exchange Commission and The Thai Greenhouse Gas Management Organization. However, there is no centralized database to track climate investments across various agencies. As a result, reporting on private climate finance is voluntary.

Thailand still lacks direct legislation or specific laws on climate change aimed at achieving climate mitigation & adaptation objectives. The current fundamental law in is the Enhancement and Conservation of National Environmental Quality Act, B.E. 2535, enacted in 1992. This act covers a wide range of pollution issues, including water pollution, air pollution, waste management, noise, and vibration. However, Thailand's Climate Change Bill is progressing through the legislative process.

Thailand's Climate Change Act is being developed to help the country achieve its commitments under the Paris Agreement. However, in response to escalating global concerns over climate change, the government sets ambitious strategies & targets through policies & plans. Thailand established the National Committee on Climate Change Policy by Order of the Office of the Prime Minister on Climate Change Implementation B.E.2550.The committee has the mandate to formulate national climate change policy.

Thailand has not yet enacted a specific law that solely addresses climate change; however, there are relevant laws and regulations governing environmental issues, such as the Enhancement and Conservation of National Environmental Quality Act, B.E. 2535; the Factory Act, B.E. 2535; the Land Transport Act, B.E. 2522; and the Energy Conservation Act, B.E. 2535.

The House of Representatives & the Senate have committees focused on environmental issues, including climate change: the Committee on Land, Natural Resources, and Environment, and the Committee on Natural Resources and Environment, respectively. Parliament plays role in monitoring government action related to climate change, handling public complaints, researching, disseminating relevant knowledge. It facilitates discussions among stakeholders, e.g. public hearings on the climate change bill.

In 2025, SAI Thailand are currently conducting both compliance and performance audits on climate change adaptation through its Central, Regional, and Provincial Audit Offices. The outcome will be a comprehensive report on domestic public climate finance.

Although one climate change lawsuit has been filed in court (Residents of Omkoi v. Expert Committee on EIA Consideration and ONEP), the Thai judiciary is well-prepared to adjudicate climate change cases. The Administrative Courts and the Supreme Court each have their own Environmental Divisions and environmental case databases. The Judiciary also conducted comparative studies and hosted the seminars on climate justice, climate change litigation adjudication and other related topics.

The National Committee on Climate Change Policy (NCCC) was established by Order of the Office of the Prime Minister on Climate Change Implementation B.E. 2550 (2007) (Amended). Chaired by the Prime Minister, the committee includes members from both the public and private sectors, as well as experts from relevant agencies. Its role is to undertake climate change policy planning and coordination management within the national framework and multilateral environmental agreements.

The NCCC comprises members from public/private sectors/experts from relevant agencies. Under NCCC, many organizations have been assigned responsibilities that involve leading, coordinating, implementing, monitoring related activities. DCCE serves as UNFCCC Focal Point  & oversees climate change missions & operations, monitoring, reporting & encouraging participation from all sectors at all levels. Though, a unified & effective system connecting all agencies is still needed.

The NCCC is composed of 7 subcommittees including members from public/private sectors and experts from relevant agencies. Each subcommittee's role is to provide comments on policy integration & strategy across various areas. They serve as channels for driving forward proposed policies, projects, plans, reducing inefficiencies caused by overlapping responsibilities. However, there is still need a unified & effective system connecting all agencies through well-functioning coordination mechanisms.

The NCCC is the core of the institutional framework for climate governance. It's responsible for reviewing & approving national climate policies as well as establishing guidelines & mechanisms for international collaboration in response to conventions & protocols on climate change. Additionally, the Department of Climate Change and Environment functions as the secretariat of the NCCC, playing a crucial role in leading and coordinating efforts at the working level.
Thailand revised the Long-term Low Greenhouse Gas Emission Development Strategy (LT-LEDS) in November 2022, which results in strengthened targets.

At COP26, Thailand committed to achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 & net zero GHG emissions by 2065. Thailand also pledged to enhance the NDC to reduce GHG emissions by 30-40% in 2030 up from previous target of 20-25%. To align with the updated NDC, LT-LEDS has been revised in accordance with national circumstances & an updated technical analysis. The revised LT-LEDS lays out climate policies, priorities, measures that will navigate towards low GHG emissions & climate-resilient development.

The revised Long-term Low Greenhouse Gas Emissions Development Strategy (LT-LEDS) does not explicitly reference the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs); however, its content is implicitly aligned with the SDGs.

Thailand has developed a database of geospatial risks from climate change by assessing climate impacts, risks, and vulnerabilities in 6 significant sectors: water management, agriculture and food security, tourism, public health, natural resources management, and human settlement and security. The risk and vulnerability assessments for climate projection are based on data as of 2021 using climate scenarios generated through the General Circulation Models (GCMs) and RCP models.

The climate scenarios generated model (GCMs and RCP models) was developed by specialists and researchers from Center of Regional Climate Change and Renewable Energy, Ramkhamhaeng University (RU-CORE). The analysis used data from the future climate projection, downscaling, non-climate factors, and socio-economic data etc.

The NAP process starts with the analysis of the risks & vulnerabilities in each sector by using global climate models under IPCC's SRES A1B emission scenario. The downscaling would enable the simulation of climate trends to be used with a risk management approach to develop the initial guidelines & measures for climate change adaptation in each sector. The risk analysis generated by the model has also been employed to address climate risk in drafting the adaptation plans at provincial level.

The NCCC, chaired by the Prime Minister, is Thailand's primary institutional mechanism for climate change policy, consisting of members from 15 ministries, 4 agencies, private sector and other organizations. It is responsible for defining national climate policies and establishing guidelines and mechanisms for international collaboration on climate change conventions and protocols, and supporting and evaluating domestic relevant agencies to ensure compliance with national policies and plans.

The NCCC meets 2-4 times annually, while the subcommittees meet 1-3 times annually to discuss climate change issues in the national context. Climate Change Convention Officers (CCCO) are stationed in 30 related government agencies to coordinate activities among relevant NCCC entities. However, as noted in the 4th NC, there remain challenges with limited integration and ineffective coordination among related agencies in certain sectors e.g. water resource management and climate data management.

Apart from the National Committee on Climate Change Policy, there is the Provincial Committee on Climate Change at the provincial level. This committee is responsible for developing climate mitigation and adaptation action plans, measures, and greenhouse gas reduction targets. Chaired by the Provincial Governor, the committee includes members from relevant regional government agencies. Representatives from local governments, private sector, and civil society may be included in the committee.

The Provincial Committee on Climate Change ordinarily meets 2-5 times annually to discuss about climate change policies in the local context. The Provincial Office of Natural Resources and Environment acts as the focal point to facilitate the coordination efforts. However, the complex & overlapping responsibilities between entities under deconcentration & those under decentralization somehow hinder effective coordination between relevant regional government actors & local governments.

Members of national and provincial climate committees are mainly from government agencies while the rest come from non-governmental sectors. Stakeholders have been consulted and engaged during the making of the 13th National Development Plans, as well as the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC), National Adaptation Plans (NAP), and public hearings organized for the development of the National Communication (NC), Biennial Update Reports (BUR), Long-Term Strategy (LTS), and updated NDC.

At the national level, members of the NCCC and its subcommittees include representatives from civil society, the private sector, and academia. At the local level, provinces have the authority to customize their climate change committee membership to align with local political, social, and economic contexts. As a result, representatives from the private sector, civil society, and academia can be included in the committee based on the specific needs of each province.

Both national and provincial climate change committees hold the meeting 2-5 times annually to discuss relevant issues related to the design and implementation of climate change policies, plans, or activities. There are provisions explicitly and implicitly allowing members of committees to express their opinion and invite individuals or representatives from the public and private sector to provide information and opinions. However, decision-making under these mechanisms appears to be top-down.

The 2022 CPEIR indicates that Timor-Leste dedicated 1.8% of the General Budget to climate action between 2018-21, with 65% of resources directed to drainage and road works, 25% to institutional capacity building and 10% to community campaigns.
Private investment in climate projects in Timor-Leste has remained limited, but some examples are notable. The country's first major public-private partnership (PPP) project was the construction of the Tibar Bay Port, inaugurated in November 2022. The government contributed US$130 million through the Viability Gap Fund, and Timor-Port (a subsidiary of the French company Bolloré) invested US$150 million, bringing the initial phase to a total of US$280 million. This infrastructure, in addition to improving maritime connectivity, was conceived as a "green port," helping to diversify the local economy. The UN-funded Blue Economy Plan also emphasizes that a "qualitative and quantitative leap" in public and private investment will be necessary to seize sustainable opportunities in the country.

The 2022 CPEIR indicates that Timor-Leste dedicated 1.8% of the General Budget to climate action between 2018-21, with 65% of the resources going to drainage and road works, 25% to institutional capacity building, and 10% to community campaigns.In 2011, the World Bank provided a US$20 million IDA credit to the Road Climate Resilience Project (P125032) to upgrade the Dili-Ainaro road and install drainage systems.Under the GCF, FP171 with US$2,098,722 was approved for early warning systems and FP109 with US$2,235,6805 for community protection.In 2023, the ADB provided $6 million in grants as part of a $16.6 million water resilience package.

Timor-Leste is actively working on tracking climate change finance, both direct and indirect. The country has established a National Climate Change Directorate and is actively involved in international collaborations to secure funding for climate action. A recent Climate Public Expenditure and Institutional Review (CPEIR) identified significant climate-related expenditures in the national budget, even during challenging periods.

Timor-Leste is actively engaged in reporting on public climate change finance, as evidenced by its Climate Public Expenditure and Institutional Review (CPEIR) and other initiatives. The country is particularly vulnerable to climate change impacts, requiring a coordinated approach across government and with development partners.

Timor-Leste receives international climate finance from various sources, including multilateral institutions like the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and the Global Environment Facility (GEF) (under the UNFCCC) and bilateral cooperation, such as the European Union. These funds are used to support both adaptation and mitigation efforts in the country.
Timor-Leste relies heavily on international cooperation to finance its climate agenda. Tunisia submitted its first NDC in 2015 and updated NDC in 2021. The updated NDC has an emissions reduction target of 45% by 2030 as compared to a 2010 baseline.
The updated NDC covers the energy, industrial processes and product use, agriculture, forestry and land use, waste, water, ecosystems, coastal zones, health, and tourism sectors.

The submission of the updated NDC, in accordance with the provisions of the Paris Agreement, represent a more ambitious mitigation and adaptation under Article 2 of the Paris Agreement. The updated NDC is also fully in line with Tunisia's economic and social development priorities, mainly through The alignment of the NDC with the UN Sustainable Development Goals(SDGs), A Significant co-benefits in terms of economic growth, job creation and poverty alleviation & A Gender integration Approach.

In order to strengthen resilience in all its different sectors, the adaptation component of the NDC is based on a framework shift and a cross-sectoral approach. Its Implementation is based on a prioritized action plan, with vertical actions that address specific sectoral issues and cross-cutting actions to 6 most vulnerable sectors: water resources, agriculture, ecosystems, the coastline, health and tourism, considering 3 new cross-cutting areas: Gender, Land Planning & Disaster Risk Reduction.

Estos acontecimientos afectan de manera significativa la estructura social, siendo las mujeres, niños, niñas y jóvenes los grupos más vulnerables ante fenómenos climáticos extremos, como las altas temperaturas y las intensas lluvias.
